articles.title: Securing an Angular Firebase AI App with Email/Password Authentication (Part 1: Emulator, AuthService, and Route Guard) [GDE]
articles.description: Anyone with the public URL can use my tokens to perform image analysis and text-to-speech, which can...
articles.body_html:
Anyone with the public URL can use my tokens to perform image analysis and text-to-speech, which can quickly drive up my billing costs. To prevent unauthorized usage, I want to convert /dashboard into a protected route by adding Email/Password authentication with Firebase Auth.

Firebase Auth supports many authentication providers out of the box, and I chose Email/Password because it is the simplest method to configure. In Part 1, we will configure the Firebase Auth Local Emulator, build a lazy-loaded AuthService and a functional route guard, and protect the /dashboard route using CanActivateFn.

Architecture & Mental Model

Part 1 focuses on running the Firebase Auth Emulator alongside the Angular dev server and configuring authentication state management.

The architecture uses Firebase's browser session persistence (browserSessionPersistence) to manage the user's authentication state, which provides two key benefits:

  • After a user authenticates successfully, Firebase persists the authentication state in sessionStorage. When the user refreshes the browser page, the browser retains their login state.
  • When the user closes the browser tab, the browser automatically clears the authentication state from sessionStorage. The next time the user visits the application, they must log in again.

Without session persistence, the application would require extra custom logic to check token expiration, explicitly purge the user state from storage, and trigger route redirection.

Similarly, because firebase/auth is a heavy third-party SDK, loading it eagerly would increase the initial bundle size. Instead, AuthService lazy-loads it via a dynamic import() to update the reactive isAuthenticated signal.

flowchart LR
    subgraph Dev["Local Development (npm run launch)"]
        NG["Angular Dev Server (:4200)"]
        EMU["Firebase Auth Emulator (:9099 & UI :4000)"]
    end

    subgraph AuthCore["AuthService (src/app/core/auth)"]
        ENSURE["ensureAuth() (Single-Flight Promise)"]
        SDK["Dynamic import('firebase/auth')"]
        STATE["onAuthStateChanged -> #user Signal"]
        COMP["isAuthenticated Computed Signal"]
        ENSURE --> SDK --> STATE --> COMP
    end

    subgraph Routing["Angular Router (app.routes.ts)"]
        GUARD["canActivateDashboard (CanActivateFn)"]
        HOME["/home (Sign-In Screen)"]
        DASH["/dashboard (Image Analysis & TTS)"]
    end

    NG --> ENSURE
    SDK -. "isLocalhost()" .-> EMU
    GUARD --> ENSURE
    COMP -- "true" --> DASH
    COMP -- "false (Redirect)" --> HOME

1. Configuring the Firebase Auth Emulator & Unified Launch Script

1.1 Enabling the Auth Emulator in firebase.json

The { "emulators": { "auth": ... } } block in firebase/firebase.json configures the Firebase Auth Emulator to run on host port 9099 (127.0.0.1:9099), while "ui": { "enabled": true } enables the Emulator UI on port 4000 (http://127.0.0.1:4000).

// firebase/firebase.json
{
  // ... rest of configuration omitted for brevity
  "emulators": {
    "auth": {
      "port": 9099
    },
    "ui": {
      "enabled": true
    }
  }
}

1.2 Installing concurrently as a Dev Dependency

This step is optional, but I prefer not to start the Firebase Auth Emulator and the Angular dev server in two separate steps—opening one terminal tab to run the emulator and a second terminal tab to run the Angular dev server. Installing concurrently allows us to run both processes with a single command so we can start development immediately.

npm install --save-dev concurrently

1.3 Adding Emulator and Launch Scripts in package.json

During local development, I connect the Angular application to the Firebase Authentication Emulator to seed a test user for login. AuthService connects to the emulator programmatically, and the new scripts in package.json launch it.

// package.json (scripts excerpt)
{
  "scripts": {
    "start": "ng serve",
    "firebase:emulate:auth": "firebase --config firebase/firebase.json emulators:start --only auth",
    "launch": "concurrently \"npm run firebase:emulate:auth\" \"npm run start\""
  }
}

Here is what each script does:

  • start: Starts the local Angular development server (ng serve) on http://localhost:4200.
  • firebase:emulate:auth: Reads the firebase/firebase.json configuration to start the Authentication Emulator only.
  • launch: Launches both the Angular client and the Firebase emulator concurrently, allowing me to prompt the Antigravity CLI to execute it in the background.

2. Creating a Test Account in the Firebase Emulator UI

Seeding a user is a manual process, so I open the Emulator UI at http://localhost:4000 to create a dummy user with the credentials aaa@example.com and 123456. Note that 123456 is a weak password created strictly to facilitate local authentication testing.


Caption: Creating a new test user with an email and password in the Firebase Emulator UI at http://localhost:4000.

Saving the form creates the user account. Because the users table displays the email address without the password, I recommend using a password that is easy to remember or saving it in a password manager.


Caption: The newly created email/password user account displayed in the Firebase Authentication Emulator.

3. Building a Lazy-Loaded, Signal-Driven AuthService

3.1 Defining the AuthCredentials Interface

The AuthCredentials interface defines the email and password properties for user login credentials.

// src/app/core/auth/auth-credentials.interface.ts
export interface AuthCredentials {
  email: string;
  password: string;
}

3.2 Implementing AuthService with Dynamic SDK Loading and Signals

First, AuthService injects WINDOW, ConfigService, and DestroyRef, and declares the #user signal, the isAuthenticated computed signal, and private fields to cache the Firebase Auth instance and SDK module:

// src/app/core/auth/auth.service.ts
import { WINDOW } from '@/core/constants/navigator.const';
import { ConfigService, isLocalhost } from '@/core/firebase';
import { computed, DestroyRef, inject, Service, signal } from '@angular/core';
import type { Auth, User } from 'firebase/auth';
import type { AuthCredentials } from './auth-credentials.interface';

const AUTH_EMULATOR_URL = 'http://127.0.0.1:9099';

@Service()
export class AuthService {
  readonly #window = inject(WINDOW);
  readonly #configService = inject(ConfigService);
  readonly #destroyRef$ = inject(DestroyRef);

  readonly #user = signal<User | null>(null);
  user = this.#user.asReadonly();
  isAuthenticated = computed(() => !!this.#user());

  #auth: Auth | null = null;
  #authSdk: typeof import('firebase/auth') | null = null;
  #authReady: Promise<void> | null = null;

Next, AuthService manages the Firebase Auth lifecycle through four core methods:

  1. loadAuth()
    • Dynamically imports firebase/auth for the first time and retrieves the current Firebase application instance.
    • Connects the Angular application to the Firebase Auth Emulator when running on localhost.
    • Sets authentication state persistence to browser session persistence (browserSessionPersistence), registers onAuthStateChanged to monitor authentication state changes, and awaits auth.authStateReady() for the initial auth state to resolve.
    • Stores the auth instance in #auth and the Auth SDK module in #authSdk. 
  private async loadAuth(): Promise<void> {
    const [firebaseApp, authSdk] = await Promise.all([this.#configService.getApp(), import('firebase/auth')]);

    const auth = authSdk.getAuth(firebaseApp);
    if (isLocalhost(this.#window)) {
      authSdk.connectAuthEmulator(auth, AUTH_EMULATOR_URL, { disableWarnings: true });
    }

    await authSdk.setPersistence(auth, authSdk.browserSessionPersistence);
    const unsubscribe = authSdk.onAuthStateChanged(auth, (user) => this.#user.set(user));

    this.#destroyRef$.onDestroy(unsubscribe);

    await auth.authStateReady();

    this.#auth = auth;
    this.#authSdk = authSdk;
  }
  1. ensureAuth()
    • Ensures loadAuth() resolves exactly once and returns both the auth instance and the #authSdk module. Keeping both in memory allows signIn() and signOut() to reuse them when logging a user in or out. 
  async ensureAuth(): Promise<{ auth: Auth; sdk: typeof import('firebase/auth') }> {
    if (!this.#authReady) {
      this.#authReady = this.loadAuth();
    }

    await this.#authReady;

    if (!this.#auth) {
      throw new Error('Auth is not initialized');
    }

    if (!this.#authSdk) {
      throw new Error('Auth SDK does not exist');
    }

    return { auth: this.#auth, sdk: this.#authSdk };
  }
  1. signIn()
    • Accepts the user's email and password, validates the arguments, and calls sdk.signInWithEmailAndPassword() to authenticate the user. When authentication succeeds, the authSdk.onAuthStateChanged(auth, (user) => this.#user.set(user)) listener observes the state change, updates the #user signal, and recalculates the isAuthenticated computed signal. 
  async signIn({ email, password }: AuthCredentials): Promise<void> {
    if (!email || !password) {
      this.#user.set(null);
      return;
    }

    const { auth, sdk } = await this.ensureAuth();
    await sdk.signInWithEmailAndPassword(auth, email, password);
  }
  1. signOut()
    • Calls sdk.signOut(auth) to sign out the currently logged-in user. Similarly, the onAuthStateChanged listener resets the #user signal to null and recalculates the isAuthenticated computed signal. 
  async signOut(): Promise<void> {
    const { auth, sdk } = await this.ensureAuth();
    await sdk.signOut(auth);
  }
}

4. Protecting the Dashboard Route with canActivateDashboard

4.1 Creating the CanActivateFn Route Guard

canActivateDashboard is a functional route guard of type CanActivateFn. It injects AuthService and Router to verify the user's authentication status and handle route redirection. Calling await authService.ensureAuth() initializes Firebase Auth (connecting to the Auth Emulator when running on localhost) and updates the isAuthenticated computed signal with the current authentication state. When the user is authenticated, the guard returns true to allow navigation to the route; otherwise, it redirects the user back to /home via router.createUrlTree([APP_LINKS.HOME]).

// src/app/core/auth/auth.guard.ts
import { AuthService } from './auth.service';
import { APP_LINKS } from '@/core/constants/routes.const';
import { inject } from '@angular/core';
import type { CanActivateFn } from '@angular/router';
import { Router } from '@angular/router';

export const canActivateDashboard: CanActivateFn = async () => {
  const authService = inject(AuthService);
  const router = inject(Router);

  await authService.ensureAuth();

  if (authService.isAuthenticated()) {
    return true;
  }

  return router.createUrlTree([APP_LINKS.HOME]);
};

Finally, we re-export the AuthCredentials interface, the canActivateDashboard route guard, and AuthService from a single barrel file (src/app/core/auth/index.ts). This gives the /dashboard route configuration—and the Sign-In component we will build in Part 2—a clean, unified import path.

// src/app/core/auth/index.ts
export * from './auth-credentials.interface';
export * from './auth.guard';
export * from './auth.service';

4.2 Wiring canActivateDashboard in app.routes.ts

The canActivate property of the dashboard route accepts the canActivateDashboard function in an array. When a user types /dashboard in the address bar or navigates to the path programmatically, the router executes this route guard function. Authenticated users proceed to the dashboard, while the guard blocks unauthenticated visitors and redirects them back to /home.

// src/app/core/constants/routes.const.ts
export const ROUTE_PATHS = {
  HOME: 'home',
  DASHBOARD: 'dashboard',
} as const;

// src/app/app.routes.ts (dashboard route excerpt)
  {
    path: ROUTE_PATHS.DASHBOARD,
    title: 'Firebase TTS',
    providers: [provideEnvironmentInitializer(() => inject(ConfigService).initialize())],
    loadComponent: () => import('./features/dashboard/dashboard.component'),
    canActivate: [canActivateDashboard],
  },

Takeaways & What's Next

In Part 1, we configured Firebase Auth to protect our image analysis and TTS endpoints:

  • Local Auth Emulator: Configured the Auth Emulator in firebase.json and used concurrently to start the emulator and Angular app together.
  • Lazy-Loaded AuthService: Dynamically imported firebase/auth once and used signals (#user and isAuthenticated) to track the login state.
  • Route Guard: Added canActivateDashboard to app.routes.ts to redirect unauthenticated users back to the home screen.

In Part 2, we will build the interactive sign-in experience on the frontend. We will use Angular 22's Signal Forms to create the form where users input their email and password, use Angular CDK Dialog to open the sign-in modal when a user clicks the Sign In button on the home screen, and connect the Sign-In component with AuthService to call the signIn() method.

Resources

  • Firebase Password Authentication
  • Firebase Auth State Persistence
  • Angular CanActivateFn

articles.title: Next.js Doesn't Render Pages Anymore. It Streams Something Stranger.
articles.description: A deep visual guide to how Next.js and React Server Components really work under the hood. Why Client Components run on the server, what the RSC Payload is, and how hydration connects them.
articles.body_html:
If you ask ten developers what the "use client" directive does in Next.js, at least eight of them will give you the same intuitive answer:

"Server Components run on the server. Client Components run in the browser. So 'use client' tells Next.js to run the component on the client."

It sounds completely logical. The directive is literally named use client. The mental model seems clean: two environments, two directives, a neat split between backend and frontend.

Except that is not how Next.js works at all.

If Client Components only ran in the browser, why does this code crash your server with ReferenceError: window is not defined?

"use client";

export default function UserProfile() {
  // 💥 Crashes during build or initial page load on the server!
  const screenWidth = window.innerWidth;

  return <div>Screen width: {screenWidth}px</div>;
}

If it were truly client-side only, window would be defined, the browser would evaluate it, and there would be no error on the server.

The truth is surprising to many developers: Client Components in Next.js also execute on the server.

The "use client" directive does not define where a component executes. It defines a module boundary that dictates what code gets packaged into your browser bundle.

To write fast, bug-free Next.js applications, you have to dismantle the "server vs. client execution" myth and understand what the rendering engine is actually doing behind the scenes.

The Core Misconception: Execution vs. Bundling

In the App Router, every file is a Server Component by default.

When you prepend "use client" to the top of a file, you are not saying "never run this on Node.js."

You are telling the bundler:

"Everything exported from this file, and anything it imports, needs to be compiled into a JavaScript bundle and sent across the network to the browser. Also, allow this sub-tree to use React hooks (useState, useEffect) and browser event listeners (onClick)."

When a user visits a route for the first time, Next.js performs Server-Side Pre-rendering (SSR) for your entire page—including your Client Components.

Here is what happens during that initial request:

  1. Server Components execute on the server. They can access databases, read files, read secret environment variables, and compute data. They output a stream of structured UI instructions called the RSC Payload.
  2. Client Components ALSO execute on the server. Next.js executes their render function once on the server to generate semantic HTML tags (<div class="profile">...</div>).
  3. The browser receives raw HTML immediately. The user sees the fully formed page almost instantly (First Contentful Paint).
  4. The JavaScript bundle downloads in the background. React runs in the browser, matches the JavaScript event listeners to the existing DOM nodes, and brings the page to life. This second step is called Hydration. 
                ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
                │             INITIAL HTTP REQUEST              │
                └──────────────────────┬────────────────────────┘
                                       │
                         Next.js Server Execution
                                       │
        ┌──────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────┐
        ▼                                                             ▼
┌───────────────────────────────┐             ┌───────────────────────────────┐
│       Server Component        │             │       Client Component        │
├───────────────────────────────┤             ├───────────────────────────────┤
│ • Runs ON SERVER ONLY         │             │ • Runs ON SERVER (Initial SSR)│
│ • Zero JS sent to browser     │             │ • Bundled into client JS      │
│ • Direct DB / Secrets access  │             │ • Re-runs in browser          │
│ • Emits: RSC Payload          │             │ • Emits: HTML + JS Bundle     │
└───────────────┬───────────────┘             └───────────────┬───────────────┘
                │                                             │
                └──────────────────────┬──────────────────────┘
                                       │
                        Combined Server Response
                                       │
              ┌────────────────────────┴────────────────────────┐
              ▼                                                 ▼
    Raw Pre-rendered HTML                          RSC Payload Stream
  (Instant paint on screen)                    (Virtual DOM data instructions)
              │                                                 │
              └────────────────────────┬────────────────────────┘
                                       │
                              Browser Environment
                                       │
                        ┌──────────────┴──────────────┐
                        ▼                             ▼
                 Fast First Paint              React Hydration
              (Non-interactive HTML)         (Attaches events & hooks)

Once you see this diagram, the window is not defined error makes immediate sense. When Next.js pre-rendered your Client Component on the server to generate that initial HTML, Node.js evaluated window.innerWidth. Because Node.js has no browser window, it blew up before the HTML ever left the server.

What Actually Is the RSC Payload?

Most developers know what HTML is, and they know what JavaScript is. But Next.js introduces a third artifact that is the true backbone of the App Router: the React Server Component (RSC) Payload.

When the server evaluates your Server Components, it does not produce HTML directly. Instead, it generates a compact, streaming binary/JSON format representing the virtual tree.

Here is a conceptual look at what an RSC Payload stream contains:

  1. Rendered HTML-like UI descriptions of all Server Components (tags, attributes, text).
  2. Placeholders ("holes") where Client Components should go.
  3. References to JavaScript chunk URLs that the browser needs to load to fill those client holes.
  4. Serialized props passed from Server Components into Client Components.

Let's look at a concrete example. Suppose you have this page:

// app/dashboard/page.tsx (Server Component by default)
import Counter from './Counter';

export default async function DashboardPage() {
  const user = await db.user.findUnique({ where: { id: 1 } });

  return (
    <main>
      <h1>Welcome back, {user.name}</h1>
      <Counter initialCount={user.savedItemsCount} />
    </main>
  );
}

And your counter component:

// app/dashboard/Counter.tsx
"use client";

import { useState } from 'react';

export default function Counter({ initialCount }: { initialCount: number }) {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(initialCount);

  return (
    <button onClick={() => setCount(c => c + 1)}>
      Saved Items: {count}
    </button>
  );
}

When Next.js renders DashboardPage, it executes the database query on the server. The code for db.user.findUnique never leaves the server. The database driver is not in your browser bundle.

Next.js then serializes the result into an RSC stream that looks conceptually like this:

[
  "$", "main", null, {
    "children": [
      ["$", "h1", null, { "children": "Welcome back, Sarah" }],
      ["$", "$L1", null, { "initialCount": 5 }]
    ]
  }
]

Notice ["$", "$L1", null, { "initialCount": 5 }].

$L1 is a reference placeholder. Elsewhere in the stream, Next.js specifies:

1:I["./app/dashboard/Counter.tsx", ["chunks/counter.js"], "default"]

The server says: "At this spot in the tree, place the component exported from Counter.tsx. You will find its code in chunks/counter.js. And give it the prop initialCount: 5."

Why does Next.js stream this payload instead of just sending plain HTML?

Because when a user navigates between pages on the client (client-side routing), Next.js does not re-download a full HTML page. It requests only the new route's RSC Payload!

React merges the new RSC Payload directly into the existing browser DOM. Any client-side state in parent components (like an active dropdown, playing audio, or scroll position) stays preserved, while the server components update seamlessly.

The Boundary Rule: What Can Cross the Line?

Because Server Components run in an isolated server context and Client Components run across both environments, the border between them has strict physics.

1. Props Must Be Serializable

When a Server Component passes props to a Client Component, those props must travel across the network inside the RSC Payload.

That means props must be serializable to JSON (with React-extended support for Promises, BigInt, Date, and Set/Map):

// ❌ FAILS: Functions cannot be serialized across the network
<ClientButton onClick={() => console.log("clicked")} />

// ❌ FAILS: Classes with methods lose their prototype
<ClientUserCard user={new UserModel("Sarah")} />

// ✅ WORKS: Plain objects, strings, numbers, booleans, arrays
<ClientUserCard user={{ name: "Sarah", role: "admin" }} />

// ✅ WORKS: Server Actions (marked with "use server")
<ClientButton action={deleteAccountAction} />

If you try to pass an inline callback function from a Server Component to a Client Component, Next.js throws an error: Functions cannot be passed directly to Client Components unless you explicitly expose it with "use server".

2. The Import Flow Is One-Way Only

You can import a Client Component into a Server Component. But you cannot import a Server Component directly into a Client Component.

"use client";

// ❌ This does NOT work as a Server Component anymore!
import ServerSecretWidget from './ServerSecretWidget';

export default function ClientModal() {
  return (
    <div>
      <ServerSecretWidget />
    </div>
  );
}

Why? Because the moment you import a file into a file marked "use client", the bundler treats that imported file as part of the client bundle too!

If ServerSecretWidget used private database credentials, the bundler would either throw a compilation error or, worse, attempt to bundle backend modules into the browser.

The Slot Pattern: Putting Server Components Inside Client Components

If Client Components cannot import Server Components, how do you put a data-fetching Server Component inside a Client Component (like an interactive animated modal or collapsible sidebar)?

This is where the Composition Pattern (or Slot Pattern) comes in, and it is one of the most elegant architectural patterns in React.

Instead of importing the Server Component into the Client Component, you pass it as a children prop:

// components/CollapsibleSection.tsx
"use client";

import { useState, ReactNode } from 'react';

export default function CollapsibleSection({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
  const [isOpen, setIsOpen] = useState(true);

  return (
    <section>
      <button onClick={() => setIsOpen(prev => !prev)}>
        {isOpen ? "Collapse" : "Expand"}
      </button>
      {isOpen && <div>{children}</div>}
    </section>
  );
}

Now, in your Server Component:

// app/page.tsx (Server Component)
import CollapsibleSection from '@/components/CollapsibleSection';
import HeavyDatabaseList from '@/components/HeavyDatabaseList';

export default async function Page() {
  return (
    <main>
      <h1>Project Feed</h1>
      {/* HeavyDatabaseList stays a Server Component! */}
      <CollapsibleSection>
        <HeavyDatabaseList />
      </CollapsibleSection>
    </main>
  );
}

How does this work?

HeavyDatabaseList is evaluated on the server by Page.tsx. Its output is converted into the RSC Payload.

CollapsibleSection receives the already-resolved React elements as children. The code for HeavyDatabaseList never touches the browser bundle.

CollapsibleSection handles the interactive toggle in the browser without ever knowing or caring what rendered inside its slot.

Three Costly Mistakes Developers Make (And How to Fix Them)

Understanding the rendering pipeline protects you from the three most common performance killers and bugs in Next.js:

Mistake 1: Placing "use client" at the Root of a Feature

When developers need a single useState or onClick handler, they often slap "use client" at the very top of the page or layout.

// ❌ Anti-pattern: The entire subtree becomes client-side bundled
"use client";

import { useState } from 'react';
import HeavyChart from './HeavyChart'; // 120 kB bundled!
import LargeDataList from './LargeDataList'; // 85 kB bundled!

export default function AnalyticsDashboard() {
  const [filter, setFilter] = useState("all");

  return (
    <div>
      <FilterDropdown value={filter} onChange={setFilter} />
      <HeavyChart filter={filter} />
      <LargeDataList filter={filter} />
    </div>
  );
}

The Fix: Push the client boundary down to the leaves.

Keep the container as a Server Component. Extract only the interactive input into a small Client Component:

// ✅ Better: Only the interactive trigger is a client component
// app/dashboard/FilterDropdown.tsx
"use client";

export function FilterDropdown({ current, onSelect }) { ... }

Keep heavy static presentation or data-fetching logic in Server Components to keep the JavaScript bundle lean.

Mistake 2: Accessing Browser APIs Outside of useEffect

Because Client Components render on the server during the initial request, accessing window, document, or localStorage during the render phase causes runtime server crashes:

"use client";

export default function ThemeWidget() {
  // 💥 Error: window is not defined during SSR
  const theme = localStorage.getItem("theme") ?? "light";

  return <div>Current theme: {theme}</div>;
}

The Fix:

Move browser API access into useEffect (which only executes in the browser after mount), or wrap it with a mount guard:

"use client";

import { useState, useEffect } from 'react';

export default function ThemeWidget() {
  const [theme, setTheme] = useState<string>("light");

  useEffect(() => {
    // ✅ Safe: useEffect runs ONLY in the browser after hydration
    const saved = localStorage.getItem("theme");
    if (saved) setTheme(saved);
  }, []);

  return <div>Current theme: {theme}</div>;
}

Mistake 3: Hydration Mismatches from Non-Deterministic Values

If the HTML produced on the server differs from what the client produces during its first hydration pass, React emits a noisy console warning:

Text content does not match server-rendered HTML.

Common triggers:

"use client";

export default function Timestamp() {
  // ⚠️ Server renders at 12:00:00.000, browser hydrates at 12:00:00.120!
  return <span>Current time: {new Date().toLocaleTimeString()}</span>;
}

When React hydrates, it expects the server HTML and the initial client render tree to match character-for-character. If they disagree, React has to throw away the server HTML and rebuild the DOM tree from scratch, degrading performance.

For values that depend on the client's local time or random numbers, defer the dynamic rendering until after mounting, or use suppressHydrationWarning on individual tags where mismatches are intentional.

Quick Reference: Server vs. Client Components

Capability Server Component (Default) Client Component ("use client")
Initial Execution Server only Server (SSR) and Browser
Shipped to Client Bundle 0 kB JavaScript Full component code + imports
React Hooks (useState, useEffect) ❌ No ✅ Yes
Browser APIs (window, navigator) ❌ No ✅ Inside useEffect or events
Direct DB & Secret Key Access ✅ Yes ❌ No
Render Output RSC Payload (virtual stream) HTML string (SSR) + Client DOM
Primary Purpose Data fetching, security, zero bundle User interactivity, state, event handlers

The Mental Shift

Next.js does not split your application into two separate worlds. It weaves them together into a single continuous pipeline.

The next time you type "use client", remember:

You are not telling Next.js where to execute the code. You are drawing a line for the compiler, telling it where interactive JavaScript needs to begin, and allowing the server to hand off the user interface smoothly to the client.

Once you treat "use client" as a boundary rather than a location, the App Router transforms from a confusing maze of hydration errors into one of the most capable full-stack architectures in modern web development.

When you first started working with the Next.js App Router, what was the mental model hurdle that tripped you up the most? And what is your favorite pattern for keeping client bundles minimal?

References:

  • Next.js Official Documentation: Server Components
  • Next.js Official Documentation: Client Components
  • React Working Group: React Server Components Architecture
  • Dan Abramov: The Two Reacts

articles.title: Claude Code Custom System Prompts in 2026: Overriding Defaults, Appending Instructions, and What You Cannot Change

articles.body_html:
Claude Code Custom System Prompts in 2026: Overriding Defaults, Appending Instructions, and What You Cannot Change

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

Developers add custom instructions to Claude Code, restart the session, and watch Claude ignore them. The instructions sit in a CLAUDE.md file, or a settings.json key, or an --append-system-prompt flag, but Claude still responds with the default behavior. This confusion stems from a misunderstanding of where each layer applies and what the system prompt actually controls.

Claude Code provides three distinct mechanisms for shaping behavior: replacing or appending to the system prompt with CLI flags, defining persistent project context in CLAUDE.md files, and configuring output styles that transform how Claude formats responses. Each mechanism operates at a different layer of the request cycle, and mixing them without understanding their boundaries produces configuration that appears broken but is working exactly as designed.

The system prompt itself is not a single editable file. Claude Code builds it from multiple sources at request time, and certain parts remain locked regardless of configuration. Understanding which parts you can change, which require a different mechanism, and which remain fixed is the difference between instructions that work and instructions that vanish.

This post examines the three ways to customize Claude Code behavior, explains what each mechanism controls, and clarifies which built-in behaviors cannot be changed no matter which layer you modify.

Key Takeaways

  • Claude Code builds the system prompt from multiple sources; replacing or appending text with CLI flags changes the core identity and tool guidance, while CLAUDE.md injects project context into the conversation separately.
  • The --system-prompt flag replaces the entire default prompt including tool descriptions and safety instructions, while --append-system-prompt preserves the default and adds extra rules on top.
  • CLAUDE.md files do not modify the system prompt; they inject content into the conversation as project context that Claude reads alongside the system prompt.
  • Output styles, skills, and permission rules shape behavior through separate mechanisms that remain active regardless of system prompt customization.
  • Built-in safety instructions, tool definitions, and API-level constraints cannot be overridden through any system prompt flag or configuration file.

Understanding System Prompt Presets: claude_code vs Custom Strings

Claude Code does not expose the full default system prompt as an editable file. The official documentation confirms this: "Claude Code's system prompt isn't published. To give Claude standing instructions, use CLAUDE.md files or the --append-system-prompt flag." Developers who expect a single text file controlling Claude's identity will not find one, because the prompt assembles from multiple internal sources at runtime.

The default prompt includes the following components:

  • Core identity and role definition
  • Tool descriptions and usage guidance for each available capability
  • Safety and security instructions
  • Coding conventions and best practices
  • Output formatting rules

When developers pass --system-prompt or --system-prompt-file, they replace all of these components with their own text. Claude Code discards the default identity, tool guidance, and safety instructions, leaving the developer responsible for defining everything from scratch.

This replacement makes sense for non-coding agents where Claude Code's default identity does not fit the task, but it creates problems when developers simply want to add domain-specific rules without rebuilding the entire prompt. For that use case, --append-system-prompt preserves the default and adds extra instructions after it.

The choice between replacement and append determines whether developers inherit Claude Code's built-in tool guidance. A replaced prompt loses descriptions of how the Bash tool works, when to use Read versus Write, and which permission checks apply before tool execution. An appended prompt keeps those descriptions and layers new instructions on top.

Appending Instructions: Extending the Default Without Starting From Scratch

The --append-system-prompt and --append-system-prompt-file flags let developers extend the default prompt without replacing it. This preserves Claude Code's identity as a coding assistant while adding project-specific conventions, output requirements, or domain context.

A typical use case: enforcing a consistent code review format. Developers want Claude to check for specific patterns in every review without changing how Claude uses tools or responds to questions. Appending instructions achieves this:

// Start Claude Code with custom review rules appended
// Shell command:
// claude --append-system-prompt-file ./review-rules.txt

// Contents of review-rules.txt:
When reviewing code, always check for:
1. Missing error handling in async functions
2. Hardcoded configuration values that should be environment variables
3. Console.log statements that should be removed before production
4. Tests that need updating after implementation changes

Format your review as:
- Summary (2-3 sentences)
- Findings (bulleted list with file:line references)
- Risk level (low/medium/high)

Claude receives the default system prompt followed by a blank line and then the appended text. The blank line separates the default instructions from the custom rules, making the boundary clear when debugging what Claude sees.

Developers can combine both inline text and file contents by passing both --append-system-prompt and --append-system-prompt-file in the same command (requires Claude Code v2.1.283 or later). The file contents appear first, followed by a blank line, then the inline text:

// Combine file and inline instructions
// Shell command:
// claude --append-system-prompt-file ./style.md --append-system-prompt "Always reply in French"

// Claude receives:
// 1. Default system prompt
// 2. Blank line
// 3. Contents of style.md
// 4. Blank line
// 5. "Always reply in French"

This ordering ensures that persistent style rules from the file remain stable across runs while allowing per-invocation overrides through the inline flag.

Claude Code system prompt layers

The appended text applies to a single session. Starting a new session without the flags returns to the default prompt. Developers who need persistent instructions that apply across all sessions should use CLAUDE.md files instead, which inject content at a different layer.

CLAUDE.md vs System Prompts: What Actually Goes Where

CLAUDE.md files do not modify the system prompt. This distinction trips up developers who expect CLAUDE.md to work like a persistent --append-system-prompt, but CLAUDE.md operates through a separate mechanism that injects content into the conversation as project context.

The Agent SDK documentation states: "CLAUDE.md takes a different path: the SDK reads it and injects its content into the conversation as project context, so it shapes behavior alongside whichever system prompt you choose." This injection happens after the system prompt is built, meaning CLAUDE.md cannot override tool guidance or safety instructions that live in the system prompt layer.

Aspect System Prompt Flags CLAUDE.md Files
Scope Single session Persistent across sessions
Timing Applied at prompt assembly Injected into conversation
Can override tool guidance Yes (with --system-prompt) No
Can define project conventions Yes (with --append) Yes
Requires restart after edit No (takes effect immediately) No (watched for changes)
Location CLI flag Project .claude/ directory

CLAUDE.md excels at defining what the project is, what conventions it follows, and what context Claude needs to understand it. System prompt flags excel at defining who Claude is and how Claude should respond. When developers put project conventions in the system prompt or try to redefine Claude's identity in CLAUDE.md, the configuration fights against the mechanism's design.

A well-structured setup uses CLAUDE.md for project facts:

// .claude/CLAUDE.md contents:
# Project: TypeScript API Server

This project uses:
- Express 4.18 with TypeScript 5.3
- Jest for testing with 80%+ coverage requirement
- Zod for runtime validation
- Prisma 5.x for database access

Conventions:
- All API routes live in src/routes/
- Database models use singular names (User, not Users)
- Environment variables are required at startup (fail fast)
- Error responses follow RFC 7807 Problem Details format

And system prompt flags for response requirements:

// Pass this flag when starting Claude Code:
// --append-system-prompt "When suggesting code changes, always include the full file path and a brief explanation of why the change is needed"

This separation lets developers change project facts without touching how Claude formats responses, and change response formatting without modifying project documentation.

What You Cannot Override: Built-In Safety, Tool Definitions, and Hard Limits

Certain parts of Claude Code behavior remain fixed regardless of system prompt configuration. These restrictions protect against unsafe operations, ensure consistent tool behavior, and enforce API-level constraints that no client-side configuration can bypass.

Three categories of behavior cannot be overridden:

Safety and security instructions. Claude Code includes built-in rules that prevent certain operations even when the system prompt requests them. These rules operate at a layer below the system prompt, meaning a custom --system-prompt text cannot remove them. Examples include refusal to generate malware, restrictions on processing sensitive data without explicit permission, and guardrails against executing commands that could compromise the system.

Tool definitions and behavior. The tools Claude Code exposes (Bash, Read, Write, Edit, and others) have fixed definitions that describe their parameters, when to use them, and what they return. A custom system prompt can provide additional guidance on tool usage, but it cannot change the tool's signature or disable built-in tool restrictions. For instance, developers cannot use --system-prompt to make the Read tool bypass permission checks or force the Bash tool to run commands without approval when project settings require it.

API and model constraints. Token limits, rate limits, and model capabilities are set by the Anthropic API and cannot be increased through configuration. A system prompt that requests "unlimited context window" has no effect because the constraint exists at the API layer, not in Claude Code's client logic.

Developers who attempt to override these restrictions through creative prompt engineering will find that Claude Code silently ignores the instructions or Claude refuses the request. The official documentation warns: "Replacing drops all of the default prompt, including tool guidance and safety instructions, so you take responsibility for whatever your task still needs." This warning applies to guidance developers can provide, not to safety checks they cannot remove.

The distinction matters when debugging why certain instructions fail. If a custom system prompt asks Claude to "always read .env files without asking," the request fails not because the prompt is malformed but because permission checks happen after the prompt is processed. The solution is not better prompt engineering but configuring permissions through the separate permissions mechanism.

Real-World Patterns: Output Styles, Skills, and Hooks That Shape Behavior Outside the System Prompt

Claude Code provides three additional mechanisms for shaping behavior that operate independently of the system prompt: output styles, skills, and hooks. Each mechanism targets a different aspect of Claude's responses, and understanding when to use each prevents configuration conflicts.

Output styles transform how Claude formats responses without changing the underlying reasoning or tool usage. An output style might enforce markdown structure, add specific headers to code blocks, or require responses to follow a template. Output styles apply after Claude generates a response, meaning they cannot change which tools Claude chooses or what logic Claude follows. The official documentation states: "an output style changes the instructions Claude Code gives Claude for every response."

Skills add specific capabilities that Claude loads on demand. A skill defines when to run (through YAML frontmatter), what dynamic context to inject (through command substitution), and what instructions to follow when active. Skills operate through the conversation context layer, not the system prompt layer, which means they remain available even when developers replace the system prompt entirely.

Hooks execute code at specific points in the request lifecycle: before a request is sent, after Claude responds, or when specific events occur. Hooks can modify the request, transform the response, or trigger external actions. They run in the Claude Code runtime, not as instructions to Claude, which gives them capabilities that system prompts cannot replicate.

A practical example demonstrates the difference. Developers building a documentation generator want Claude to:

  1. Read TypeScript source files
  2. Extract JSDoc comments and type definitions
  3. Format the output as markdown with specific section headers
  4. Inject the result into a template
  5. Write the final documentation to a file

This workflow spans multiple mechanisms:

// 1. CLAUDE.md defines project conventions
// .claude/CLAUDE.md:
# Documentation Standards
All exported functions must have JSDoc comments with @param and @returns tags.
Type definitions use TypeScript 5.3 syntax.

// 2. Skill provides dynamic context
// .claude/skills/doc-gen/SKILL.md:
---
description: Generate documentation from TypeScript source files
---
## Current files
!`find src -name "*.ts" -not -path "*/test/*"`

## Instructions
Extract JSDoc comments and type definitions from the files above.

// 3. Output style enforces format
// .claude/output-styles/docs/style.md:
Format documentation as:
## Function Name
Description from JSDoc

**Parameters:**
- param: type - description

**Returns:** return type - description

// 4. Hook writes to file
// .claude/hooks/after-response.ts:
export default async function(response, context) {
  if (context.skill === 'doc-gen') {
    await writeFile('./docs/api.md', response.text);
  }
}

Attempting to implement this workflow through a single --system-prompt flag would fail because the system prompt cannot read files dynamically (skill functionality), format output conditionally (output style functionality), or write files after Claude responds (hook functionality). Each mechanism exists because it solves a problem the system prompt cannot address alone.

Claude Code configuration mechanisms

The documentation's guidance remains relevant: "For persistent personas you can switch between and share across a project, use output styles. For project conventions Claude should always follow, use CLAUDE.md." System prompt flags are for identity and per-invocation instructions, not for persistent behavior that should survive across sessions.

Common Mistakes: Why Your System Prompt Feels Ignored

Developers report that Claude ignores custom system prompts, but the problem usually sits in one of three areas: recording behavior, layer mismatches, or permission conflicts. Understanding these failure modes prevents hours of debugging configuration that is working correctly but not in the way developers expect.

Recording behavior in resumed conversations. By default, Claude Code builds the system prompt once on the first request of a conversation and records it. Later requests in the same conversation reuse that recorded prompt, even if developers pass different --system-prompt flags when resuming with --continue. The official documentation explains: "Until the conversation is compacted, every later request uses that recorded prompt, including after you return to the conversation with --resume or --continue."

This design optimizes for consistent behavior across a multi-turn conversation, but it surprises developers who expect system prompt changes to apply immediately. The solution is passing --system-prompt-snapshot off, which rebuilds the prompt on every request. This flag is essential during development when iterating on prompt wording:

// Iterate on system prompt wording without starting new sessions
// Shell command:
// claude --append-system-prompt "Draft rules v3" --system-prompt-snapshot off --continue

// Each run rebuilds the prompt with the new text
// Perfect for testing different phrasings

Layer mismatches. Developers put instructions in CLAUDE.md expecting them to override tool behavior, or they put project facts in --system-prompt expecting persistence across sessions. Both configurations fail because the instructions sit in the wrong layer. CLAUDE.md cannot override tool guidance that lives in the system prompt, and system prompt flags do not persist across sessions without being passed on every launch.

The fix is moving instructions to the correct layer: tool behavior overrides go in --system-prompt (which replaces the default including tool guidance), project conventions go in CLAUDE.md, and per-session response formatting goes in --append-system-prompt or output styles.

Permission conflicts. A system prompt can request specific tool behavior, but permission checks run separately and take precedence. If a system prompt says "always read package.json without asking" but project permissions require approval for Read operations, the permission check blocks the read regardless of what the system prompt requests. The official documentation confirms: "an allowed-tools grant goes through the normal permission flow."

Developers who encounter this conflict must configure permissions through the separate permissions mechanism (allow/ask/deny rules in settings.json or through permission prompts) rather than attempting to bypass permissions through prompt engineering. The permissions documentation describes the full syntax, and our production guide covers common permission patterns.

A fourth category of confusion stems from character restrictions in skill names and frontmatter. If a skill appears to load but its command does not work, the official documentation lists characters that Claude Code refuses: "Claude Code refuses a command name or a frontmatter name that contains characters such as: zero-width space or control character, private-use or unassigned character, character that changes text direction, blank other than one plain space, < or >." Renaming the skill folder or editing the name field in frontmatter resolves the issue, and the debug log (claude --debug) shows which names were refused.

Frequently Asked Questions

How do I make my custom system prompt persist across all sessions?

You cannot make a --system-prompt or --append-system-prompt flag persist automatically. These flags apply to the session you start them with. For instructions that should apply to all sessions in a project, put them in a CLAUDE.md file in the project's .claude/ directory. For cross-project conventions, create a script or alias that starts Claude Code with your preferred flags.

Why does Claude ignore my CLAUDE.md file?

CLAUDE.md does not modify the system prompt and cannot override built-in tool behavior or safety instructions. It injects content into the conversation as project context, which means it works best for defining what the project is and what conventions it follows, not for changing how Claude uses tools or formats responses. If your CLAUDE.md contains instructions about tool usage or response formatting, move them to an --append-system-prompt flag or an output style.

Can I disable Claude Code's safety instructions through a custom system prompt?

No. Safety and security checks operate at a layer below the system prompt. Even when you replace the entire default prompt with --system-prompt, the API-level safety checks remain active. This restriction exists to prevent accidental or intentional misuse and cannot be bypassed through any client-side configuration.

What happens when I pass both --system-prompt and --append-system-prompt?

Claude Code uses both. The --system-prompt flag replaces the default prompt, and then --append-system-prompt adds your extra text after that replacement. This combination is useful when you need a non-coding identity (through replacement) but still want to add per-invocation instructions (through append). With Claude Code v2.1.283 or later, you can also combine the inline and file forms of the same flag.

How do I debug which system prompt Claude is actually receiving?

Claude Code does not publish the full system prompt text, but you can confirm which sources loaded by running /status inside a session and checking the "Setting sources" line. For more details, run claude --debug from your shell and search the debug log for prompt-related entries. The log shows which settings files loaded and which system prompt flags applied, though it does not dump the full prompt text.

Conclusion: Choosing the Right Layer for Your Custom Instructions

System prompt customization in Claude Code requires understanding three distinct layers: the prompt itself (controlled through CLI flags), project context (injected through CLAUDE.md), and behavior modifications (implemented through output styles, skills, and hooks). Developers who put every instruction in the system prompt discover that some work, some vanish, and some conflict with other mechanisms. The configuration is not broken but is fighting against the layer where each mechanism operates.

Replace the system prompt when the default identity does not fit the task. Append to it when you need per-invocation instructions that preserve tool guidance. Use CLAUDE.md for project facts that should persist across sessions. Configure output styles for response formatting, skills for on-demand capabilities, and hooks for request lifecycle modifications. The official documentation at code.claude.com/docs covers each mechanism in detail, and the memory strategies guide explores how these layers interact with Claude's context handling.

articles.body_html:
Hey folks, it's me again! :)

Today, I would like to share with you how you can use Lighthouse CI to audit various software qualities of your project in Continous Integration but also how you can set up a Web Performance Budget strategy to not ship unintentional regressions.

I used this techique in various kinds of projects and I really liked the outcome of it.

Enjoy!

Problem

In Software Development, we always aimed to develop and ship fast. Nowadays with the growing popularity of AI agents that help us ship code even faster, being able to set certain quality guardrails (i.e. in Continous Integration/Continous Deployment) is essential to maintain software quality.

This is especially visible in the area of Web Performance where we can very easily ship performance regressions by adding a third party script, an unoptimized image or multiple custom fonts.

To maintain good performance and exceptional user experience, we need to find a way to warn us early about unexpected regressions. This is where Lighthouse CI can help us.

Solution

Lighthouse CI is a tool that can be used both in local development as well (and primarily) in the CI GitHub Action. The idea is simple:

  1. Define a configuration file
  2. Add a GitHub action/step
  3. See results and react to them before they reach production

The basic example could just be like following:

name: CI
on: [push]
jobs:
  lighthouseci:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 22
      - run: npm install && npm install -g @lhci/cli@0.15.x
      - run: npm run build
      - run: lhci autorun

But this will run the test in a basic setup - in our case we want to add some more configuration that will allow us to define our custom budget, and update it on the go to more restrict setup after time.

ci:
  collect:
    numberOfRuns: 5
    startServerCommand: rails server -e production
    url:
      - http://localhost:3000/
      - http://localhost:3000/pricing
      - http://localhost:3000/support
  assert:
    preset: lighthouse:recommended
    assertions:
      first-contentful-paint:
        - error
        - maxNumericValue: 2000
          aggregationMethod: optimistic
      largest-contentful-paint:
        - error
        - maxNumericValue: 2500
          aggregationMethod: optimistic
      cumulative-layout-shift:
        - error
        - maxNumericValue: 100
          aggregationMethod: optimistic
  upload:
    target: lhci
    serverBaseUrl: https://lhci.example.com

This configuration can either be in the yaml,js,json or any other supported format. What is important is that with it, you can be warned early about unexpected regressions and update the budget later to match your needs and goals better.

And if you would like to compare one LHCI result to the previous one to show instant improvements/regressions, here is a great example for that https://github.com/adevinta/actions-lighthouseci-compare

articles.title: I deleted 2,000 lines of code and shipped zero new features. It was the best thing I did all year.
articles.description: The biggest pull request I opened all year was two thousand lines long. And every single one of them...
articles.body_html:
The biggest pull request I opened all year was two thousand lines long. And every single one of them was red.

No new feature. No new endpoint. Nothing a user would ever see. Just a minus sign in front of two thousand lines of code that already existed, that were running in production right now, that I was asking to simply delete.

I sat with my finger over the button for a long time before I opened it. Deleting code you didn't write, in a path you're not sure you fully understand, feels exactly like defusing something. Every line I was cutting was a line someone had added on purpose, once, for a reason — and if I was wrong about even one of them, I wasn't shipping a feature that didn't work. I was pulling out a guardrail that something real was leaning on.

I shipped it anyway. It was the most important thing I did all year, and it's not close. And the reason why is the exact opposite of how I'd spent the previous two years measuring my own work.

The pile

The two thousand lines weren't one person's mistake. They were sediment.

There was a write path in our app — the part that saves a user's work — that had been quietly flaky for as long as anyone could remember. Not broken. Flaky. Every few weeks someone would report that something they'd saved wasn't there, nobody could reproduce it, and the ticket would go cold.

And every time it flared, somebody did the reasonable thing. They added a retry. Then a second retry with a backoff. Then a cache, so the UI could still show the work even when the read came back empty. Then a try/catch that swallowed the error "so it wouldn't crash the page." Then a background job that reconciled the cache against the database every few minutes to paper over the gap. Each layer got written fast — a lot of it by an AI, prompted by someone just trying to make the bug report stop — and each layer was, on its own, a locally sensible patch.

Nobody was lazy. Nobody was stupid. The pile was built entirely out of reasonable responses to a problem no one had ever actually sat down and looked at. Two thousand lines of scar tissue grown over a splinter nobody had removed.

What was actually under it

I only started pulling the layers off because I was chasing that same cold ticket for the third time. And the way you come to understand code like that is you delete it — locally, one piece at a time — and watch what actually breaks versus what you were only afraid would break.

The retries came off. Nothing broke. The cache came off. Nothing broke — except now, with the cache gone, I could finally see the real behaviour instead of the smoothed-over version. And there it was, naked, the thing all two thousand lines had been built to hide:

The write path acknowledged the request before it had actually persisted the row.

It said saved! to the user — and to every layer stacked above it — the instant the request arrived, not the instant the data was durable. Ninety-nine times out of a hundred the row landed a few milliseconds later and no one noticed. But let a retry hit at the wrong moment, or the connection blip at the wrong moment, and the ack had already gone out the door. The user saw saved. The save never landed. Their work was gone, and the app had cheerfully told them it was fine.

That was the splinter. Ack-before-persist. Every retry, every cache, every reconciliation job was a layer of code added to survive a lie the system was telling at the very bottom. We had spent two thousand lines making the symptom quieter instead of spending twenty making the cause go away.

And it had hurt someone. Not hypothetically — there was a real user, months back, who had lost an evening of work to exactly this and sent a furious, and completely correct, message about it. We'd "fixed" it at the time by adding another layer. We hadn't fixed anything. We'd just buried the body deeper.

The fix was twenty lines

When I finally understood it, the actual fix was almost insultingly small. Move the acknowledgement to after the row is durably written. Let the write fail loudly if it fails. Then delete every single layer that existed only to cope with the fact that it used to lie.

Two thousand lines out. About twenty lines in. The PR did not add a feature. It removed the reason five features' worth of defensive code had to exist at all.

That red, featureless, two-thousand-line-deletion pull request was the best code I wrote all year. And for the two years before it, I would have been incapable of seeing that — because I'd been measuring myself, like most of us do, by the green. By lines added. By features shipped. By the size of the diff in the direction that feels like progress.

The part that isn't free anymore

Here's the reframe, and it's the whole point.

Adding code is free now. I don't mean cheap — I mean free. I can describe a feature to a machine and have four hundred plausible lines back before my coffee's cool. So can you. So could every person who added a layer to that write path. The part of the job that generates code got infinitely fast and infinitely tireless this year, and the proof is sitting right there in the pile: two thousand lines accrete a lot faster when adding them is nearly effortless.

But deleting a line is not free, and it never will be, because deletion is the one move you cannot make without actually understanding what the code does. To add the retry, you only had to believe it might help. To delete the retry, I had to know what it was holding up — what leaned on it, what would fall over without it, and what was only there out of fear. Addition runs on hope. Subtraction runs on understanding. That's the whole difference, and it's the entire reason one of them got free this year and the other one didn't.

Anyone can add a line. Deleting one means knowing what it was holding up. That's the part that was never free.

The machine wrote most of that pile in minutes. It took me three days to be sure which lines were safe to remove — and those three days, not the minutes, were the actual engineering. The gap between "I can generate this" and "I understand this well enough to take it away" is exactly the gap that stopped being automatable the moment generation stopped being hard.

To be clear — this is not "stop writing code"

I need to be fair here, because the lazy version of this post is "real engineers delete, juniors add," and that's garbage.

I am not anti-code. I add code all day. I let a machine write most of it, and I'd never go back — it's genuinely one of the best things to happen to this job. Adding is good. Features are the point. An app that only ever shrinks is a product dying on a schedule. Every one of those two thousand lines got written by someone trying, in good faith, to help a user, and most of the individual patches were reasonable the day they shipped. Writing code is not the problem and never was.

The point is narrower, and I think more useful: addition was never the scarce part, so getting faster at it didn't make me better — it just let me accumulate the expensive problem faster. The scarce thing — the only thing that turned that flaky write path from a two-year-old cold ticket into a solved problem — was the judgment to look at code that already existed and ask the question nobody adding a layer ever asks: does this need to exist, and what breaks if it doesn't? The machine made the output free and did absolutely nothing about that question. It can't. It generates confidently in whichever direction you point it — including straight onto the pile.

Why this is exactly how I build now

I build an agent platform now, and this one pull request is more or less the whole thesis of it.

The industry's reflex this year is to worship the author — the thing that generates. Look how much it ships! A whole feature from a sentence! But an author with no counterweight doesn't hand you a clean codebase. It hands you that write path: two thousand confident, plausible, locally-reasonable lines piled on top of a lie at the bottom, because generating the next layer was always easier than questioning the last one. I've watched it happen by hand. The author is how the pile gets built.

So the part I care about isn't the author — I already assume the author. Everyone has one now. What I'm hunting for is the skeptic and the human. The author writes the code, fast and free. The skeptic is the part that asks the question I didn't ask for two years — does this need to exist? what does it do under a retry? — and whose best possible output is often a giant red diff and nothing new. And the human is the one who owns the real person on the other end, the one whose evening of work quietly vanished, who can see the blast radius the model never will. Author, skeptic, human. That separation is the entire shape of xenition — and it's the same thing one deletion taught me the hard way: generating the thing is free and always will be; knowing what to take away, and what it costs the person on the other end if you're wrong, is the whole job, and the only part anyone ever actually pays for.

My best pull request last year added nothing and deleted two thousand lines. For two years I'd have called that a week with no output. It was the opposite. It was the week I finally did the part that wasn't free.

Next time you open a file you're afraid to touch, don't ask what you can add to make it better. Ask what's in there that nobody understands anymore — and what it might be quietly hiding.

articles.body_html:
When an e-commerce storefront or SaaS application suffers from poor Google Core Web Vitals, the immediate business penalty is quantifiable: lower search rankings in Google SERPs, higher ad acquisition costs, and elevated cart abandonment rates. On mobile networks, every 100ms of latency degrades conversion by up to 1%.

Yet the standard response from many agencies—installing third-party "speed optimization" plugins or app overlays—often makes the underlying problem worse. These tools inject speculative prefetchers, delay scripts via brittle DOM rewrites, and introduce layout jitter that destroys Interaction to Next Paint (INP) while masking actual server and rendering bottlenecks.

A senior engineering approach treats Core Web Vitals as a systems measurement problem: diagnose the exact phase of the critical rendering path, eliminate root-cause bottlenecks in code and server delivery, and verify with lab and field metrics.

The Three Vital Pillars: Diagnostic Breakdown

1. Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) < 2.5s

LCP measures the time from initial page load until the largest visual content element (typically a hero banner, product image, or main heading block) is completely rendered in the viewport.

LCP time breaks down into four sequential phases:

  • Time to First Byte (TTFB): Server processing, database query latency, and edge CDN routing.
  • Resource Load Delay: The elapsed time between TTFB and when the browser actually begins fetching the LCP resource.
  • Resource Load Duration: The time required to download the LCP asset over the wire.
  • Element Render Delay: The time between asset download completion and the paint event, often blocked by synchronous JavaScript execution or web font loading.

Root-Cause Remediation for LCP:

  • Direct Edge Preloading: Never let the browser discover your hero image through deeply nested CSS classes or client-side JavaScript hydration. Declare priority hints in the document <head>: 
  <link
    rel="preload"
    as="image"
    href="/images/hero-mobile.webp"
    imagesrcset="/images/hero-mobile.webp 600w, /images/hero-desktop.webp 1200w"
    imagesizes="(max-width: 768px) 100vw, 1200px"
    fetchpriority="high"
  />
  • Modern Asset Encodings & Right-Sizing: Serve modern formats (AVIF or WebP) with proper responsive srcset definitions. An uncompressed 2MB PNG scaled down via CSS to 400px will reliably fail LCP on 4G cellular links.
  • Edge Cache Invalidation & TTFB Reduction: Cache static HTML at the edge via Cloudflare Workers or Cache Rules with stale-while-revalidate headers. Aim for edge TTFB under 150ms.

2. Interaction to Next Paint (INP) < 200ms

Replacing FID (First Input Delay), INP measures page responsiveness across the entire lifecycle of a user session—capturing the delay from clicks, taps, or key presses to the visual frame update on screen.

Poor INP is almost always caused by Long Tasks (tasks executing on the main thread for longer than 50ms) blocking user input handling.

Common INP Bottlenecks:

  • Third-party analytics and tracking scripts (Meta Pixel, TikTok, Hotjar, multiple tag managers) running un-debounced event listeners on window scroll, touch, or click.
  • Heavy React, Vue, or Next.js hydration passes recalculating entire component trees on mobile hardware.
  • Synchronous DOM mutations occurring within click event handlers (e.g., cart drawer toggles, filter accordions) instead of deferring heavy re-renders.

Root-Cause Remediation for INP:

  • Yielding to the Main Thread: Break massive JavaScript execution loops into discrete chunks using scheduler.yield() or microtask timeouts: 
  async function handleFilterUpdate(filterCriteria) {
    // 1. Immediately update critical UI state (spinner / button feedback)
    setLoadingState(true);

    // 2. Yield control back to browser to paint input feedback
    if ('scheduler' in window && 'yield' in window.scheduler) {
      await window.scheduler.yield();
    } else {
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 0));
    }

    // 3. Execute heavier filtering / DOM recalculations
    applyCatalogFilters(filterCriteria);
    setLoadingState(false);
  }
  • Audit Third-Party Tag Ingestion: Move third-party tracking pixels to Web Workers via tools like Partytown or execute them via server-side edge webhooks (Cloudflare Workers / Zaraz) to completely remove them from the user's main thread.
  • Debouncing Global Event Listeners: Ensure custom scroll, resize, or keyup handlers use passive: true listeners and requestAnimationFrame throttling.

3. Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) < 0.1

CLS measures visual stability: unexpected layout jumps that occur as elements shift while new resources load asynchronously.

Root-Cause Remediation for CLS:

  • Explicit Aspect Ratios on Media Elements: Always specify width and height attributes on <img>, <video>, and <iframe> elements, or define aspect-ratio in CSS so the browser reserves layout space before media arrives: 
  .product-gallery-image {
    width: 100%;
    height: auto;
    aspect-ratio: 1 / 1;
    content-visibility: auto;
  }
  • Reserve Space for Dynamic Embeds & Banners: Promotional banners, cookie consent bars, and dynamic price notices must render inside fixed-height placeholders rather than pushing existing content down by 80px upon arrival.
  • Font Display Strategy: Mitigate Flash of Unstyled Text (FOUT) and Flash of Invisible Text (FOIT) layout shifts by pairing font-display: swap with font metric overrides (size-adjust, ascent-override) matching system fallback fonts.

The Anti-Pattern: Plugin Stacking vs. Native Code

In platforms like Shopify and WooCommerce, store owners frequently install multiple caching, compression, and minification plugins hoping for a quick fix. In practice:

  • Plugins concatenate scripts into massive render-blocking bundles.
  • Speculative preloaders flood mobile cellular data connections with unnecessary requests.
  • App scripts fight each other for execution priority, spiking total blocking time (TBT).

The sustainable solution is native code remediation:

  1. Remove deprecated apps, theme fragments, and dead tracking pixels.
  2. Build custom sections in clean HTML/Liquid/TypeScript instead of heavy third-party page builders.
  3. Establish edge caching rules and proper HTTP cache-control semantics.

Measuring Your Baseline

Before changing code, establish an objective performance baseline using real lab data and field telemetry.
