articles.title: pointer-events: none doesn't disable an element. It hands the press to whatever is underneath.
articles.description: In a fanned hand of cards, I pressed a card I wasn't allowed to play, and the game played a different...
articles.body_html:
In a fanned hand of cards, I pressed a card I wasn't allowed to play, and the game played a different card: the one lying under it. The click handler was fine. The card I pressed had pointer-events: none, and that property doesn't stop a press. It takes the element out of hit-testing, the step where the browser works out which element is under the pointer, so the press goes to the next element down, and in a fan the next element down is the neighbouring card.

This post has the minimal repro, a table of where the press lands in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit for five ways of switching an element off, and the fix.

The repro 

<!doctype html>
<style>
  .hand { position: relative; height: 140px; margin: 20px; }
  .card { position: absolute; top: 0; width: 80px; height: 120px; }
  .card:nth-child(1) { left: 0; }
  .card:nth-child(2) { left: 40px; }
  .card:nth-child(3) { left: 80px; }
  .off { pointer-events: none; opacity: .5; }
</style>
<div class="hand">
  <button class="card" id="a">A</button>
  <button class="card off" id="b">B</button>
  <button class="card" id="c">C</button>
</div>
<script>
  document.querySelector('.hand').addEventListener('click', (e) => {
    console.log('played', e.target.id);
  });
</script>

Three cards, each covering the right half of the one before it. B is dimmed and has pointer-events: none. Click the strip of B that you can see, between A and C. The console says played a.

You can ask the browser what a press at that spot would hit:

const r = document.getElementById('b').getBoundingClientRect();
document.elementsFromPoint(r.left + 20, r.top + 60).map((el) => el.id || el.tagName);
// ["a", "DIV", "BODY", "HTML"]

B isn't in the list at all. That is what the spec asks for. CSS UI 4 says that with none, hit-testing "acts as if the boxes generated by the element were not there, effectively causing the element behind the pointer-events: none element to become the target of hit-testing-based events instead."

The part I had wrong was "the element behind". It isn't the page background. It is whatever hit-testable box comes next in paint order, and if that box is another live control, the press is now a press on that control.

Five ways to switch B off, in three engines

I disabled B five different ways and pressed its visible strip in Chromium 148, Firefox 150 and WebKit 26.4: once with Playwright's mouse, once with Playwright's emulated touchscreen, and once by tabbing to it from A and pressing Enter. A capturing listener on window logged the target of every pointer, touch, mouse and click event.

B is switched off with pointerdown lands on click, mouse click, touch Tab from A, then Enter
nothing (control) B B B focuses B, clicks B
pointer-events: none A A A focuses B, clicks B
inert A A A skips B, focuses C
disabled B no click no click; A in WebKit skips B, focuses C
aria-disabled="true" B B B focuses B, clicks B

The three engines agree everywhere except the one cell marked WebKit. Four things fall out of it.

pointer-events: none switches off the pointer, not the element. Every event in the sequence, from pointerdown to click, went to A, with the mouse and with touch. The keyboard is untouched: B still takes focus, and Enter clicks it. The spec says so too: "pointer-events: none does not inhibit sequential focus navigation." So a card switched off this way plays its neighbour when you click it and plays itself when you press Enter on it.

inert behaves the same for the pointer. inert is an HTML attribute that switches off an element and everything inside it, and the HTML spec defines it this way. The first rule in its list for an inert node is "Hit-testing must act as if the 'pointer-events' CSS property were set to 'none'." It also takes B out of the tab order, which is why Tab went from A straight to C. It is the right tool for a whole region the user can't reach, such as the page behind a modal, and the wrong one for a single item that sits on top of other live items.

disabled keeps the press on B, but not every event. Hit-testing stops at the disabled button. With the mouse, no engine dispatched a click anywhere, and with touch, Chromium and Firefox didn't either. But pointerdown and pointerup still fired on B in all three engines, so a handler on pointerdown gets no protection from disabled. And with emulated touch in WebKit, pointerdown and touchstart went to B while the mousedown, mouseup and click that follow a tap went to A. That happened when the element under B was another button; with a <div> under B, nothing received a click, even with a click listener on it. disabled also only exists on form controls, so a card built from a <div> can't use it.

aria-disabled changes nothing about the press. Every event landed on B, in every engine, from every input. That is the behaviour you want: the press reaches the element the user aimed at, and your code decides what it means.

The fix

Keep every item hit-testable and refuse the press in the handler. Against the repro, replace the .off rule, mark B with the attribute instead of the class, and check it in the handler:

.card[aria-disabled="true"] { opacity: .5; }

<button class="card" id="b" aria-disabled="true">B</button>

document.querySelector('.hand').addEventListener('click', (e) => {
  const card = e.target.closest('.card');
  if (!card) return;
  if (card.getAttribute('aria-disabled') === 'true') {
    console.log('refused', card.id);
    return;
  }
  console.log('played', card.id);
});

A press on B's strip now logs refused b in all three engines, with the mouse, with touch, and with Tab and Enter. elementsFromPoint at the same spot returns ["b", "a", "DIV", "BODY", "HTML"]: B is back on top of the stack, with A under it where it belongs. The dimming and the refusal read the same attribute, so they can't disagree.

pointer-events: none is still the right tool when you want the press to go to whatever is underneath: a label floating over a canvas, or a drag preview that follows the pointer while you hit-test for the drop target under it. Use it for things that should be transparent to the pointer, never as a way to say "this control is off".

Two caveats. These are Playwright's synthesized mouse, touch and keyboard input, not a physical mouse or a finger on a phone, so test the devices you ship to. In particular, the WebKit touch result comes from Playwright's WebKit build with emulated touch; I haven't reproduced it on an iPhone, so treat it as a reason to check Safari, not as a fact about it.

How much of a fan it hits

In a fan, most of the part of a card you can see lies on top of the card before it. With pointer-events: none on the cards you can't play, a press on one of them goes to the card underneath, and on down the stack until it reaches a card that takes presses, or the table. It only plays the wrong card when an unplayable card lies on a playable one.

I measured how much of a hand that is in a game of Spades, where the hand is sorted by suit and, when you have the suit that was led, only that suit may be played. I dealt eight hands, four at 1280×900 with the mouse and four at 390×844 with emulated touch, and stopped at the first trick where I had to follow suit. For each card I couldn't play, I sampled its visible area on a 2 px grid with elementFromPoint, then switched back to the old rule, under which only playable cards take presses, and checked what each sampled point hit.

  • In four hands, the playable suit was the last one in the fan. Nothing lay on it, and every stray press fell to the table.
  • In the other four, the card lying on the end of the playable run had 50–89% of its visible area over a playable card. The 50% was the last card in the hand, whose whole face shows.
  • At phone size the fan is tighter, and the card after that one still had 7% of its visible area over the same playable card: a press can fall through two cards.

In all four of those hands, a press on that card played the playable card under it with the old rule, and played nothing with the fix in place. The fixed hand is in this Spades game: when you have to follow suit, a press on a card you can't play does nothing.

Takeaways

  • pointer-events: none doesn't disable an element. A press goes to whatever hit-testable box is underneath, and the keyboard still reaches the element itself.
  • inert does the same to the pointer, by definition, and also removes focus. Use it for whole regions, not single items in a stack.
  • disabled stops click but not pointerdown or pointerup, and exists only on form controls.
  • In any UI where items overlap, keep each item hit-testable and refuse the press in your handler. document.elementsFromPoint(x, y) shows you what a press at a point would hit.

articles.title: Vue provide/inject: Why You Should Never Skip readonly()
articles.description: Vue's guide says wrap provide() state in readonly() — most tutorials skip it. The mutation bug that causes, verified against Vue 3.5, plus a cheat sheet.
articles.body_html:
A teammate asks you why cart.total changed. You open the component that renders it — nothing there mutates it. You check its parent — nothing there either. Twenty minutes later you find it: a <PromoBanner> three levels down, nowhere near the cart, called cart.items.push(...) because it had a reference to the object and nobody stopped it. Vue didn't do anything wrong. provide/inject handed that component the exact same reactive object the cart store holds, and JavaScript let it write to what it was handed. The bug isn't in Vue's reactivity — it's in a contract nobody enforced.

What You'll Learn

By the end of this article you'll be able to:

  • Explain why an injected value is a live reference, not a snapshot or a message
  • Reproduce the "mutation from anywhere" bug on purpose, so you recognize it in a real codebase
  • Apply Vue's own fix — readonly() on the provided value, paired with an exposed mutator function — and know exactly what it does and doesn't stop
  • Type provide/inject with InjectionKey<T> so TypeScript catches a missing provider at compile time
  • Decide when provide/inject is still the right tool and when a store (Pinia) earns its weight

Who this is for: you've used ref, reactive, and basic provide/inject in a Vue 3 Composition API app, and you want the version of this pattern that survives more than two components.

Contents

  • Why this breaks: provide/inject shares the object, not a copy
  • The mental model
  • The fix: readonly() and a mutator function
  • Typing it with InjectionKey
  • Edge cases and gotchas
  • Best practices
  • FAQ
  • Cheat sheet
  • Key takeaways

This is written against Vue 3.5 (verified 3.5.44 on npm's latest tag, October 2026). Everything here is Composition API with <script setup>; there is no Options API equivalent worth writing, since this.$options.provide was always the weaker version of this same idea.

Why this breaks: provide/inject shares the object, not a copy

Here's the setup almost every provide/inject tutorial shows, including Vue's own introductory example:

<!-- CartProvider.vue -->
<script setup>
import { reactive, provide } from "vue";

const cart = reactive({ items: [], total: 0 });

function addItem(item) {
  cart.items.push(item);
  cart.total += item.price;
}

provide("cart", cart);
provide("addItem", addItem);
</script>

<!-- PromoBanner.vue, three components deep -->
<script setup>
import { inject } from "vue";

const cart = inject("cart");

function applyFreeGift() {
  // "I just need to add one thing, calling addItem felt like overkill"
  cart.items.push({ id: "free-sticker", price: 0 });
}
</script>

Run this and it works. cart.items updates, the cart badge re-renders, nothing throws. That's exactly why it's dangerous: there is no error to notice, no test that fails, no lint rule that fires. inject("cart") returned the same reactive() proxy the provider created — not a message describing a change, not a frozen snapshot — the object itself. Anything with a reference to it can write to it, from anywhere in the tree, and Vue's reactivity system will faithfully propagate that write, because propagating writes is its entire job.

The bug only shows up later, as a debugging problem: cart.total is wrong, or cart.items has an entry nobody can explain, and the mutation could be coming from any of the components that called inject("cart"). Vue devtools' state inspector will show you the current value, but it won't point you at the nine places across the tree that are allowed to change it.

The mental model

The mental model: provide/inject is Vue's version of passing a reference down an arbitrarily deep call stack — it shares the exact object, with none of the access control a function's parameters would give you. A prop is already a one-way, shallow-readonly-by-convention handoff that Vue warns about if you mutate it directly. provide/inject has no equivalent warning built in, because the whole point of the API is to skip the explicit, typed handoff of props — and that convenience is also the hole.

Vue's own guide is explicit about the fix, and about whose job it is: "it is recommended to keep any mutations to reactive state inside of the provider whenever possible," and when a descendant genuinely needs to change something, the provider should expose "a function that is responsible for mutating the state" rather than the state's writable surface. That single line is doing a lot of work, and it's easy to skip because unlike a type error, skipping it doesn't break anything today.

The fix: readonly() and a mutator function

The fix is two changes to the provider, and zero changes to how descendants read the value.

<!-- CartProvider.vue -->
<script setup>
import { reactive, readonly, provide } from "vue";

const cart = reactive({ items: [], total: 0 });

function addItem(item) {
  cart.items.push(item);
  cart.total += item.price;
}

// Descendants get a read-only view of the state...
provide("cart", readonly(cart));
// ...and the only sanctioned way to change it.
provide("addItem", addItem);
</script>

Now the PromoBanner from earlier doesn't quietly succeed:

const cart = inject("cart");
cart.items.push({ id: "free-sticker", price: 0 });
// [Vue warn] Set operation on key "0" failed: target is readonly.
// [Vue warn] Set operation on key "length" failed: target is readonly.

readonly() wraps the value in a second proxy that intercepts writes and, in development, logs a warning naming the exact key that was targeted instead of silently applying — Vue's reactivity docs show this same message for a plain mutation attempt on a readonly() copy of a reactive object. The write doesn't happen; the original, writable cart inside the provider is unaffected. PromoBanner has no way to change the cart except by calling the addItem function it was also given — which means every mutation path is now a named function you can grep for, breakpoint, or log.

Key concept: readonly() doesn't make the data immutable — the provider can still mutate its own cart freely. It makes the injected reference refuse writes, which is what turns "any of nine components might have done this" back into "only addItem could have done this."

readonly()'s wrapping is deep: nested objects and arrays reached through the readonly proxy are themselves readonly, so cart.items.push(...) is caught, not just reassigning cart.items itself. If you only need the top level protected (rare, and usually a sign the shape should be flatter), shallowReadonly() exists, but reach for plain readonly() by default — a one-level gap is exactly where the next PromoBanner finds the one key that still writes.

Typing it with InjectionKey

String keys ("cart") work but give TypeScript nothing to check — a typo in the key, or injecting before the provider ever renders, both fail silently at runtime. InjectionKey<T> fixes both:

// keys.ts
import type { InjectionKey, DeepReadonly } from "vue";

export interface CartState {
  items: { id: string; price: number }[];
  total: number;
}

// Keyed as DeepReadonly<CartState>, because that's what provide(cartKey, readonly(cart))
// actually hands out — typing it as plain CartState fails to compile, since readonly()'s
// nested readonly arrays aren't assignable to CartState's mutable ones.
export const cartKey: InjectionKey<DeepReadonly<CartState>> = Symbol("cart");
export const addItemKey: InjectionKey<(item: CartState["items"][number]) => void> =
  Symbol("addItem");

// CartProvider.vue <script setup lang="ts">
import { reactive, readonly, provide } from "vue";
import { cartKey, addItemKey, type CartState } from "./keys";

const cart = reactive<CartState>({ items: [], total: 0 });
function addItem(item: CartState["items"][number]) {
  cart.items.push(item);
  cart.total += item.price;
}

provide(cartKey, readonly(cart));
provide(addItemKey, addItem);

// PromoBanner.vue <script setup lang="ts">
import { inject } from "vue";
import { cartKey, addItemKey } from "./keys";

// cart: DeepReadonly<CartState> | undefined — TypeScript now forces you to
// handle the "no provider" case instead of finding it at 2am.
const cart = inject(cartKey);
const addItem = inject(addItemKey);

The symbol key means a typo can't collide with an unrelated provide("cart", ...) elsewhere in the tree, and inject()'s return type is now narrowed to DeepReadonly<CartState> | undefined — the undefined is real, because inject without a default genuinely returns undefined when there's no matching provider above the component, and the type system now makes you prove you've considered that.

Edge cases and gotchas

  • readonly() on a ref warns the same way. provide("count", readonly(count)) means inject("count").value = 5 from a descendant logs the same "target is readonly" warning instead of applying. The pattern isn't specific to reactive() objects.
  • computed() needs no wrapping. A computed ref is already read-only by construction — assigning to .value is a TypeScript error (or a runtime no-op without a custom setter) regardless of readonly(). If the provided value is derived, not stored, provide the computed() directly.
  • The provider can still forget the function. readonly() stops the descendant from writing; it does nothing if the provider itself exports a mutable reference alongside the readonly one by mistake. The discipline is "provide state read-only, provide every allowed change as a named function" — both halves matter.
  • This is a dev-mode warning, not a runtime guarantee you should rely on for security. It protects you from accidental mutation in your own codebase, not from a determined caller bypassing Vue's proxy in production. Don't use it as an access-control boundary for untrusted code.
  • It's the single-request version of the shared-state trap. The same "one object, many writers" shape that bites provide/inject across a component tree also bites module-scope state across requests on a Vue SSR server — that's a different failure mode with a different fix, covered in this series' composables shared-state piece.

Best Practices

Reach for provide/inject (with this pattern) when the state is genuinely tree-scoped — a form wizard's shared step state, a modal's context, a design-system component's configuration — and you want to avoid prop-drilling it through components that don't care about it.

Pair every provide() of mutable state with:

  1. readonly() (or shallowReadonly()) around the value itself.
  2. One or more named functions for every change a descendant is allowed to make.
  3. An InjectionKey<T> instead of a string, once more than one file touches the key.

Reach for Pinia instead when the state needs to be read or changed from components that aren't descendants of a single provider — a cart that's also read from the header nav and a checkout page outside that subtree, for instance. provide/inject is scoped to a component subtree by design; a store isn't. Using provide/inject for truly global, cross-tree state usually means re-providing it near the root anyway, at which point a store does the same job with less wiring.

FAQ

Does readonly() also stop the provider from mutating the value?

No. readonly(cart) returns a new proxy; the original cart reference the provider holds is still the plain reactive() object, fully writable. Only the reference that goes through provide() is wrapped.

Does wrapping a large object in readonly() cost performance?

The wrapping itself is cheap — it's a proxy, created once, not a deep clone. Reads are tracked the same way reactive() reads are. You won't notice this on anything short of a very large, deeply nested object being read in a tight loop, and that's a different problem to measure separately.

Can a child still mutate the state through a method it calls?

Yes, and that's correct, not a hole. If the provider exposes addItem(), a child calling addItem() is mutating state through the one sanctioned path — that's the entire point. readonly() blocks direct property writes on the injected value; it was never meant to block the mutator functions you provide alongside it.

Does this replace Pinia?

No — it's the right tool for state scoped to one part of the tree, not a general store replacement. See "Best practices" above for the line between them.

What happens if a component injects a key with no matching provider?

Without a default, inject() returns undefined at runtime. With InjectionKey<T>, TypeScript types that return as T | undefined, so a missing provider becomes a type error you fix during development instead of a crash a user finds. You can also pass a default as inject(key, defaultValue).

Cheat Sheet

Task Code Notes
Provide read-only state provide(key, readonly(state)) Deep by default; descendants can read, not write
Provide the allowed mutation provide(mutateKey, mutateFn) One named function per allowed change
Type the key const key: InjectionKey<T> = Symbol("x") inject(key) is now typed `T \
Inject with a safe default {% raw %}inject(key, fallback) Avoids undefined entirely when a sane default exists
Top-level-only protection shallowReadonly(state) Rare — nested objects stay mutable
Readonly a single ref provide(key, readonly(myRef)) Same warning-on-write behavior as an object 
// keys.ts
import type { InjectionKey, DeepReadonly } from "vue";
export interface CartState { items: { id: string; price: number }[]; total: number }
export const cartKey: InjectionKey<DeepReadonly<CartState>> = Symbol("cart");
export const addItemKey: InjectionKey<(item: CartState["items"][number]) => void> = Symbol("addItem");

// Provider
const cart = reactive<CartState>({ items: [], total: 0 });
function addItem(item: CartState["items"][number]) {
  cart.items.push(item);
  cart.total += item.price;
}
provide(cartKey, readonly(cart));
provide(addItemKey, addItem);

// Any descendant
const cart = inject(cartKey);       // DeepReadonly<CartState> | undefined
const addItem = inject(addItemKey); // the only legal way to change it

Key Takeaways

  • provide/inject hands descendants the live reactive object, not a copy — any component with the reference can mutate it, and Vue will propagate that write exactly as designed.
  • Vue's own guide already tells you the fix: keep mutations in the provider, and provide a function for anything a descendant is allowed to change. The gap is that most example code skips it.
  • readonly() (or shallowReadonly()) turns a silent, untraceable write into a dev-mode warning naming the exact key — wrap every provided value that descendants shouldn't mutate directly.
  • InjectionKey<T> replaces a magic string with a typed, typo-proof key and makes the "no provider above me" case a compile-time | undefined instead of a runtime surprise.
  • This isn't a Pinia replacement — it's the right shape for state scoped to one part of the tree; state read or written from outside that subtree belongs in a store instead.

That PromoBanner bug from the top is now impossible to write by accident: there's no writable cart to reach for, only an addItem call that shows up in a stack trace with your name on it. articles.title: I Deleted My Scroll-Lock Library's Ugly Hack. `scrollbar-gutter` Replaces It.
articles.description: Opening a modal shifts your whole page sideways because the scrollbar vanishes with it — the bug every scroll-lock library papers over with a JS width measurement and a padding-right hack. `scrollbar-gutter: stable` fixes it in one line now that Safari finally caught up.
articles.body_html:
You open a modal. For one frame, before you can even read what it says, the page behind it flinches — the whole column of text shifts a few pixels to the right, like the browser flinched too.

Close the modal and it snaps back. Nobody styled that. Nobody asked for it. And if you build UI on Windows or Linux, you've shipped it to production without noticing, because on a Mac with the default trackpad scrollbars, it's nearly invisible. That's the part that makes this bug so sticky: the person who can see it and the person who has to fix it are usually not using the same operating system.

The fix everyone reaches for first

The standard explanation is that overflow: hidden on <body> — the thing every modal, drawer, and dropdown uses to stop the page scrolling behind it — also removes the vertical scrollbar. Removing the scrollbar hands its width back to the content. The content reflows into that space. The page shifts.

So people fix it the only way CSS used to allow: measure the scrollbar, then pay it back in padding.

function lockScroll() {
  const scrollbarWidth = window.innerWidth - document.documentElement.clientWidth;
  document.body.style.paddingRight = `${scrollbarWidth}px`;
  document.body.style.overflow = "hidden";
}

function unlockScroll() {
  document.body.style.paddingRight = "";
  document.body.style.overflow = "";
}

This works. It's also the entire reason body-scroll-lock, react-remove-scroll, and half a dozen modal libraries ship their own copy of this exact measurement. Every one of them is solving the same problem: find out how wide the scrollbar would have been, then fake its presence with padding so nothing moves.

Before you keep reading — guess how many pixels of padding a 100-line copy-pasted "scroll lock" utility is usually off by, on the one OS nobody tested it on. The answer is almost always "enough to notice," because scrollbar width isn't a constant. It's roughly 17px on Windows across Chrome and Firefox alike, 0px on a Mac with overlay scrollbars — and the measurement has to run before you lock, every single time, or it reads the wrong number.

Why the shift happens at all

Here's the part the padding hack never actually fixes, it just hides: a classic scrollbar — the opaque kind with a visible track, standard on Windows and Linux — is laid out inside the element's content box. The browser treats it the same way it treats a sidebar: it eats width from whatever would otherwise render there. Turn the scrollbar off, and the content box grows back to full width. Turn it on, and the content box shrinks to make room. The content isn't "jumping" — it's being resized, every time, and resized fast enough that it reads as a flinch.

macOS's default overlay scrollbars don't do this. They float on top of the content without claiming any layout space, so toggling them on and off never changes anything's width. That's the whole reason this bug is invisible to a developer who only ever tests on their own Mac: the platform they build on structurally can't reproduce the thing their users are reporting.

The padding-right hack works around the resize by adding back exactly the width the scrollbar would have taken — but it only works if you already know the scrollbar is about to disappear, and you measured it correctly, before it does. It's compensating for a resize instead of preventing one.

scrollbar-gutter: stable: tell the layout to stop flinching

CSS has a property for exactly this now, and the name says what it does: reserve the scrollbar's gutter, stably, whether a scrollbar is currently needed or not.

html {
  scrollbar-gutter: stable;
}

Set this once, and the browser carves out the scrollbar's width in the layout permanently — for overflow: auto, scroll, and hidden. When your modal flips overflow to hidden to lock the page, the gutter is already reserved from before the modal ever opened. There's no width to give back, so there's nothing to resize, so there's nothing to flinch.

function lockScroll() {
  document.body.style.overflow = "hidden"; // that's it — no measuring, no padding
}

function unlockScroll() {
  document.body.style.overflow = "";
}

That's the whole fix for the layout-shift half of what a scroll-lock library does. You still need something to stop the page actually scrolling under a modal on touch devices — overflow: hidden alone doesn't catch every edge case there, and that part of a scroll-lock library can stay. But the width-measuring, padding-compensating dance that most of these libraries built their reputation on? scrollbar-gutter: stable makes it dead code.

There's a second value for layouts that center content and need symmetry on both sides:

html {
  scrollbar-gutter: stable both-edges;
}

both-edges mirrors the reserved gutter to the opposite inline edge, so if space is held open on the right, matching space opens on the left too — useful when a scrollbar appearing on only one side would visibly knock a centered layout off-center.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

The part that's easy to get wrong: overlay scrollbars opt out of this too

Here's the honest asterisk, and it's the same one from earlier in reverse: scrollbar-gutter: stable only reserves space for classic scrollbars. MDN says it plainly — "When using overlay scrollbars, the gutter will not be present." On a system with overlay scrollbars, setting this property changes nothing, because there was never any layout space being given up in the first place.

That means you can't fully verify this fix by eyeballing your own Mac. You need a Windows or Linux machine, a Windows/Linux VM, or Chrome DevTools' device toolbar won't help either — it emulates viewport size, not the host OS's scrollbar rendering mode. The honest test is someone, or something, running an actual classic-scrollbar environment.

Is this safe to ship today?

Yes, with one small caveat worth knowing rather than discovering. Chrome and Edge have supported scrollbar-gutter since version 94 (2021), and Firefox since version 97 (2022) — this has quietly worked for most of your users for years. Safari was the holdout; it landed support in Safari 18.2, released in December 2024, which is also what pushed scrollbar-gutter to Baseline "newly available" that same month. If you need to support Safari versions older than 18.2, the property is simply ignored there — no error, no warning, the page just behaves exactly like it always did. That's a safe degrade, not a broken one, so there's no reason to gate this behind a feature query unless you want to show a different UI specifically for browsers that lack it.

The next time a modal makes your page twitch, you'll know exactly why — and now you know the one-line reason to stop paying JavaScript to measure a number CSS can just reserve for you.

Still carrying a scroll-lock library in your bundle for this exact problem? Go check what it actually does under the hood — there's a decent chance half of it just became unnecessary.

articles.title: SortedDictionary Kept Sorting My Insertion Order Away
articles.description: I grabbed SortedDictionary to keep my config in insertion order and it alphabetised everything instead. Here's why the generic OrderedDictionary<,> from .NET 9 is the one you actually want, and what the old boxing version was costing in allocations.
articles.body_html:
A config loader I wrote was reading feature-flag rollout steps out of a file, keyed by flag name, and the order those steps are declared in actually matters. They get applied top to bottom. So I reached for SortedDictionary<string, int> without really thinking about it, because some lazy corner of my brain had filed "sorted dictionary" under "the dictionary that keeps its order." It does keep an order. Just not mine.

The flags came back alphabetised. checkout-v2 was first in the file and showed up third in the output, sitting behind ai-suggest and beta-dashboard, two flags I hadn't touched in weeks. SortedDictionary sorts by key. That's the entire point of the type, and it's right there in the name once you stop misreading it. My insertion order was gone the moment I added the second entry.

Here's the setup. Five steps, in the order they live in the file:

var steps = new (string Name, int Percent)[]
{
    ("checkout-v2", 5),
    ("new-search", 50),
    ("dark-mode", 100),
    ("beta-dashboard", 25),
    ("ai-suggest", 10),
};

var sorted = new SortedDictionary<string, int>();
foreach (var (name, pct) in steps) sorted[name] = pct;

And what it printed:

SortedDictionary order:
  ai-suggest = 10
  beta-dashboard = 25
  checkout-v2 = 5
  dark-mode = 100
  new-search = 50

Alphabetical. Exactly what SortedDictionary promises, and exactly wrong for what I wanted.

The one that actually remembers

For years the only built-in that kept insertion order was System.Collections.Specialized.OrderedDictionary, the non-generic one from back in 2005 that stores everything as object. It works. But every int you put in gets boxed, and you cast your way back out again. .NET 9 finally shipped a generic version, System.Collections.Generic.OrderedDictionary<TKey, TValue>, and it's the thing I should have grabbed in the first place.

var ordered = new OrderedDictionary<string, int>();
foreach (var (name, pct) in steps) ordered[name] = pct;

OrderedDictionary<string,int> order:
  checkout-v2 = 5
  new-search = 50
  dark-mode = 100
  beta-dashboard = 25
  ai-suggest = 10

Declaration order, untouched. It's still a dictionary, so you get O(1) lookup by key like always, and it happens to remember the sequence you added things in. Because it tracks that sequence, you also get index access on top of the key access:

ordered.GetAt(0).Key;         // "checkout-v2", the first step
ordered.IndexOf("dark-mode"); // 2

GetAt, SetAt, RemoveAt, IndexOf, Insert. The list-shaped API sits right next to the dictionary one. I've hand-rolled the "Dictionary<,> plus a List<string> of keys to remember order" dance more than once, and this deletes all of it.

What the boxing was costing

I got curious about what the old Specialized one had been charging people all these years, so I measured instead of guessing. A hundred thousand string -> int entries, built and then read straight back, with the keys generated up front so their string allocations stay off the scorecard. Best of five runs, GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() wrapped around each build, and a checksum on the way out so nothing gets optimised away. This is a cloud container on workstation GC, not a lab bench, so I care about the ratio and not the raw milliseconds.

Legacy OrderedDictionary (boxes)     10,154,696 bytes   checksum 4999950000
OrderedDictionary<string,int>         3,041,792 bytes   checksum 4999950000

Same answer, a third of the memory. The old one boxes a hundred thousand ints into a hundred thousand tiny heap objects. The generic one stores them inline and never allocates a single box. The figure came back byte-for-byte identical on every run, which is the one nice thing about counting allocations: it doesn't drift the way a stopwatch does.

So if you're still typing Specialized.OrderedDictionary out of muscle memory, the generic drop-in is nicer to use and cheaper. That's about as close to a free upgrade as these things ever get.

Where it isn't a free lunch

One honest caveat, because OrderedDictionary<,> is not just "Dictionary<,> but better at everything." To keep its order, it stores entries in an array underneath. Inserting or removing anywhere other than the end shifts everything after it, which is O(n) work that a plain Dictionary would never do. RemoveAt(0) on a big one moves every remaining entry down a slot. If your access pattern is a lot of churn in the middle of the collection, that cost is real, and you'll want to feel it coming before you reach for this type.

My rule of thumb: use it when the order is part of the data. Config, column definitions, a pipeline of steps, anything you're going to hand back to someone who expects it the way they wrote it. For a hot lookup table where the order means nothing, plain Dictionary<,> is still the right call. The mistake was never picking SortedDictionary. It was picking it for a job the type never claimed it could do.

Here's the full runnable sample if you want to poke at the numbers yourself. It's a console app on net10.0. Drop it in a folder and dotnet run -c Release:

using System.Collections.Generic;
using LegacyOrderedDictionary = System.Collections.Specialized.OrderedDictionary;

var steps = new (string Name, int Percent)[]
{
    ("checkout-v2", 5),
    ("new-search", 50),
    ("dark-mode", 100),
    ("beta-dashboard", 25),
    ("ai-suggest", 10),
};

Console.WriteLine("== Does it keep insertion order? ==\n");

var sorted = new SortedDictionary<string, int>();
foreach (var (name, pct) in steps) sorted[name] = pct;

Console.WriteLine("SortedDictionary order:");
foreach (var kv in sorted) Console.WriteLine($"  {kv.Key} = {kv.Value}");

var ordered = new OrderedDictionary<string, int>();
foreach (var (name, pct) in steps) ordered[name] = pct;

Console.WriteLine("\nOrderedDictionary<string,int> order:");
foreach (var kv in ordered) Console.WriteLine($"  {kv.Key} = {kv.Value}");

Console.WriteLine($"\nFirst declared step via GetAt(0): {ordered.GetAt(0).Key}");
Console.WriteLine($"Index of 'dark-mode': {ordered.IndexOf("dark-mode")}");

Console.WriteLine("\n== Building 100,000 ordered entries (string -> int) ==\n");

const int N = 100_000;
var keys = new string[N];
for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) keys[i] = $"flag-{i}";

long legacyBytes = Measure(() =>
{
    var d = new LegacyOrderedDictionary(N);
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) d.Add(keys[i], i);       // int boxed on the way in
    long sum = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) sum += (int)d[keys[i]]!;  // unboxed on the way out
    return sum;
}, out long legacyChecksum);

long genericBytes = Measure(() =>
{
    var d = new OrderedDictionary<string, int>(N);
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) d.Add(keys[i], i);       // no boxing
    long sum = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) sum += d[keys[i]];
    return sum;
}, out long genericChecksum);

Console.WriteLine($"Legacy OrderedDictionary (boxes)   {legacyBytes,12:n0} bytes   checksum {legacyChecksum}");
Console.WriteLine($"OrderedDictionary<string,int>      {genericBytes,12:n0} bytes   checksum {genericChecksum}");
Console.WriteLine($"\nRatio: {(double)legacyBytes / genericBytes:0.0}x");

static long Measure(Func<long> build, out long checksum)
{
    checksum = 0;
    long best = long.MaxValue;
    for (int run = 0; run < 5; run++)
    {
        GC.Collect();
        GC.WaitForPendingFinalizers();
        GC.Collect();
        long before = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
        checksum = build();
        long after = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
        best = Math.Min(best, after - before);
    }
    return best;
}

Anyone else been hauling the Dictionary plus List<string> ordering hack around out of pure habit? I'm curious how many quiet little corners this new type replaces.

articles.title: gp-grid: A Free, Open-Source TypeScript Data Grid for React, Vue, and Angular (No Paywalled Features)
articles.description: An open-source data grid can look impressive with 1,000 rows and still struggle when your application...
articles.body_html:
An open-source data grid can look impressive with 1,000 rows and still struggle when your application needs to handle 100,000 or more. The same goes for features: you might find sorting and filtering in a free library, only to discover that row grouping, pivot tables, or other advanced capabilities require an enterprise license.

gp-grid takes a different approach. It is an open-source TypeScript data grid for React, Vue, and Angular, released under the Apache 2.0 license. It has zero external dependencies, supports large datasets through virtual scrolling, and includes all its features without paywalls.

In this article, we'll explore what makes a data grid useful, how gp-grid works, how to get started in your framework, and how it compares with AG Grid in features, bundle size, and published performance benchmarks.

TL;DR

gp-grid is a free, open-source TypeScript data grid for React, Vue, and Angular, licensed under Apache 2.0. It combines virtual scrolling, advanced data handling, and spreadsheet-style interactions without locking features behind a paid enterprise tier.

Its core features include:

✅ Row and column virtualization: Render only the visible rows and columns, plus an overscan buffer, to keep large and wide grids responsive.
✅ Sorting and filtering: Support multi-column sorting and advanced filter conditions.
✅ Cell selection and editing: Work with selected ranges, keyboard navigation, inline editing, and a fill handle.
✅ Custom rendering and styling: Customize cells, headers, filters, themes, and dark mode.
✅ Live and server-side data: Manage streaming updates or fetch rows on demand for larger datasets.
✅ Flexible layouts and analytics: Reorder, resize, pin, and freeze columns, with row grouping, aggregation, and pivot tables.
✅ AI coding agent support: Use the official gp-grid skill to help coding agents integrate the correct APIs, framework bindings, and data-source patterns.

gp-grid 1.0.0 supports both row and column virtualization, using overscan to render the visible viewport efficiently. Its published one-million-row benchmark reports 56.2 average FPS during the measured scrolling test, although results depend on the workload and test environment.

What Is a Web Data Grid?

A web data grid is an interactive component for displaying, sorting, filtering, selecting, and editing tabular data in a browser. Unlike a plain HTML table, a data grid can provide spreadsheet-style interactions, customizable cells, and virtual scrolling, which renders only the rows needed for the current viewport.

The distinction matters when you're building an admin dashboard, CRM, analytics platform, financial application, or any interface where people work with large datasets.

A standard HTML <table> gives you the basic structure for displaying rows and columns. You can add the behavior you need, but you'll have to build features such as sorting, filtering, and keyboard navigation yourself.

A headless table library such as TanStack Table handles much of the table logic while leaving the markup and presentation to you. This offers considerable flexibility, although your team remains responsible for building the interface.

A full data grid component comes with a more complete UI, including built-in interactions and configurable behavior. For teams that need a spreadsheet-like experience without implementing every interaction from scratch, this can save substantial development time.

The challenge is finding a grid that handles your dataset, fits your framework, and includes the features your application needs without creating unnecessary bundle weight or licensing costs.

What Features Really Matter in a Web Data Grid?

When choosing an open-source data grid, start with a practical checklist: performance, data operations, editing, customization, framework compatibility, accessibility, and licensing. The right balance depends on your application's workload and the experience your users expect.

Here are the capabilities worth evaluating before committing to a library:

  • Virtual scrolling: Keeps large datasets responsive by rendering visible rows and a small buffer instead of mounting every row in the DOM.
  • Sorting and filtering: Supports everyday data exploration, including multi-column sorting, advanced filter conditions, and server-side operations.
  • Selection and editing: Provides cell and range selection, keyboard navigation, inline editing, and spreadsheet-style conveniences such as a fill handle.
  • Customization and theming: Lets you create custom cell renderers, format values, apply application-specific styling, and support dark mode.
  • TypeScript and framework support: Offers reliable types and bindings that fit your existing React, Vue, or Angular application.
  • Bundle size and dependencies: Affects initial loading costs and the number of third-party packages your project must maintain.
  • Accessibility and keyboard support: Makes common grid interactions available through the keyboard and provides appropriate accessibility semantics.
  • Licensing: Clarifies whether grouping, pivot tables, and other advanced features are available under the free license.

That final point deserves attention. A library can be free to install while charging for the capabilities your application eventually needs. Check the licensing of individual features before making your decision.

gp-grid addresses this checklist with a TypeScript-first architecture, virtual scrolling, spreadsheet-style interactions, and an Apache 2.0 license that covers its complete feature set.

What Is gp-grid?

gp-grid is an open-source TypeScript data grid for React, Vue, and Angular, built around virtual scrolling, a framework-agnostic core, and a data-source abstraction. The library is released under Apache 2.0 and announces its 1.0.0 release with all features available for free.

Its architecture follows three main principles:

  • Slot-based virtual scrolling: gp-grid recycles a pool of DOM containers as users scroll, keeping the number of rendered elements controlled even when the underlying dataset contains millions of rows.
  • Instruction-based core: The core emits declarative instructions describing UI changes, separating grid logic from framework-specific rendering and allowing the wrappers to share the same underlying behavior.
  • Flexible data sources: You can work with data held in browser memory or fetch rows from a server on demand, depending on your application's needs.

The project separates its functionality into four packages: @gp-grid/core, @gp-grid/react, @gp-grid/vue, and @gp-grid/angular. They are available through npm and JSR.

Installation and Quick Start: React, Vue, and Angular

Getting started with gp-grid requires installing the package for your framework, defining your columns, and providing your data. The library recommends TypeScript 5.0 or higher, includes its own type definitions, and supports React 18+ and Vue 3 through dedicated wrappers.

Install the package

Choose the framework package you need and install it with your preferred package manager:

npm install @gp-grid/<framework>
# Replace <framework> with react, vue, or angular

The package names and component bindings are summarized below.

Framework Package Component Data helper
React @gp-grid/react Grid useGridData
Vue @gp-grid/vue GpGrid createGridData
Angular @gp-grid/angular gp-grid (GpGridComponent) provideGridData
Custom adapter @gp-grid/core GridCore createClientDataSource

Build your first React data grid

Define your columns and pass them to the Grid component alongside your rows. This example includes an editable name column and a basic email column.

import { Grid, type ColumnDefinition } from "@gp-grid/react";
import "@gp-grid/react/dist/styles.css";

const columns: ColumnDefinition[] = [
  { field: "id", cellDataType: "number", width: 80, headerName: "ID" },
  { field: "name", cellDataType: "text", width: 150, editable: true },
  { field: "email", cellDataType: "text", width: 250, headerName: "Email" },
];

const data = [
  { id: 1, name: "Alice", email: "alice@example.com" },
  { id: 2, name: "Bob", email: "bob@example.com" },
];

export default function App() {
  return (
    <div style={{ width: "100%", height: "400px" }}>
      <Grid columns={columns} rowData={data} rowHeight={36} />
    </div>
  );
}

One detail can save you a frustrating debugging session: the grid fills its parent, so that parent needs an explicit height.

Remember to import the stylesheet once at your application's root. Vue and Angular use their own component bindings but follow the same column-definition model.

gp-grid Core Features

The core features of gp-grid cover performance, data exploration, spreadsheet-style editing, customization, and different ways of loading data. Here are the capabilities worth examining when deciding whether the library fits your application.

Slot-Based Virtual Scrolling and Million-Row Performance

gp-grid uses slot-based virtualization to keep the rendered DOM small as datasets grow. Starting with version 1.0.0, it virtualizes the entire grid viewport, including both rows and columns. It maintains reusable DOM containers and updates their assignments as users scroll vertically or horizontally, rendering only the visible area and the surrounding overscan buffer.

The same overscan logic applies to both dimensions, helping preserve smooth scrolling behavior in both directions. This means gp-grid can handle large datasets and wide grids without mounting every row and column in the DOM. By reusing rendering slots as the viewport moves, it reduces the overhead associated with repeatedly creating and destroying DOM elements.

For large client-side datasets, sorting can also run in a Web Worker, enabled by default in the client data source. Developers can tune overscan, wheelDampening, and maxFlingVelocity to adjust scrolling behavior for their interface and input devices.

According to gp-grid's benchmarks, its test with one million rows recorded:

  • 56.2 average FPS while scrolling, with zero dropped frames.
  • 652 ms for ascending sorting and 188 ms for text filtering.
  • Approximately 254.7 MB of memory after loading the dataset.

These results are promising, but they're not universal performance guarantees. The benchmark tested @gp-grid/react 0.19.0, so keep that version in mind when comparing the figures with the project's newer 1.0 release.

Multi-Column Sorting and Advanced Filtering

Sorting and filtering help users find useful information without manually scanning thousands of records. gp-grid enables sorting by default: clicking a column header changes its sort order, while holding Shift and clicking another header adds a secondary sort criterion.

Filter controls support text, numeric, and date operators, along with a checkbox-based mode for selecting distinct values. For more complex searches, users can combine conditions with AND/OR logic, making expressions such as (A AND B) OR C possible.

You can disable sorting globally through sortingEnabled or set sortable: false on an individual column. Custom comparators and custom filter components also provide room for application-specific behavior.

For example, a finance dashboard could sort transactions by date and then amount, while a CRM user could filter contacts by status and region. These operations are available without requiring a separate enterprise feature license.

Cell Selection, Keyboard Navigation, and Excel-Like Editing

gp-grid supports cell selection, drag-to-select ranges, Shift-click to extend a selection, and Ctrl-click to toggle individual cells. Keyboard navigation includes arrow keys, Tab, Enter, Home, End, and common Ctrl-based shortcuts, allowing users to work through data without constantly reaching for the mouse.

To enable inline editing, set editable: true on a column. Users can start editing with a double-click, Enter, F2, or by typing. Enter and Tab commit changes, while Escape cancels an edit.

The fill handle adds another useful spreadsheet-style interaction: users can drag the small handle at the corner of a selected range to copy values across the target cells. Custom edit renderers and validators can support more specialized inputs and validation rules.

Custom Renderers, Styling, Highlighting, and Dark Mode

A data grid needs to fit your application's interface, especially when cells communicate status, money, dates, or other values that benefit from custom presentation. gp-grid supports custom cell, edit, and header renderers, either directly in column definitions or through renderer registries.

The valueFormatter option is useful when the displayed value differs from the raw data. For example, a salary column can show currency formatting while sorting and value-based operations continue to use the underlying numeric value.

{
  field: "salary",
  cellDataType: "number",
  width: 140,
  cellRenderer: SalaryRenderer,
  valueFormatter: (value) =>
    "$" + (value as number).toLocaleString(),
}

Styling is also flexible. The darkMode prop enables dark styling, and the built-in CSS uses zero-specificity :where() selectors, making it easier to override defaults with your own classes. Tailwind's @apply directive is supported, while highlighting callbacks can add row, column, or cell classes for hover states, alternating rows, and crosshair effects.

Live Data Streaming and Server-Side Data

gp-grid supports both continuously changing datasets and data loaded from a server on demand. This makes it suitable for interfaces such as stock tickers, operational dashboards, and administrative tools where records can change while users are working.

For live updates in React, the useGridData hook provides a mutable data source with helpers such as addRows and removeRows. You can also update individual cells or rows through the data source. Its debounceMs option batches rapid changes into fewer transactions, helping the grid handle frequent updates efficiently.

When your dataset is too large to keep entirely in browser memory, createServerDataSource lets the grid request specific row ranges from your API, along with sorting and filtering information.

import { Grid, createServerDataSource } from "@gp-grid/react";

const dataSource = createServerDataSource(async (request) => {
  const res = await fetch("/api/grid-data", {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify(request),
  });

  return res.json(); // { rows, totalRows }
});

<Grid columns={columns} dataSource={dataSource} rowHeight={36} />

Your endpoint must return the requested rows and the total row count. For datasets exceeding roughly 10 million rows, gp-grid's performance guide recommends server-side data loading.

Flexible Layout: Drag, Resize, Pin, Freeze, and Group Columns

A useful data grid should let users arrange information around their workflow. gp-grid supports dragging columns into a new order, resizing columns with minimum and maximum constraints, pinning columns to either side, and freezing rows beneath the header.

Column virtualization also limits the number of mounted columns when working with wide datasets. The grid supports right-to-left layouts, configurable column sizing, nested column groups, and row heights that can vary by row identity.

For example, a CRM could keep contact names visible while users scroll horizontally through company details, activity dates, and account values. A financial dashboard could freeze important summary rows while users inspect the records below them.

The library also provides ARIA grid roles and keyboard support. However, its documentation does not claim full accessibility compliance, so applications with strict accessibility requirements should perform their own audits and testing.

Row Grouping, Aggregation, and Pivot Tables

gp-grid includes row grouping, aggregation, and pivot tables under its free Apache 2.0 license. These features help turn flat records into structured summaries, giving users ways to explore large datasets without requiring a separate enterprise license.

Row grouping organizes records into expandable groups, with aggregates and totals available for summarizing values. Depending on the data source, grouping calculations can happen locally or be loaded from the server on demand.

Pivot tables let you transform dimensions into columns and summarize the resulting data, either locally or through precomputed pivot tables. This is useful for analytical interfaces where users need to compare categories, examine totals, or reorganize information around different dimensions.

The project also provides further guides covering write commands, history, and columnar data sources. Because gp-grid is a young project, review the relevant guides and try these capabilities with your own data before making them a core dependency.

AI coding agents can save time when building data-heavy interfaces, but they need accurate library-specific guidance to generate code that works. gp-grid provides an official skill that helps coding agents use the correct imports, column definitions, renderers, and data-source APIs across its supported frameworks.

The skill includes a main SKILL.md file and framework-specific references for React, Vue, Angular, and the framework-agnostic core. It also covers common integration mistakes, such as forgetting to set the grid container's height, missing the stylesheet import, or using the wrong date data type.

gp-grid vs AG Grid: Features, Cost, and Performance

Choosing a React data grid involves more than comparing performance. Feature availability and licensing can have a major impact on the total cost of a project. AG Grid follows a Community and Enterprise model: its Community edition is free, but several advanced capabilities, including row grouping and pivoting, require an Enterprise license. gp-grid takes a different approach by making all its features available under the Apache 2.0 license, with no Enterprise tier or feature-based licensing restrictions.

Who Should Use gp-grid?

gp-grid is worth considering if you need a feature-rich, open-source data grid without an enterprise license. It can be a good fit for:

articles.title: Claude's Watermark Disappears When You Tune Temperature
articles.description: Anthropic retrofitted watermarks onto older Claude models for EU compliance, but changing temperature quietly drops the injection.
articles.body_html:
Anthropic sent an update to API customers this weekend outlining a rollout of statistical text watermarks across older production models, including Claude Opus 4.6 and Claude Sonnet 4.6. The update is part of the compliance push ahead of the European Union AI Act deadline in December.

The announcement contained a technical condition that caught my attention. On Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6, the watermark only activates when developers leave three specific sampling parameters at their default values: temperature, top_p, and top_k.

If you pass a custom temperature in your API payload, the watermark does not attach to the response. Anthropic noted this directly in the customer email, advising teams who rely on the watermark for compliance reporting to keep their sampling settings at default values.

On newer architectures such as Claude Opus 5.5, the watermarking routine runs regardless of your request configuration. On the 4.6 generation, adjusting temperature from 1.0 to 0.7 turns the watermarking step off.

How logit watermarking breaks under sampling transforms

To understand why a sampling parameter disables the watermark, you have to look at how statistical text watermarking functions in token generation.

Anthropic uses an approach derived from Google DeepMind's SynthID scheme. These systems do not append hidden metadata, invisible Unicode tags, or cryptographic signatures to the completed response text. They operate inside the model's vocabulary projection layer while each token is being sampled.

During inference, the model produces a vector of unnormalized log-probabilities across its vocabulary. Before converting those logits into a probability distribution via softmax, the watermarking algorithm computes a pseudo-random hash using a private key and the tokens that immediately precede the current position. That hash partitions the vocabulary into two buckets, conventionally termed green and red token sets. The algorithm then applies a positive bias to the logits in the green set.

When the model samples from this adjusted distribution, it selects green tokens at a rate higher than pure chance would predict. A detector holding the private key reads the text, computes the expected fraction of green tokens across thirty or forty words, and runs a hypothesis test. If the green token density crosses a statistical threshold, the detector flags the output as synthetic.

This mechanism relies on a predictable relationship between logit shifts and selection probabilities.

When you alter sampling parameters, you modify that probability landscape. Temperature divides the unnormalized logits by a scalar constant before exponentiation. A temperature of 0.2 sharpens the distribution, driving probabilities toward the highest logit and suppressing the rest. Top-k drops all tokens outside the top k candidates, regardless of whether they belong to the green set. Top-p calculates cumulative probability mass and truncates the distribution tail dynamically.

If your sampling kernel was written for static defaults, running dynamic temperature scaling and nucleus truncation on top of logit offsets complicates the detector's math. The detector relies on an assumed null hypothesis distribution. When the generator truncates logits or sharpens distributions unevenly, the detection score drifts.

The engineering compromise behind legacy endpoints

Modern foundation models integrate watermarking directly into their custom Triton or CUDA sampling kernels. Those newer kernels compute the logit bias, scale by temperature, apply nucleus masks, and sample in a single fused pass.

Retrofitting that fused math onto existing high-throughput production clusters for older models is an operational hazard. Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6 serve heavy enterprise production traffic. Rebuilding and redeploying their core sampling kernels carries latency risks, memory footprint regressions, and numerical precision shifts that could alter output behavior for existing production workflows.

Anthropic chose the pragmatic path. The inference router checks the incoming request payload. If temperature, top_p, and top_k match the provider defaults, the request routes through the watermarking sampler. If the developer specifies custom sampling values, the router falls back to the original un-watermarked sampling path.

The trade-off is clean from an infrastructure stability standpoint. It avoids breaking changes on legacy model instances while satisfying regulatory deployment checklists.

The gap between compliance assumptions and production configs

The operational problem lives on the client side.

Most production software built on top of LLM APIs never runs at default sampling settings. When building structured extraction pipelines, developers frequently drop temperature to 0.0 or 0.2 to reduce token variance. When writing narrative drafts or creative copy, teams often nudge temperature to 0.7 or 0.8 while capping top_p at 0.95 to eliminate degenerate tails.

Every developer team doing that on Claude Opus 4.6 is now generating unwatermarked text, regardless of what their compliance dashboard claims.

Many teams assume that model-level watermarking is an ambient environmental property like TLS encryption or tenant isolation. If a provider announces that a model family is watermarked, engineers assume the output carries the watermark automatically.

In this case, an ordinary client configuration change silently changes the compliance status of your data pipeline. If an enterprise relies on Anthropic's private preview detection API to audit generated assets against EU regulatory records, documents generated with tuned sampling parameters will register as unverified third-party text.

Practical checks for API pipelines

If you run Claude in production and need to track watermarking status, you need to audit your client calls directly.

First, inspect your client abstraction layer. Check whether your SDK wrappers inject default sampling overrides. Many internal frameworks default temperature to 0.7 across all outgoing completions unless explicitly overridden. On Opus 4.6, that single line invalidates the watermark.

Second, separate your compliance workflows from your precision workflows. If a specific task requires auditable model watermarking under the EU AI Act, run that task on Claude Opus 5.5 where watermarking persists across parameter changes, or lock your 4.6 calls to default sampling values and handle variance through prompt structure.

Text watermarking remains fragile at the boundaries where statistical math meets real-world inference systems. A client request configuration should never be treated as an irrelevant implementation detail.

articles.title: One Contains Call, 375 Million Comparisons
articles.description: A membership check that reads like plain English was doing 375 million comparisons for 100,000 lookups. Here is what List.Contains in a loop actually costs, and when a HashSet is not worth the bother.
articles.body_html:
A nightly reconciliation job that cross-checks incoming orders against a list of active SKUs crept from "instant" to "noticeable," and the profiler pointed straight at a line I'd have sworn was free. It was a membership check. One Contains. The kind of thing you write without thinking because it reads like plain English: is this SKU allowed?

var allowed = GetActiveSkus();      // a List<Sku>
foreach (var order in incoming)
    if (allowed.Contains(order.Sku))
        keep.Add(order);

Reads fine. Does the right thing. And on a list of a few thousand SKUs with a hundred thousand orders flowing through, it was doing an absurd amount of work I never asked for.

The thing I forgot is what List<T>.Contains actually does. It has no index and no shortcut. It starts at the front and compares element by element until it finds a match or runs off the end. For an item that's present that's on average half the list. For an item that isn't present, a SKU that got retired say, it's the whole list, every time, because the list can't say "no" until it has checked all of them.

Making the list tell on itself

I didn't want to argue from a hunch, so I made the comparison count itself. I wrapped the SKU in a little struct whose Equals bumps a counter every time it runs:

readonly struct Sku(int value) : IEquatable<Sku>
{
    public readonly int Value = value;

    public bool Equals(Sku other)
    {
        Probe.Comparisons++;
        return Value == other.Value;
    }

    public override int GetHashCode() => Value;
}

Then I ran the same check two ways over the same data, once against the List<Sku> and once against a HashSet<Sku> built from it, and counted. Five thousand allowed SKUs, a hundred thousand orders to check, with about half the incoming SKUs deliberately not in the allowlist so the misses do their worst. Best of seven, JIT warmed first. This is a container, not a lab bench, so I care about the ratios and not the exact millisecond.

// the list way
foreach (var sku in incoming)
    if (allowed.Contains(sku)) matches++;

// the set way
var allowedSet = new HashSet<Sku>(allowed);
foreach (var sku in incoming)
    if (allowedSet.Contains(sku)) matches++;

Allowlist size:   5,000
Incoming checks:  100,000
Matches agree:    True (49,960)

List.Contains   comparisons:     375,031,117   best:    808.6 ms
HashSet.Contains comparisons:         49,960   best:      1.1 ms

Comparison ratio: 7507x
Time ratio:       733x

Three hundred and seventy-five million comparisons to answer a hundred thousand yes/no questions. That works out to about 3,750 comparisons per question, which is exactly what you'd expect: a miss walks all 5,000, a hit walks around 2,500, and it's a coin-flip which one you get.

The set did the same work in 49,960 comparisons, which is identical to the match count. That's not luck. HashSet finds the right bucket by hash code and only calls Equals when something is actually sitting in that bucket to confirm it. Every miss got answered by the hash alone, with no comparison at all, so the only Equals calls left are the real hits.

Why the shape matters more than the speed

The 733x is the headline, but it's the wrong thing to fixate on, because it's tied to my specific sizes. Double the allowlist and the list version roughly doubles its work while the set barely moves. That's the actual problem with Contains in a loop: it's O(n×m), and both of those numbers tend to grow in production while nobody is looking. The version that was fine with 500 SKUs in testing is the one that falls over at 5,000 in March.

The fix is boring, which is the best kind. Build the set once, query it in the loop:

var allowedSet = allowed.ToHashSet();   // pay O(n) once
foreach (var order in incoming)
    if (allowedSet.Contains(order.Sku)) // O(1) each
        keep.Add(order);

When I wouldn't bother

One honest caveat, because "always use a HashSet" is how you end up making the opposite silly mistake. The set isn't free. You pay to build it, and every element has to be hashed. If the collection is tiny, or you only probe it once or twice, that build cost is the whole story and the plain list wins.

So I checked. Same hundred thousand lookups, but against a ten-item allowlist:

10-item allowlist, 100k checks -> List: 1.27 ms   HashSet: 1.33 ms

The set is actually a hair slower there. At ten items, walking the list is so cheap that hashing is just ceremony. My rough rule: if the thing you're searching has more than a few dozen elements and you search it more than a couple of times, reach for the set. Below that, a List.Contains is clearer and costs nothing worth measuring.

If I had one opinion to leave you with, it's that this is the bug I personally re-introduce more than any other, because each individual Contains call looks completely innocent in review. Nobody flags "is this allowed?" The cost only exists in the loop wrapped around it, and the loop is usually three files away.

Here's the whole thing if you want to run the numbers yourself. New console project on the .NET 10 SDK, dotnet run -c Release:

using System.Diagnostics;

// A lookup key wrapping an int. The only reason it's a struct and not a
// plain int is so Equals can tell on itself: every comparison bumps a
// counter, which is how we watch List.Contains do O(n) work per call.
readonly struct Sku(int value) : IEquatable<Sku>
{
    public readonly int Value = value;

    public bool Equals(Sku other)
    {
        Probe.Comparisons++;
        return Value == other.Value;
    }

    public override bool Equals(object? obj) => obj is Sku s && Equals(s);
    public override int GetHashCode() => Value; // identity hash, stable buckets
}

static class Probe
{
    public static long Comparisons;
}

static class Program
{
    const int AllowedCount = 5_000;
    const int IncomingCount = 100_000;

    static void Main()
    {
        // Allowlist: even-numbered skus from 0..9998.
        var allowed = new List<Sku>(AllowedCount);
        for (int i = 0; i < AllowedCount; i++)
            allowed.Add(new Sku(i * 2));

        // Incoming skus across 0..9999, so roughly half are present (even)
        // and half miss (odd). A miss walks the whole list before saying no.
        var incoming = new Sku[IncomingCount];
        var rng = new Random(1234);
        for (int i = 0; i < IncomingCount; i++)
            incoming[i] = new Sku(rng.Next(0, AllowedCount * 2));

        var allowedSet = new HashSet<Sku>(allowed);

        // Warm the JIT.
        _ = CountWithList(allowed, incoming.AsSpan(0, 1000));
        _ = CountWithSet(allowedSet, incoming.AsSpan(0, 1000));

        var (listMatches, listComparisons, listMs) = BestOf(7, () => CountWithList(allowed, incoming));
        var (setMatches, setComparisons, setMs) = BestOf(7, () => CountWithSet(allowedSet, incoming));

        Console.WriteLine($"Allowlist size:   {AllowedCount:N0}");
        Console.WriteLine($"Incoming checks:  {IncomingCount:N0}");
        Console.WriteLine($"Matches agree:    {listMatches == setMatches} ({listMatches:N0})");
        Console.WriteLine();
        Console.WriteLine($"List.Contains   comparisons: {listComparisons,15:N0}   best: {listMs,8:F1} ms");
        Console.WriteLine($"HashSet.Contains comparisons:{setComparisons,15:N0}   best: {setMs,8:F1} ms");
        Console.WriteLine();
        Console.WriteLine($"Comparison ratio: {(double)listComparisons / setComparisons:F0}x");
        Console.WriteLine($"Time ratio:       {listMs / setMs:F0}x");
    }

    static int CountWithList(List<Sku> allowed, ReadOnlySpan<Sku> incoming)
    {
        int matches = 0;
        foreach (var sku in incoming)
            if (allowed.Contains(sku)) // walks the list, every single call
                matches++;
        return matches;
    }

    static int CountWithSet(HashSet<Sku> allowed, ReadOnlySpan<Sku> incoming)
    {
        int matches = 0;
        foreach (var sku in incoming)
            if (allowed.Contains(sku)) // one hash, maybe one compare
                matches++;
        return matches;
    }

    static (int matches, long comparisons, double ms) BestOf(int rounds, Func<int> work)
    {
        double best = double.MaxValue;
        int matches = 0;
        long comparisons = 0;
        for (int r = 0; r < rounds; r++)
        {
            Probe.Comparisons = 0;
            var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
            matches = work();
            sw.Stop();
            comparisons = Probe.Comparisons;
            best = Math.Min(best, sw.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds);
        }
        return (matches, comparisons, best);
    }
}
