articles.title: Why your image won't update in Gmail, Apple Mail, GitHub and Slack
articles.description: When Gmail, Apple Mail, GitHub's Camo, Slack and Facebook fetch your image, how long they keep it, and the two URL patterns that stop stale images.
articles.body_html:
You replaced the image on your server. Your browser shows the new version. The README, the email sitting in your inbox, the Slack message and the LinkedIn preview all still show the old one, and a hard refresh changes nothing.

Your browser was never involved. When an image appears inside someone else's product, the reader almost never asks your server for it. A proxy run by Google, Apple, GitHub, Slack or Meta fetches it once and hands its copy to everyone who looks. The proxy decides when to ask you again, and several of them never read your Cache-Control header.

We first published this on the HTML to Image blog as Why your image won't update: how Gmail, Apple Mail, GitHub and Slack cache images. This is the same guide: the per-platform cheat sheet, the header measurements and the two URL patterns that fix it.

Two minutes or thirty days

The spread is what catches people out.

The blue bars are clocks somebody chose. Shields.io sends max-age=120 on a badge that changes and max-age=432000 on one that never does, and GitHub's proxy honours both. The grey bars are clocks you cannot touch: Facebook refreshes on its own 30-day cycle, X on roughly seven days, and Apple Mail keeps whatever it prefetched for two to three days whatever headers you send.

Those two colours give the rule for everything that follows. Where the platform reads your headers, set them. Where it does not, change the URL.

The chart itself is an image URL like any other. It comes from RenderChart's chart image API, which turns chart parameters into a PNG at a URL. Even here it has been through a proxy: dev.to serves every image in a post from its own media2.dev.to copy, so you are looking at dev.to's version of the file, not RenderChart's.

The cheat sheet

Each row comes from the platform's own documentation or a published test. The GitHub row was also checked with live requests on 28 October 2026. Where a platform publishes nothing, the table says so.

Where the image shows Who fetches it When Reads your Cache-Control? How to get a new image shown
Gmail (web and apps) Google's image proxy, user agent contains GoogleImageProxy When the email is opened Yes, no-cache makes it fetch again Send no-cache, or use a new URL
Apple Mail with Mail Privacy Protection Apple's proxy, user agent a bare Mozilla/5.0 In the background after delivery, before any open No Nothing reaches an email already delivered
Outlook desktop The reader's own machine On every open Yes Not needed
Outlook.com Microsoft's image proxy On open Not documented New URL
Yahoo Mail Yahoo's caching proxy On open Not documented New URL
GitHub READMEs, issues, comments Camo, camo.githubusercontent.com First view after its copy expires Yes, your header is passed through Short max-age, curl -X PURGE on the Camo URL, or a new URL
Slack messages and previews Slack-ImgProxy and Slackbot When the message is shown Not documented New URL
Discord embeds Discord's media proxy (the embed's proxy_url) Not documented Not documented New URL
Facebook link previews facebookexternalhit When the link is first shared No, it refreshes every 30 days Sharing Debugger, then a new image URL
X cards Twitterbot When the link is first shared No, it re-indexes about every 7 days New image URL
LinkedIn previews LinkedInBot When the link is first shared Not documented Post Inspector

Email clients disagree with each other

Gmail fetches on open and listens to no-cache

Since December 2013, Gmail on the web and in its apps loads every remote image through Google's proxy. The image in the message points at a googleusercontent.com address with your original URL after a #, and the proxy only calls your server when someone opens the email. Filippo Valsorda's test from the week it launched also showed the proxy re-encoding the file. The image the reader saw had a different hash and size from the one he served. Google changes your bytes.

The first version told every client to keep each image for 24 hours, which froze countdown timers and live charts. Gmail changed that in March 2014: a no-cache response now makes it fetch again on the next open. Reelevant, which serves live images in email, sends this on every response:

Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store, max-age=0
Pragma: no-cache
Expires: -1

The request comes from Google's address, not the reader's. Anything you vary by the requester's location, such as local weather or the nearest store, sees a Google data centre.

Apple Mail fetches before anyone opens the email

With Mail Privacy Protection on, Apple Mail downloads remote images in the background after a message arrives, through Apple's proxy, whether or not the person ever opens it. In FreshInbox's tests the download usually came about 20 minutes after delivery, sometimes hours later. Opening the email made no new request. The copy lasted two to three days, Cache-Control was ignored, and an image URL used in several emails was fetched once for all of them. Those tests ran on the iOS 15 beta in 2021, and Reelevant's current documentation still lists Apple as caching images soon after delivery despite no-cache headers.

So in Apple Mail a countdown timer shows the time left at delivery, and a "live" chart shows the numbers from when the email landed. Headers cannot change that. What you can do is make the frozen version true: draw the timestamp into the image ("Figures at 09:00 on Monday 2 November") and write the surrounding copy so it still reads correctly a day later. Give each send its own image URL as well, so last week's prefetched copy is never reused for this week's email.

Outlook and Yahoo

Outlook for desktop has no proxy, unless your organisation's security tooling adds one. It fetches from your server on every open and respects no-cache.

Outlook.com loads external images through a Microsoft proxy, and Yahoo Mail has served images from its own caching proxy since 2018. Neither publishes how long it keeps a copy. Reelevant reports that Outlook on the web sometimes returns a cached image and Yahoo often does. Treat both as caches you cannot clear.

For the design side of email images, the guide to images that render in every email client covers retina scaling and dark mode.

GitHub's Camo copies your headers

Every external image in GitHub Markdown, from READMEs to issue comments, is rewritten to a camo.githubusercontent.com address: an HMAC of the original URL, then the original URL in hex. The first viewer after a copy expires triggers a fetch, and everyone else gets the copy from GitHub's CDN.

Camo trusts your server. It keeps its copy for as long as your headers say, and here is a Shields.io commit-activity badge requested through Camo twice, three seconds apart, with the headers trimmed:

HTTP/2 200
cache-control: max-age=120, s-maxage=120
content-type: image/svg+xml;charset=utf-8
via: 1.1 varnish
age: 0
x-cache: MISS

HTTP/2 200
cache-control: max-age=120, s-maxage=120
via: 1.1 varnish
age: 3
x-cache: HIT
x-cache-hits: 1

That cache-control line is Shields.io's own. The same badge requested straight from img.shields.io returns max-age=120, and the GitHub Actions status badge returns max-age=60. Static badges go out with max-age=432000, five days, because nothing about them will change. A badge or stats card on a README stays current only as far as its server's max-age allows.

If your image server sends no Cache-Control header at all, GitHub's troubleshooting page tells you to add Cache-Control: no-cache. When a wrong image has to go immediately, right-click it on GitHub, copy the image address (that is the Camo URL) and purge it:

curl -X PURGE "https://camo.githubusercontent.com/<hmac>/<hex-encoded-url>"

Camo replies with {"status": "ok", ...}. GitHub warns that a purge forces every viewer to re-request the image, so keep it for mistakes. Let max-age handle routine updates.

Assume Slack and Discord keep a copy

Slack fetches images through Slack-ImgProxy and link previews through Slackbot, and publishes no cache lifetime for either. The one documented rule concerns previews: a link shared in the same conversation within the past hour does not expand again. If you post through Block Kit, the image block takes an image_url of up to 3,000 characters pointing at a PNG, JPG or GIF. SVG is not on that list, so the SVG badge from your README is the wrong format for a Slack image block.

Discord's API describes each embed image's proxy_url as a proxied copy of the image, and documents nothing about how long that copy lives.

For both, a changed image needs a changed URL. Any difference counts, even a query string your server ignores (?v=2026-10-28), though the first pattern below does it properly.

Link previews hold on the longest

A link preview stacks two caches: the platform's copy of your page's og:image tag, and its copy of the image that tag points at.

Facebook is the slowest. Its crawler refreshes link metadata every 30 days. To force it sooner, run the page through the Sharing Debugger or call POST /?id={url}&scrape=true on the Graph API. Meta's own advice for a replaced image is to give it a different URL, so the cached file is not reused. X's crawler re-indexes card tags roughly every seven days and gives the same advice: add a parameter to the image URL. LinkedIn's Post Inspector fetches the page again on demand.

Caching is only one way a preview goes wrong. Relative og:image paths, missing dimensions, the wrong aspect ratio and tags added by JavaScript are covered in why your OG image isn't showing, and the Open Graph checker shows what a crawler sees on your page right now.

Two URL patterns that make the cache work for you

Every fix above is one of two moves.

New content, new URL

If the URL changes whenever the image changes, no proxy can show a stale version, because no proxy has seen the new URL yet. You can then cache as hard as you like, since the content behind any one URL never changes.

Derive the version from the inputs, so the same data always gives the same URL and any change gives a new one:

import { createHash } from 'node:crypto';

function versionedImageUrl(base, data) {
  const v = createHash('sha256')
    .update(JSON.stringify(data))
    .digest('hex')
    .slice(0, 12);
  return `${base}?v=${v}`;
}

versionedImageUrl('https://example.com/og/launch-week.png', { title: 'Launch week', stars: 1240 });
// https://example.com/og/launch-week.png?v=f4fb944a18e4

versionedImageUrl('https://example.com/og/launch-week.png', { title: 'Launch week', stars: 1241 });
// https://example.com/og/launch-week.png?v=d7b608bef371

Then serve each versioned URL with a long lifetime:

Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable

Rendering APIs give you this pattern without the hashing. Every render from HTML to Image comes back at its own CDN address, so a redesigned email banner or a corrected certificate gets a URL no proxy has a copy of. A RenderChart chart URL carries its data in the query string (type=bar&x=Mon,Tue,Wed&y=4200,3900,5100), so next week's numbers are a different URL by construction, and a weekly chart in an email never shows last week's figures, in Gmail or in Apple Mail.

The pattern needs you to control where the URL gets written: the email template, the message your bot posts, the meta tag on the page.

Same URL, short max-age

Sometimes you cannot change the URL. It is pasted into a README, a Notion page, a wiki or somebody's email signature, and it has to keep working there. Then the content behind the URL changes, and your only lever is a short max-age for the proxies that read it:

location /badges/ {
    add_header Cache-Control "public, max-age=300" always;
}

Pick the number by weighing how stale you can tolerate against how much traffic you want reaching your server. Shields.io uses 60 to 120 seconds for badges that change. RenderChart's live short URLs send max-age=300 for the same reason: edit the data behind one and the same URL shows the new chart within about five minutes, wherever the proxy honours the header.

This pattern stops where the header stops being read. In Apple Mail and in link previews, a fixed URL shows whatever was fetched first.

Finding out what the proxy has

Before you blame a cache, check what the proxy actually holds.

Request the proxied URL rather than your own. Copy the image address from the place where it looks wrong, a Camo URL on GitHub or a googleusercontent.com URL in Gmail, and run curl -sI on it. The age, x-cache and cache-control headers show if you are looking at a copy, and how old it is.

Then log user agents on your image route. Each fetcher names itself: GoogleImageProxy, Slack-ImgProxy, Slackbot-LinkExpanding, facebookexternalhit, Twitterbot, LinkedInBot and Discordbot, with Apple Mail's requests arriving as a bare Mozilla/5.0. If opening the email in Gmail produces no request, Gmail is serving a copy it already has. An Apple request a few minutes after delivery tells you exactly when the frozen version was taken.

The original lives on the HTML to Image blog.

Have you hit a proxy that ignored your headers in a way that isn't in the table? Tell us which one in the comments.

articles.title: George Hotz Calls Coding Agents a Costly Mistake. He's Right About Who Pays
articles.description: Hotz says agent code is broken in ways that are harder to detect. Karpathy calls it bloaty. Same diagnosis: the risk is the reviewer who can't spot it.
articles.body_html:
• Book: LLM Observability Pocket Guide
  • Also by me: Thinking in Go (2-book series) — Complete Guide to Go Programming + Hexagonal Architecture in Go
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

"I'm calling it now, the adoption of AI agents into software development will be one of the most costly mistakes in the field's history." That's George Hotz, opening The Eternal Sloptember on May 24, 2026. Decrypt and The Decoder covered it the next day.

The post is five months old now. The line from it I keep coming back to: "The output is broken, but in a way that's getting harder and harder to detect."

Most replies at the time argued about whether Hotz is right that agents can't program. I think that's the less interesting part. The sharper claim is buried a few paragraphs in, and it's about who catches the breakage.

What Hotz actually said

Hotz didn't write this from the sidelines. He says he spent about six months trying to make agents work, across models, harnesses and prompts. He used them on parts of tinygrad, his deep learning framework, and on reverse-engineering the firmware of a USB-to-PCIe chip. Each time, he writes, he felt he could have done it better and faster by hand.

His description of the pattern will sound familiar if you've run an agent on a real codebase. In his words, "the agent frontloads all the progress." Most of the work appears fast. Then you're pulling a slot machine lever, hoping the last stretch of polish shows up. In his telling, it never quite does.

Strong engineers, he argues, read code carefully and keep correcting it, and that acts as a self-check. "The bottom performers won't have that self check." Those are the people who can now turn out far more code than before, and he expects the average quality at large companies to drop as their volume rises. He also asks: "Do you think macOS will get better or worse in the next 2 years?"

Hotz also says he is now in the "LeCun/Marcus camp" (The Decoder): he thinks real programming agents will need world models, not better language models.

The optimist says the same thing

Andrej Karpathy sits on the other side. He has argued that agents have already changed how software gets written. Five days before Hotz's post, he joined Anthropic's pre-training team (Decrypt).

Here is Karpathy at Sequoia's AI Ascent 2026, in a talk with Stephanie Zhan that The Decoder quoted in its coverage. Looking at what agents write, "sometimes I get a little bit of a heart attack because it's not super amazing code necessarily all the time. And it's very bloaty. And there's a lot of copy-paste. And there's awkward abstractions that are brittle." (transcript)

In the same talk, he says what the human is left holding: "You basically still have to be in charge of the aesthetics, the judgment, the taste, and a little bit of oversight." And he paraphrases a tweet: "you can outsource your thinking, but you can't outsource your understanding."

Put the two quotes side by side. The pessimist says the output is broken in ways that are hard to see. The optimist says the output works but is bloated, copy-pasted and brittle, and that a human with understanding has to stay in charge. They disagree about the trajectory. They describe the same code.


Hotz and Karpathy describe the same defect. What differs is who looks closely enough to see it.

The model isn't the one who pays

The cost Hotz predicts lands at an approval. Somewhere, a person who can't tell brittle code from good code clicks merge on a diff that looks fine. The model produced the bug; the approval is what lets it into production, and the team that runs that code is the one that pays.

Hotz's own framing points there. High performers catch the errors because they know what correct looks like in that codebase. Karpathy says the same in his own words: you can't outsource the understanding. Neither of them says the fix is a better model.

So the knob most teams turn is the wrong one. Agent rollouts get planned by seat count: who gets a license, how many tasks a day, which agents are allowed. None of that says anything about whether the person approving the diff could have written it.

The knob I'd turn instead is autonomy per area of code, tied to how well the reviewer knows that area:

Reviewer knows this code Agent autonomy
Owns it, has debugged it in production Larger tasks, review at the end of each turn
Has worked in it, not an owner Small tasks, plan approved first, owner signs off
New to it Agent explains and proposes, human writes or pairs

None of this needs new tooling to start. GitHub already lets you route review by path. A CODEOWNERS file in .github/ names who owns what:

# Agent or not, these paths need someone who knows them
/src/billing/     @your-org/payments
/src/auth/        @your-org/identity
/firmware/        @your-org/firmware

Turn on "Require review from Code Owners" in the branch protection rule, and a diff touching billing can't land without an approval from the team that owns billing. The rule doesn't care whether a human or an agent wrote the diff, only whether someone from that team signed off.

Where Hermes fits

I build Hermes IDE, so weigh this section with that in mind. Hermes is a desktop app that runs agents like Claude Code and Codex in their own terminals, each task on its own hermes/<name> branch and worktree.

The part relevant here is review. Hotz's complaint is partly about size: the agent frontloads a lot of change, and a big diff is where breakage hides. Hermes saves every agent turn, so you can diff or restore a single turn, with undo. The Review Desk (⌘G, Ctrl+Shift+G on Windows and Linux) shows changes by turn or by file, with risk flags, and you can send a line comment back to the agent that wrote the line.


The Review Desk (⌘G) in By turn view: two Claude Code turns, turn 1's diff of src/db.ts, the changed files and a commit message drafted from the turns.

Reading turn by turn maps onto the table above. An owner can let the agent take bigger turns and read each one as it lands. Someone newer to the code can keep turns small and push questions back as line comments instead of approving what they don't follow.

Hermes doesn't know whether the code is right. Risk flags point your eyes somewhere; they don't replace knowing the codebase. Hermes is free to download, source-available under BSL 1.1 (GitHub), and runs on macOS, Windows and Linux. It isn't affiliated with Nous Research or its Hermes Agent.

Where I think Hotz goes too far

"Agents cannot program" is a claim about the model. His evidence is about the work: a framework he wrote and knows deeply, and firmware reverse-engineering, which is about as far from boilerplate as code gets. On that work, he was the reviewer best placed to see what the agent got wrong, and he decided he'd rather do it himself. That's a reasonable call for him. It doesn't follow that nobody should use agents anywhere.

Karpathy's position covers the other case: agents are useful, and the human still owns the judgment. Both positions fail in the same way when the human approving the code doesn't have that judgment for the code in front of them.

If Hotz's prediction comes true, it will come true one merge at a time, approved by someone who couldn't have written the diff, on a team that counted its rollout in seats.

How does your team decide who can approve agent work today: by seniority, by code ownership, or not at all? Tell me in the comments.

If this was useful

Hotz's warning is about breakage that gets harder to detect, and detection is a measurement problem as much as a review one. The LLM Observability Pocket Guide covers the tracing and evals tools that tell you what an LLM system actually did, so you're not relying on a diff that merely looks fine. If you want to review agent turns one at a time, Hermes IDE is free on macOS, Windows and Linux.

articles.description: so i made a programming language.  it's called catscript. you print with cat, functions are called...
articles.body_html:
so i made a programming language.

it's called catscript. you print with cat, functions are called hunt, lists are called litter, and if you type fetch anywhere in your code it refuses to run, because this is a cat household.

try it in your browser: https://yupthatscole.github.io/catscript

(no install. the first load takes a few seconds because it's loading python into your browser.)

what it looks like 

hunt double(x) {
    bring x * 2
}

kittens = litter["mochi", "pip", "clover"]
cat("there are", size(kittens), "kittens")
cat("double 21 is", double(21))

there are 3 kittens
double 21 is 42

   /\_/\
  ( ^.^ )  purr. it worked.
   > ^ <

every program ends with a cat. a happy one if it worked. an angry one if it didn't.

the cat words

  • cat(x) prints something (it's also the linux command for printing files, so it's a pun twice)
  • pspsps("name? ") asks the user for input. you're literally calling them over
  • hunt makes a function, bring returns something, because cats bring you things
  • litter[1, 2, 3] is a list
  • purr and hiss are true and false
  • empty_bowl is null
  • knock(x) deletes a variable. knocks it off the table
  • try { } pounce { } catches errors

errors

errors get a hiss code, a line number, and an insult.

  HISS-404 (line 2): never heard of 'y'. did you make it up?
  did you write this while walking across the keyboard?

   /\_/\
  ( >.< )  HISS.
   > ^ <

dividing by zero is HISS-500: you can't split the fish into zero pieces. a function that calls itself forever is HISS-508: your cat is chasing its tail.

and the dog words (fetch, bark, goodboy, woof, sit, wag) are just banned:

  HISS-403 (line 1, col 1): 'fetch'?? this is a cat household.

how it works

i always assumed making a programming language was some crazy thing. it's actually three parts:

  1. the lexer reads your code and chops it into pieces. cat("hi") becomes cat, (, "hi", )
  2. the parser turns those pieces into a tree, so it knows 1 + 2 * 3 means do the 2 * 3 first
  3. the interpreter walks through the tree and actually runs it

the whole thing is about 1,100 lines of python with no libraries.

the bug

the first time i typed my own code into the playground instead of using the examples, it crashed with a huge python error.

turns out the lexer looks two characters ahead to catch stuff like == and >=. if your code ended on something like ) with nothing after it, it looked at a character that didn't exist and fell off the end of the file.

it worked fine for me because all my example files ended with a blank line. so it only broke the second someone else used it. classic.

now if catscript itself ever crashes, you get HISS-999: catscript tripped over its own tail. this one's not your fault. instead of a wall of python.

it also runs in your browser and vs code

the playground runs the exact same python files in your browser using pyodide, so there's no separate version to keep updated.

there's also a vs code extension that gives .meow files syntax highlighting, a little cat icon, and a run button. dog words get a red squiggle.

try it

  • playground: https://yupthatscole.github.io/catscript
  • code: https://github.com/yupthatscole/catscript

write something in catscript and put it in the comments. i want to see what you make

meow

articles.title: Cell Towers Are Optional: At 16, I Built a Hybrid 800m Off-Grid Mesh Protocol for Smartphones (No LoRa Required)
articles.description: How I combined BLE, Wi-Fi Direct, UWB, and Delay-Tolerant Networking into AirPin — a zero-server P2P...
articles.body_html:
How I combined BLE, Wi-Fi Direct, UWB, and Delay-Tolerant Networking into AirPin — a zero-server P2P engine that turns regular phones into an encrypted relay network.

What happens when cell towers go down, Wi-Fi is dead, or you are deep in the wilderness—and you don't have specialized LoRa hardware like a Meshtastic node in your backpack?

Every modern smartphone already carries a ridiculous amount of radio silicon: Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE), Wi-Fi Direct, and Ultra-Wideband (UWB). Yet almost every off-grid messenger on the market locks itself into a single transport layer (usually BLE), suffering from terrible bandwidth, short range, or rapid battery drain.

Over the past year, I decided to fix this. I designed and built AirPin—a hybrid, multi-protocol P2P mesh routing engine that dynamically switches between radio interfaces and uses Delay-Tolerant Networking (DTN) to bounce encrypted messages from phone to phone without the internet or central servers. It serves as the core engine of my upcoming super-app ecosystem, Prux.

Here is the story and technical breakdown of how AirPin works under the hood, how multi-hop relay behaves in real-world field tests, and the architectural problems I had to solve along the way.

Why Single-Radio Offline Messengers Fail

If you look at classic off-grid apps like Bridgefy or Briar, they hit a hard physics wall:

  • BLE-only mesh: Great for background discovery and low battery usage, but throughput is tiny, and real-world range drops sharply in dense environments.
  • Wi-Fi Direct: High bandwidth and up to 200+ meters line-of-sight range, but keeping Wi-Fi Direct awake 24/7 destroys smartphone batteries and triggers aggressive OS background killers on iOS and Android.

Instead of choosing one radio, I built AirPin as a dynamic link-layer router that treats BLE, UWB, and Wi-Fi Direct as a single adaptive pipeline.

Inside the AirPin 4-Layer Stack

AirPin operates automatically in the background across four distinct stages, choosing the right radio for the right moment:

  1. Always-On Discovery: Devices running Prux broadcast lightweight, rotating cryptographic beacons over Bluetooth Low Energy. Because BLE uses almost zero power, it acts as a silent radar. Short text messages and initial handshakes go straight through BLE without waking heavier radios.
  2. Spatial Ranging & Direction (UWB): When supported by the phone's hardware, Ultra-Wideband gives centimeter-accurate distance and directional vectors between peers. Instead of blindly flooding packets to every phone nearby, AirPin knows which nodes are physically moving toward the destination or holding the strongest link.
  3. High-Speed Burst Escalation (Wi-Fi Direct): When you send voice notes, images, or need maximum single-hop distance (up to 200+ meters in open terrain), AirPin negotiates a handshake over BLE, spins up a temporary Wi-Fi Direct P2P tunnel for a few seconds, blasts the encrypted payload across, and immediately puts the high-power radio back to sleep.
  4. Store-and-Forward Relay (DTN): What if there is no continuous chain of users between you and your friend right now? AirPin uses Delay-Tolerant Networking. A message hops across intermediate phones like a baton in a relay race (reaching 750–800 meters across 4 hops in field tests). If the chain breaks, an intermediate phone securely caches the encrypted packet in an isolated sandbox and forwards it minutes later when it walks past another user.

Zero-Server Security: Can Strangers Read My Relayed Messages?

Bouncing your private messages through strangers' phones sounds terrifying at first. To make it bulletproof, AirPin enforces strict cryptographic isolation:

  • End-to-End Encryption (E2EE) at the Edge: Messages are encrypted on the sender's device before they ever touch the AirPin router. Intermediate relay phones only see an opaque encrypted envelope, a randomized packet hash (to prevent infinite broadcast loops), and a hop counter (TTL).
  • Zero Cloud Storage: Off-grid messages never touch a central server. Even when Prux operates in standard online mode, message history stays strictly on user devices.
  • SunFlower Visual Codes: You can't trust a central key server when you are offline. I created custom visual SunFlower codes (a specialized alternative to standard QR codes) so users can verify identities and exchange encryption keys face-to-face in a split second.

Real-World Field Tests & Recognition from Chipmakers

Testing a mesh protocol in an IDE simulator is easy; testing it in the real world is brutal. I live on the Pacific coast of the Russian Far East, surrounded by steep hills, dense taiga, and coastline where dead cellular zones are an everyday reality.

In field tests across urban and open terrain, AirPin achieved:

  • 40–80 meters single-hop range indoors and in dense city blocks.
  • 200+ meters single-hop range in open line-of-sight.
  • 750–800 meters end-to-end delivery across a 4-hop chain of smartphones without internet or cell service.

Earlier this year, I pitched and defended the AirPin architecture in English at the 40th CASTIC international science and engineering competition in China. Out of 600+ projects, AirPin placed in the Top 20 and won the Unisoc Innovation Award directly from UNISOC, one of the world's largest mobile processor and baseband chipmakers. The technology is also officially registered with Rospatent (Software Reg. #2026607225, Patent Pending #2026112785).

Why I Wrapped a Mesh Protocol Inside a "Liquid Glass" Super-App

Here is the dirty secret of every standalone offline messenger: nobody has it installed when an emergency actually happens. People delete single-purpose emergency apps because they don't use them on a normal Tuesday.

To make a smartphone mesh network work in the real world, you need node density—people actually keeping the app on their phones every day. That is why I built Prux around AirPin, featuring a custom "Liquid Glass" UI for iOS, Android, and macOS. Alongside the off-grid messenger, Prux includes daily-driver mini-apps:

  • Prux Mail: Built-in email client aggregating multiple accounts in one clean inbox.
  • Loud Music: Offline-capable music player.

  • ZheykPay: Integrated crypto wallet.

  • Red Panda & Mahjong Blast: Language learning tools and mini-games.

The more people use Prux for music, mail, or everyday chatting, the stronger and wider the invisible AirPin mesh network becomes whenever the grid goes down.

Follow the Build & Join the Beta

I am currently running closed beta tests and fine-tuning background BLE/Wi-Fi Direct wake-locks ahead of the public launch in Spring 2027.

I'm building Prux and AirPin in public and sharing raw engineering logs, range test videos, and UI previews over on X. If you love mesh networking, P2P protocols, or mobile systems engineering, come say hi and follow the journey:

  • Follow me on X (Twitter) for live dev updates: https://x.com/Prux_Messenger
  • Telegram Channel: https://t.me/Prux_channel
  • Official Website: https://www.prux.su

Questions for the devs here:

  • If you've fought iOS and Android background execution limits for BLE/Wi-Fi Direct, what are your cleanest workarounds for keeping discovery alive without killing the battery?
  • Would you be interested in an open standalone SDK for AirPin so you could drop offline mesh messaging into your own mobile apps?

articles.title: I kept correcting AI until I realised what was actually broken
articles.description: You corrected the AI yesterday. Today, it made the exact same mistake again.  Maybe it used an...
articles.body_html:
You corrected the AI yesterday. Today, it made the exact same mistake again.

Maybe it used an outdated price, invented a product feature you do not offer, or missed an important step in a client proposal.

You correct it in the chat, get the answer you wanted, and move on.

But what happens when someone else on your team asks the same question tomorrow?

The AI makes the same mistake all over again. Nobody knows it was already corrected, and someone has to spend time fixing it from scratch.

This is one of the most overlooked problems with using AI in everyday business workflows. Teams spend hours correcting AI outputs, but they rarely have a system to make sure those corrections actually improve future results.

If you want to get more real, dependable work out of AI, you have to stop treating prompts like one-off chat conversations. You need to treat them like code and build a Feedback and Learning Loop.

Why "More AI Output" Usually Means More Work

When teams talk about wanting more AI output, they usually focus on speed. They look at how fast a model types, how many pages it can generate in a minute, or how many questions it answers in an hour.

In practice, raw speed does not help if the answers are unreliable. An AI can draft a ten-page technical spec in five seconds, but that does not save time if an engineer has to spend thirty minutes reading every single line to catch errors.

+------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                      THE AI PRODUCTIVITY TRAP                          |
|                                                                        |
|  High Volume + Unreliable Output = Hours Spent Proofreading Mistakes   |
|  Controlled Volume + Reliable Output = Real Time Saved Every Week      |
+------------------------------------------------------------------------+

When AI outputs become more consistent and predictable, reviewing them becomes much easier. Your team spends less time fixing recurring blunders and more time focusing on the details that genuinely need human attention.

Why In-Chat Corrections Get Lost

It is easy to assume that if you correct an AI once, it will remember the lesson. But in reality, language models do not automatically learn from in-chat corrections.

If you tell an AI that your product price changed from \$99 to \$149, that does not mean the model will remember that change in another session.

Whether that information carries forward depends entirely on how your application is built. Some advanced setups use conversation logs, persistent memory, or external knowledge retrieval (like RAG). But unless your application is specifically designed to store, verify, and reuse those corrections, the model starts every new session with the same baseline.

In traditional software development, when a function returns bad data, you never just rerun it and hope the bug disappears. You look at the code, find the mistake, write a test case, and patch the source.

A Feedback and Learning Loop brings that same engineering discipline to your prompts.

+------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                    THE 5-STEP AI FEEDBACK LOOP                         |
|                                                                        |
|  1. Clear Rules     -> Define strict formats and negative limits       |
|  2. Failure Log     -> Record bad outputs in a shared table            |
|  3. Root Cause Fix  -> Update source facts, system rules, or examples  |
|  4. Regression Test -> Re-run past test questions before deploying     |
|  5. Track Metrics   -> Measure review time and repeat error trends     |
+------------------------------------------------------------------------+

Step 1: Define Clear Rules and Negative Boundaries

Most prompts fail because the instructions are too open-ended. When an AI receives fuzzy instructions, it fills the missing context by guessing. In technical work, guessing leads directly to hallucinations.

Before sharing any prompt with your team or putting it into an automated script, set three clear boundaries:

  1. The exact output structure: Tell the AI how to format the response. If you need a markdown table, state the exact column names. If you need JSON, provide the required keys and data types.
  2. The single source of truth: Give the AI the exact document, database record, or URL it must pull facts from. Instruct it to rely strictly on that source.
  3. Handling missing or conflicting information: Tell the AI what to do when it does not know the answer. Give it an explicit negative rule: "Never invent pricing, dates, or technical specs. If a detail is missing from the provided document, return 'NEEDS_HUMAN_REVIEW'."

Giving the AI an approved escape hatch stops it from inventing facts when the source material is incomplete.

Step 2: Keep a Simple Failure Log

When an AI produces a bad response, the worst thing you can do is backspace it, fix it in private, and move on. That guarantees someone else will hit the exact same failure later in the week.

Set up a shared tracking sheet or a simple issue board where your team can log bad outputs in under thirty seconds.

A practical failure log only needs four simple columns:

Column What to Record Example Entry
The Prompt The exact prompt and context sent "Generate client proposal for monthly maintenance"
The Bad Output What the AI got wrong Quoted \$99/mo instead of the updated \$149/mo rate
The Correct Output The version the human approved Quoted \$149/mo with 24/7 emergency response included
The Root Cause Why the failure happened The connected price sheet was out of date

After logging twenty or thirty mistakes, you will notice that errors are rarely random. They almost always cluster into a few recurring categories: outdated documents, fuzzy instructions, or missing format rules.

Step 3: Fix the Root Cause, Not Just the Prompt String

Once a failure pattern appears in your log, you need to fix the actual source of the problem. In an AI workflow, issues usually trace back to one of three layers:

1. The Source Data Layer

If the AI keeps quoting old prices or obsolete API endpoints, updating the prompt to say "make sure the price is \$149" is a fragile band-aid. The real fix is updating the source document or knowledge base.

However, updating the file is only half the battle. You also have to verify that your system is actually retrieving the updated version, rather than pulling an older cached copy or missing the relevant paragraph during search.

2. The Instruction Layer (System Rules)

If the AI keeps skipping a required disclaimer or misses error handling in generated code, your prompt lacks explicit procedural boundaries. Add a mandatory checklist:

Before returning the final output, verify:
1. Did you include the 30-day refund policy note?
2. Are all database queries parameterized?
3. Did you use the client's current legal company name?

3. The Few-Shot Example Layer (Tone and Style)

If the AI writes stiff, unnatural sentences full of buzzwords, do not just tell it to "sound natural." Instead, include two real-world examples of approved past work inside the prompt. Language models follow patterns in examples much better than they follow abstract adjectives.

Step 4: Test Old Questions Before Rolling Out Changes

Whenever you update a system prompt or change a knowledge source, you risk breaking outputs that were previously working fine. Just like in standard software development, prompt changes require regression testing.

You do not need a massive enterprise testing platform to get started. You can begin with a simple script that replays your logged failure cases against your updated prompt:

import json

# Load past failure cases from our mistake log
with open("test_cases.json", "r") as f:
    test_cases = json.load(f)

for case in test_cases:
    prompt = case["prompt"]
    required_value = case["must_contain"]
    banned_value = case["must_not_contain"]

    # Run the prompt through your updated AI system
    response = run_ai_prompt(prompt)

    # Basic rule-based validation
    if banned_value in response:
        print(f"[FAIL] Output still contains outdated mistake: {banned_value}")
    elif required_value not in response:
        print(f"[FAIL] Output is missing required information: {required_value}")
    else:
        print(f"[PASS] Prompt handled test case correctly: {case['id']}")

Understanding the Limits of Keyword Checks

While simple keyword checks are a great starting point for checking numbers and forbidden phrases, natural language is flexible. An AI might say "The plan is priced at \$149" instead of "The plan costs \$149", and a strict string match would fail even though the answer is completely correct.

For more mature setups, you can combine three layers of evaluation:

  • Rule-based checks: Verify JSON syntax, required fields, and banned keywords.
  • Model-based evaluation (LLM-as-a-judge): Use a separate prompt to ask whether the generated answer factually matches the approved reference answer.
  • Human spot-checks: Review edge cases that automated checks flag as uncertain.

What Does an Automated AI Feedback Loop Look Like?

A manual spreadsheet works well when a team is experimenting with a few prompts. But as your team scales up its use of AI, manually copying and pasting errors into a table becomes impractical.

In a production setting, you can turn this feedback loop into an automated quality-control pipeline:

[User Request]
       │
       ▼
[AI Generates Output]
       │
       ▼
[Automated Validation Checks] ──(Fails rules)──► [Flagged for Human Review]
       │                                                    │
       ▼ (Passes)                                          ▼
[Delivered to User]                              [Human Corrects Output]
       │                                                    │
       │                                                    ▼
       └────────────────────────────────────────► [Stored in Eval Dataset]
                                                            │
                                                            ▼
                                              [Tested Before Deployment]

Here is how the automated flow works step by step:

  1. User triggers the request: An employee or customer interacts with the AI workflow.
  2. Predefined validation checks run: The output is automatically screened against basic rules (valid formatting, presence of required data, absence of banned terms).
  3. Exceptions are flagged: If an output violates a rule or receives a negative user rating (like a thumbs-down), it is automatically routed to a review queue.
  4. Human reviews and corrects: An engineer or domain expert inspects the failure and logs the correct response into an evaluation dataset.
  5. Prompt updates are tested: The engineering team reviews the failure dataset, updates the instructions or source data, and runs the entire test suite before pushing the changes live.

Crucial Rule: Never allow user corrections to automatically rewrite production system prompts on the fly. Doing that creates unpredictable prompt drift. Every update should be reviewed, tested against historical failure cases, and deliberately approved.

Step 5: Track Review Hours and Recurring Mistakes

The goal of a feedback loop is to make AI a genuine productivity boost rather than an ongoing maintenance headache.

To see whether your process is working, track two practical numbers over time:

  1. Review time spent per task: How many minutes do team members spend proofreading, correcting, and re-running AI outputs?
  2. Recurring defect frequency: How often does an error you previously fixed reappear in production?

It is important to be realistic: AI systems are probabilistic, and you will never reduce mistakes to absolute zero. New edge cases will always appear as your business evolves.

However, a healthy feedback loop ensures that mistakes become manageable exceptions rather than daily frustrations. Instead of spending twenty minutes rewriting broken drafts, your team spends thirty seconds reviewing outputs they can reasonably trust.

Moving Beyond One-Off Prompting

At EnactOn, we believe building useful AI automation workflows involves much more than connecting an API and writing a good prompt. The real work is making sure the system uses verified source data, handles exceptions gracefully, and improves steadily through testing and human feedback.

That is what separates an AI workflow that looks impressive in a demo from one that people can actually depend on in their daily work.

Stop relying on the "Regenerate" button. The next time your AI makes a mistake:

  • Capture the error instead of discarding it.
  • Identify whether the breakdown happened in your data, your rules, or your examples.
  • Fix the underlying cause rather than editing the temporary chat tab.
  • Test your changes against past mistakes before rolling them out.

That is how you turn AI from an unpredictable assistant into a reliable part of your team's workflow.

What is the one mistake your team's AI tools keep making no matter how many times you correct them? How are you tracking and testing prompt updates in your team? Let's discuss in the comments below.

articles.title: How nice it is to talk — BeeDialogue lands in BeeEngine 2.11.0
articles.description: Hi. I'm Antonio. I'm 53. I build things out of pure passion.  I don't talk much. But when I do…...
articles.body_html:
Hi. I'm Antonio. I'm 53. I build things out of pure passion.

I don't talk much. But when I do… BeeDialogue comes out.

From “dialogue” to a dialogue plugin

BeeEngine is a small 2D HTML5 Canvas engine I keep shaping in the open. Physics, scenes, sprites, tiles, audio buses, an inventory plugin, a locale plugin. Useful pieces. Quiet pieces.

What was missing for story-shaped games was obvious: a place for NPCs to say something without me inventing a new if tree every weekend.

So v2.11.0 adds BeeDialogue.

Not a chatbot. Not a voice synthesizer. A dialogue tree: speakers, lines, branching choices, straight-line advances. The kind of thing you wire to a blue rectangle that pretends to be a guide on a bridge.

The engine stays blind (on purpose)

BeeEngine has a plugin contract I take seriously. The core does not import plugins. A plugin attaches itself.

import { BeeEngine } from 'beeengine';
import { BeeDialogue, BeeLocale } from 'beeengine/plugins';

const game = new BeeEngine('c', 800, 480);
const locale = new BeeLocale({ /* strings… */, engine: game });

const dialogue = new BeeDialogue({ engine: game, locale, cancelKey: 'Escape' });
// attach() registers it as 'dialogue' — detach() unregisters

No monkey-patch of loop(). No hijacking of update / render. BeeDialogue has no tick of its own and no DOM listeners. Your scene calls the verbs:

  • handleInput(input) from scene.update
  • draw(ctx) from scene.draw (screen space, after the camera)

The motor stays a motor. The plugin stays a plugin. I sleep better.

A tree you can read

You load a tree once. Nodes can be an array (easier to skim) or a map. Literal text / speaker work. Or textKey / speakerKey if you pass an optional BeeLocale (constructor, setLocale, or engine.plugin('locale')).

dialogue.load({
  start: 'intro',
  nodes: [
    {
      id: 'intro',
      speakerKey: 'guide',
      textKey: 'hi',
      choices: [
        { textKey: 'ask_map', next: 'map', data: { topic: 'map' } },
        { textKey: 'bye', next: null, data: { topic: 'bye' } }
      ]
    },
    { id: 'map', speakerKey: 'guide', textKey: 'map', next: 'tip' },
    { id: 'tip', speakerKey: 'guide', textKey: 'tip' }
  ]
});

Rules that saved me from myself:

  • Node without choices → advance() follows next (or ends).
  • Node with choices → choose(index).
  • The wrong verb returns false and warns. Good. I need warnings more than cleverness.
  • start() while already open does a clean restart (end with reason restart, then start again).

Drawing choices (without becoming a second renderer)

BeeDialogue is not BeeText.drawHUD. It draws a simple panel when you ask.

const scene = {
  update(_dt, input) {
    if (input.wasPressed('KeyE') && !dialogue.isOpen()) dialogue.start();
    dialogue.handleInput(input); // Space / Enter advances or confirms; arrows move the highlight
  },
  draw(ctx) {
    dialogue.draw(ctx, { x: 40, width: ctx.canvas.width - 80 });
  }
};

onChange reports start, node, choice, advance, and end (with a reason: finished, cancel, restart, reload, missing-node…). Enough to feed a future quest plugin without hard-wiring anything today.

And yes — toJSON / fromJSON save the tree and where you stood, so you can tuck the DTO into BeeSave next to inventory slots. Definitions stay yours; restore reopens on the saved node and emits node (not a fake second start).

About that demo label

The demo is examples/dialogue.html. Press E.

The English string does not say “E to talk”.

It says “E to interact”.

Because BeeDialogue does not talk. It does not clear its throat. It does not do regional accents. It advances nodes. The joke writes itself, and I left it in the locale table on purpose (talk: 'E to interact'). Press L if you want Italian. The guide still will not speak aloud. She will, however, mention a village east of a bridge, which is already more social than most of my week.

Why this shape

I like small contracts:

Piece Job
BeeLocale t(key) — pure read
BeeInventory stacks, use, equip — no draw loop
BeeDialogue tree state — you draw and feed input

Together they feel like a tiny RPG toolkit without pretending to be one. Next ideas on the shelf (one at a time): Quest, Post FX, scene Transition, action remapping… Lights, Spine, Net later. Those touch more surface area. Dialogue was the polite guest who hangs its coat on attach and leaves with detach.

Try it

  • Repo: BeeEngine-V2.5.0 (package beeengine 2.11.0)
  • Demo: examples/dialogue.html
  • Tests: node scripts/test-beedialogue.mjs
  • Import: import { BeeDialogue } from 'beeengine/plugins'

If you break it, tell me how. If you use it in a jam game with three lines of dialogue and a torch tip, tell me that too. Short messages welcome — I don't talk much.

But when I do… you already know what comes out.

— Antonio

articles.title: Canada Stopped Falling Back. Your Scheduler Is Now in the On-Call Rotation.
articles.description: Canada has not abolished Daylight Saving Time. It has made the time-zone support matrix more...
articles.body_html:
Canada has not abolished Daylight Saving Time. It has made the time-zone support matrix more interesting, which is exactly the sort of distinction a scheduler will exploit at 02:00 on a Sunday.

On November 1, 2026, British Columbia, Alberta, Manitoba and the Northwest Territories did not turn their clocks back. They now use fixed offsets of UTC-7, UTC-6, UTC-5 and UTC-6 respectively. Yukon has used UTC-7 throughout the year since 2020. This is not a national policy. Ontario, for example, still follows the North American seasonal schedule.

For a person, the change means fewer arguments with the microwave clock. For a software team, it means that civil-time rules changed underneath future meetings, recurring jobs, reports, settlement windows and every system that confidently stores 09:00 without first asking "09:00 where?"

The good news is that time-zone databases exist. The bad news is that they require us to install them, update them and believe they are part of the product. Apparently time has dependencies now. Again.

What changed in Canada

Jurisdiction New year-round offset Effective change
Most of British Columbia UTC-7 March 2026, following the spring change
Alberta UTC-6 November 1, 2026
Manitoba UTC-5 November 1, 2026
Northwest Territories UTC-6 Regulations in force August 21, 2026; no fall-back November 1
Yukon UTC-7 Since 2020

The labels vary. B.C. calls its new zone Pacific Time. Alberta calls UTC-6 Alberta Time. Manitoba calls UTC-5 Manitoba Standard Time, even though it preserves what had been daylight time. That naming exercise is understandable. It is also a useful reminder that an abbreviation is not a reliable time-zone model.

Use an IANA zone identifier such as America/Vancouver, America/Edmonton or America/Winnipeg in data and code. Do not use PST, MST, or a bare offset as a substitute for a location's rules. Those labels are small traps wearing name badges.

Canada is not alone, and the rules do not move together

Mexico ended seasonal time changes in most of the country in 2022, while many northern border municipalities retained a seasonal schedule to align with the United States. Cuba's October 2026 IANA update says it will remain on UTC-4 through November 7, 2027 rather than falling back this weekend. Meanwhile, the European Union still changes clocks: its 2018 proposal to stop the practice has no final decision or timetable.

This is why "DST is ending" is too vague to be useful in a code review. The question is always: which legal jurisdiction, which location-based time zone, which effective date, and which version of the rules does this runtime know?

IANA's Time Zone Database recorded British Columbia in its 2026b release, Alberta in 2026c, the Northwest Territories in 2026d, and Manitoba in 2026e. That sequence is the part I find oddly revealing. Governments announce a change. Time-zone maintainers publish the rules. Operating systems, language runtimes, containers, browsers, phones, calendar vendors and long-lived services catch up at different times. Somewhere in the middle, a recurring meeting scheduled six months ago starts negotiating with a laptop that has not restarted since the last fiscal year.

That is not a clock problem. It is a deployment problem with better branding.

What can break

Storing timestamps in UTC remains the right default for an event that happened at a specific instant. It does not preserve the meaning of a rule such as "run at 09:00 every weekday in Vancouver." That rule needs both a local time and an IANA zone. A UTC timestamp alone cannot tell you what the organiser meant after a jurisdiction changes its rules.

The systems I would inspect first are the ones with future intent:

  • Recurring calendar events and reminders created before the rule update.
  • Cron-like jobs defined in local time.
  • Payroll, billing, market, booking and service windows that describe a local business day.
  • Reports grouped by local date or hour.
  • Mobile and desktop clients that ship their own time-zone data.
  • Containers and older hosts with a stale tzdata package.

Microsoft's own guidance for the Canadian changes tells Outlook users to choose the new zone and verify or migrate future and recurring meetings. That is an unusually direct production test case from a calendar vendor. Do not assume an event is safe merely because its display looks correct this afternoon.

A small model that saves a larger incident

For a scheduled appointment or recurring business rule, keep the local meaning alongside the instant you calculate from it.

// Illustrative model. The zone is part of the business rule.
type Appointment = {
  localStart: "2027-01-15T09:00";
  timeZone: "America/Vancouver";
};

// Resolve this with a current IANA time-zone database,
// then store the resulting UTC instant for the occurrence.

The example is deliberately boring. Boring is a feature when a customer expects a 09:00 appointment to remain a 09:00 appointment. The application can calculate a UTC instant for each occurrence, but it should retain the local rule and zone that created it. If the time-zone data changes, regenerate future occurrences and show the difference before quietly moving anyone's meeting.

Also test the calendar around the transition. Create fixtures before and after the effective date, including a recurring event created before the update that extends past it. Assert the local display, the UTC instant, the notification time and the downstream integration payload. A passing unit test that only checks new Date() in the developer's current zone is how time gets promoted to principal engineer.

The practical checklist

  1. Inventory where each service gets its time-zone data: operating system, container base image, runtime, database, client or vendor API.
  2. Patch those dependencies deliberately and record the version. IANA publishes the rules, but it does not teleport them into a six-month-old container.
  3. Store instants in UTC. Store a location-based IANA zone whenever a human set a future local-time rule.
  4. Recalculate and review future recurring events after a rule change. Pay special attention to events created before the vendor update.
  5. Test local business boundaries, not only timestamp formatting.

The annual clock change may be disappearing in more places. Civil time is not becoming simpler. It is becoming more explicit, which is a much better deal for everyone except the code that has been pretending PST was a data type.

Sources

  • British Columbia: permanent year-round daylight saving time
  • Alberta: permanent Alberta Time
  • Manitoba: no more falling back
  • Northwest Territories: seasonal time change ended
  • Yukon Standard Time
  • IANA Time Zone Database releases
  • Mexico's 2022 time-zone law summary
  • EU Council: seasonal clock changes remain in force
  • Microsoft: Outlook guidance for Canadian changes

articles.title: Node Runs .ts Files Natively. Inside node_modules It Refuses, on Purpose
articles.description: Node strips TypeScript types by swapping them for whitespace. It still refuses .ts files under node_modules, by design. Here's what to ship instead.
articles.body_html:
• Book: TypeScript in Production
  • Also by me: The TypeScript Library — the 5-book collection
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

You stop compiling. Your package's exports points straight at ./src/index.ts, every script in the monorepo runs with plain node, and the tests are green. Then someone installs the package from the registry, runs their app, and Node stops with ERR_UNSUPPORTED_NODE_MODULES_TYPE_STRIPPING.

No flag turns it off. The Node.js TypeScript docs give the reason in one sentence: "To discourage package authors from publishing packages written in TypeScript, Node.js refuses to handle TypeScript files inside folders under a node_modules path."

The refusal makes sense once you see how little Node does to a .ts file.

How Node runs a .ts file without compiling it

Type stripping landed in v22.6.0, became the default in v23.6.0 and v22.18.0, and was marked stable in v25.2.0 and v24.12.0. Current releases of every LTS line on the Node releases page (22, 24 and 26, with v26.13.0 the newest LTS release listed there at the time of writing) have it on by default. You opt out with --no-strip-types.

The mechanism is deliberately dumb. Node doesn't compile anything. It finds the TypeScript syntax and overwrites it with spaces. This is the example from the node:module docs:

import { stripTypeScriptTypes } from 'node:module';
const code = 'const a: number = 1;';
const strippedCode = stripTypeScriptTypes(code);
console.log(strippedCode);
// Prints: const a         = 1;

The = 1 is still in the column where you typed it. An interface that spans twelve lines becomes twelve blank lines. Because nothing moves, a stack trace points at the right line of your .ts file, and the docs note that "source maps are unnecessary for correct line numbers in stack traces; and Node.js does not generate them." The parser doing this is Amaro, a wrapper around SWC's TypeScript parser compiled to WebAssembly.

Being dumb has consequences, and they're all in the docs. There is no type checking. Node ignores tsconfig.json, so paths aliases don't work. Imports need their real extension (./user.ts, not ./user). Type-only imports must say import type, or Node treats them as values and fails at runtime. .tsx is unsupported.


Type stripping removes the annotations and leaves the gaps, so every line and column stays where it was.

The syntax whitespace can't erase

If stripping is "replace with spaces", anything that needs Node to write new JavaScript is out. The Node docs list the main cases: enums, namespaces with runtime code, parameter properties and import aliases. Hitting one throws ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX.

The reason is visible in what tsc emits for them. An enum is a real object at runtime, so the compiler has to generate the code that builds it. A parameter property is shorthand for an assignment the compiler writes into the constructor. Neither exists in your source as JavaScript, so blanking characters can't produce it.

// Rejected by type stripping
class User {
  constructor(public name: string) {}
}

enum Role { Admin, Viewer }

The erasable versions say the same thing in syntax that's already JavaScript once the types are gone:

class User {
  name: string;
  constructor(name: string) {
    this.name = name;
  }
}

const Role = { Admin: 0, Viewer: 1 } as const;
type Role = (typeof Role)[keyof typeof Role];

You don't want to find these one runtime crash at a time. TypeScript 5.8 added erasableSyntaxOnly for exactly this: with it on, tsc errors on enums, namespaces and modules with runtime code, parameter properties, import = and export =. The tsconfig reference adds <number>value-style assertions to the list. The Node docs recommend TypeScript 5.8 or newer with erasableSyntaxOnly, verbatimModuleSyntax and rewriteRelativeImportExtensions turned on.

There used to be an escape hatch. --experimental-transform-types arrived in v22.7.0 and was removed in v26.0.0, along with the transform mode of stripTypeScriptTypes. On Node 26 the built-in path is strip-only. For full TypeScript, the docs point you to a third-party runner such as tsx.

Reproduce the refusal (your monorepo hides it)

Here's a two-package npm workspace where the library ships raw TypeScript:

greet-demo/
├── package.json          "workspaces": ["packages/*"]
└── packages/
    ├── greet-ts/
    │   ├── package.json
    │   └── src/index.ts
    └── app/
        ├── package.json
        └── main.ts

The library's manifest points exports at source:

{
  "name": "greet-ts",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "type": "module",
  "exports": "./src/index.ts"
}

// packages/greet-ts/src/index.ts
export function greet(name: string): string {
  return `hello, ${name}`;
}

// packages/app/main.ts (app has "type": "module")
import { greet } from "greet-ts";
console.log(greet("ada"));

Run npm install at the root, then node packages/app/main.ts, and it should run. That's because npm symlinks each workspace into node_modules. By default Node dereferences symlinks and uses the module's "real path" as its identity. As Jake Bailey points out in nodejs/typescript#14, the "is this in node_modules" check looks at that real path. So Node sees packages/greet-ts/src/index.ts, with no node_modules anywhere in it, and strips it happily.

Your consumers don't get a symlink. They get a copy. Pack the library the way the registry would and install the tarball somewhere else:

cd ~/code/greet-demo/packages/greet-ts
npm pack
mkdir ~/code/consumer && cd ~/code/consumer
npm init -y
npm install ~/code/greet-demo/packages/greet-ts/greet-ts-1.0.0.tgz

Copy main.ts over as main.mts (.mts always runs as ESM, whatever npm init wrote into type) and run node main.mts. The library's index.ts now lives at node_modules/greet-ts/src/index.ts. That is the case the errors reference describes for ERR_UNSUPPORTED_NODE_MODULES_TYPE_STRIPPING: "Type stripping is not supported for files descendant of a node_modules directory." I haven't run this exact repro myself; the error code and its trigger come straight from those docs. npm's install-links setting, which packs file: dependencies (not workspaces) instead of symlinking them, is another way to get the same copy-not-link setup in CI.


A symlinked workspace package resolves outside node_modules and runs. The same files installed from a tarball sit inside node_modules and are refused.

Why Node says no

The request to lift the restriction is nodejs/typescript#14, and it was closed as not planned. The issue's author makes a fair case: Bun, Deno and JSR already run or host TypeScript source, so Node holding out alone won't stop the trend. Replies in the thread explain the other side. Matteo Collina wrote that "TypeScript is designed so that only .d.ts files are shared across projects." Jake Bailey raised the problem that a published .ts file gets type-checked under the consumer's tsconfig, not the author's. Jordan Harband added that, as he understood it, the TypeScript team opposes the idea too, because it would mean they could never make breaking changes to TypeScript's syntax again.

TypeScript's own compiler options guide shows the type-checking cost. A separate outDir is "necessary for libraries that publish their input files. Otherwise, extension substitution will cause the library's consumers to load the library's .ts files instead of .d.ts files, causing type errors and performance problems." Raw .ts in node_modules hands the consumer's compiler your source and your strictness assumptions.

If you control both ends, there is a workaround. One commenter in the thread shares a loader built on module.registerHooks() and stripTypeScriptTypes(), both "release candidate" stability. That loader calls stripTypeScriptTypes() in transform mode, which Node 26 removed, so on current Node the same idea would have to use the default strip mode and handle erasable syntax only. That fits an internal app. It isn't something to ask the users of a public package to install.

What your package still ships

Your own scripts and tests can run the .ts files directly. The thing you publish is still compiled JavaScript plus declarations. One tsconfig covers both, combining the Node recommendations with the library settings from the TypeScript guide:

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "es2022",
    "module": "nodenext",
    "strict": true,
    "erasableSyntaxOnly": true,
    "verbatimModuleSyntax": true,
    "rewriteRelativeImportExtensions": true,
    "declaration": true,
    "rootDir": "src",
    "outDir": "dist"
  }
}

rewriteRelativeImportExtensions (TypeScript 5.7) is what lets one source tree serve both: you write import { x } from "./x.ts", Node runs it as-is, and tsc rewrites it to ./x.js in dist. Then the manifest points at the build output:

{
  "name": "greet-ts",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "type": "module",
  "exports": {
    ".": {
      "types": "./dist/index.d.ts",
      "default": "./dist/index.js"
    }
  },
  "files": ["dist"],
  "scripts": { "build": "tsc -p tsconfig.json" }
}

Key order matters in conditional exports: "earlier entries have higher priority," and the types condition "should always be included first." Node doesn't type-check, so keep a tsc --noEmit step in CI.

JSR: the registry that compiles for you

JSR is the one registry where publishing TypeScript source is the expected path. It "supports and encourages publishing TypeScript source code rather than pairs of .js + .d.ts files." The catch is what reaches Node. Through JSR's npm compatibility layer, "this source code is transpiled to JavaScript," and .d.ts files "are generated for all TypeScript files." A Node user who runs npx jsr add, or installs with pnpm 10.9+ or Yarn 4.9+, gets JavaScript in node_modules.

That's also why JSR enforces its "slow types" rule on exported functions, classes and variables: explicit types are what let it generate declarations for the npm layer.

If this was useful

Getting a package from "it runs in my repo" to "it runs in yours" is most of what TypeScript in Production covers: tsconfig choices, build tools, monorepos, exports maps, dual ESM/CJS and publishing to JSR. If your team has started running .ts directly and is wondering what still needs a build, that book is the one to grab.

It's the fifth book in The TypeScript Library:

  • TypeScript Essentials — types, narrowing, modules, async, daily-driver tooling
  • The TypeScript Type System — generics, mapped/conditional types, infer, template literals, branded types
  • Kotlin and Java to TypeScript — JVM developers moving to TypeScript
  • PHP to TypeScript — PHP 8+ developers moving to TypeScript
  • TypeScript in Production — tsconfig, build tools, monorepos, library authoring, dual ESM/CJS, JSR

Books 1 and 2 are the core path. If you're coming from the JVM or PHP, swap in book 3 or 4 for those. Book 5 is for anyone shipping TypeScript at work, which, if you read this far, is probably you.

All five books ship in ebook, paperback, and hardcover.

articles.title: Five Agents in Split Panes: How xterm.js Draws Text With a WebGL Glyph Atlas
articles.description: Five coding agents streaming into five panes all share one main thread. How xterm.js draws text, DOM vs WebGL, and a benchmark you can run.
articles.body_html:
• Book: System Design Pocket Guide: Interviews
  • Also by me: Thinking in Go (2-book series) — Complete Guide to Go Programming + Hexagonal Architecture in Go
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

You split the window five ways. Claude Code is printing a diff in one pane, Codex is running a test suite in another, and a third agent is dumping a 4,000-line build log because you asked it to "check why CI fails." Every one of those panes is a terminal emulator, and in an Electron or Tauri app, or in a browser tab, every one of them is JavaScript drawing characters into the same web page.

Nobody picks an agent setup by asking how the terminal paints glyphs. But when five streams arrive at once, the renderer decides whether the window stays responsive or whether your keystrokes land late. Here is how xterm.js, the terminal component inside VS Code, actually puts text on screen, and a small page you can use to measure it on your own machine.

A terminal is a grid with a 16.6 ms budget

A terminal emulator holds a grid of cells. Each cell has a character, a foreground color, a background color and style flags. Bytes from the process go through a parser that updates the grid, and a renderer turns the visible rows into pixels.

At 60 frames per second you get 16.6 ms per frame for everything on the page's main thread. That number is the budget the VS Code team used when they moved the terminal renderer from the DOM to canvas in 2017, and it still frames the problem.

xterm.js does not redraw on every write. Its RenderDebouncer asks for one requestAnimationFrame and, while that request is pending, widens the dirty range with Math.min on the start row and Math.max on the end row. A thousand writes inside one frame become one render of the rows they touched. Only rows in the viewport get drawn, never the scrollback.

So the renderer's cost is per frame, not per byte. The parser is the part that scales with output. Keep those two apart, because they behave differently when you add panes.

The DOM renderer: spans, layout, garbage

The renderer built into xterm.js core builds HTML. Since xterm.js 6.0 removed the canvas addon, it is that or WebGL. For each dirty row, DomRenderer calls replaceChildren with fresh nodes from DomRendererRowFactory. The factory is careful: it creates one <span> per run of adjacent cells that share background, foreground and style, rather than one per cell. Plain log lines collapse into a few spans per row.

Color-heavy output does not collapse. Agent output is full of ANSI color: green tool names, red diff lines, dim timestamps. Every color change starts a new span. After that the browser has to style, lay out and paint those nodes, and the old nodes become garbage.

The 2017 VS Code post put the ceiling plainly: with a DOM renderer, "performance will always have the hard cap imposed by the layout engine." It also says that composing and laying out the elements "could take longer than a frame (16.6ms) all by itself," and that under heavy output the old renderer dropped "below 10 FPS" (source). That post describes an older DOM renderer, but the shape of the cost is the same: more spans per frame, more layout per frame.


The atlas idea: draw each glyph once into a texture, then copy tiles out of it for every cell that needs that glyph.

The WebGL renderer: rasterise on first use, then copy quads

@xterm/addon-webgl replaces all of that with a WebGL2 renderer. The trick is the glyph atlas.

The first time a cell needs a glyph in a given style, TextureAtlas draws it with the 2D canvas API into a texture page and caches its coordinates. The cache key is the character plus its background, foreground and extended attributes, so a red x and a green x are two entries. Every later cell with that same key is a lookup, not a draw. Pages start at 512 px; when the atlas runs out of page slots, four same-sized pages are merged into one page twice as wide and twice as tall, as long as that stays under the texture-size limit (4096 px when no other limit is set). If they can't be merged, the atlas is evicted and starts over. During idle callbacks it also pre-fills printable ASCII so the first screen of output is mostly cache hits.

Then the drawing. GlyphRenderer keeps a typed array with 11 floats (44 bytes) per cell: offset, size, texture page, texture coordinates, texture size and cell position. Each of those attributes advances once per instance. The whole visible grid then goes to the GPU in a single call:

gl.drawElementsInstanced(
  gl.TRIANGLE_STRIP, 4, gl.UNSIGNED_BYTE, 0,
  bufferLength / Constants.INDICES_PER_CELL
);

That is one unit quad with four vertices, drawn once per cell. The CPU's job per frame shrinks to filling a float array for the dirty rows; there are no DOM nodes to lay out and no discarded spans to collect. The fragment shader picks the right texture page from an array of samplers, up to 32 pages or the device's texture-unit limit, whichever is lower.

One detail matters for split panes. In CharAtlasCache, terminals whose font and color configuration match share one atlas: the cache finds an entry with an equal config and adds the new terminal to its ownedBy list. Five panes with the same theme rasterise a glyph once, not five times.

What WebGL does not fix

The xterm.js flow control guide puts the terminal's input throughput at "5 - 35 MB/s", against producers that can push "several GB/s." Most of that is parsing, and the parser is the same code under both renderers. write() buffers and returns at once, and the buffer has a hard limit: "Any data beyond that limit gets discarded." Five agents flooding at once still share that parsing time on one main thread. WebGL frees up the frame budget the DOM renderer was spending on layout, and that time goes back to parsing and to your input.

WebGL can also go away under you. The addon's README warns that browsers "may drop WebGL contexts for various reasons like OOM or after the system has been suspended," and exposes onContextLoss so the app can dispose the addon. When an app does that, it ends up back on the DOM renderer. VS Code's default, per its terminal appearance docs, is auto: try WebGL, "fall back to the DOM renderer" if that fails. The same page lists Linux VMs, browsers without WebGL and outdated drivers as places where WebGL may not work well.

In code, the defensive load looks like this:

import { WebglAddon } from '@xterm/addon-webgl';

function loadWebgl(term) {
  try {
    const webgl = new WebglAddon();
    webgl.onContextLoss(() => webgl.dispose());
    term.loadAddon(webgl);
    return true;
  } catch {
    return false; // stays on the DOM renderer
  }
}

If you have ever seen one pane in a terminal app suddenly feel slower after the laptop woke from sleep, a dropped context and a silent fallback is one candidate worth checking.

A benchmark you can run

Save this as bench.html, serve the folder (npx serve . works), and open it twice: once with ?r=dom and once with ?r=webgl. It writes about 200,000 colored log lines in 200 chunks, waits for each chunk's write callback, and records how often the page managed to paint while it was busy.

<!doctype html>
<link rel="stylesheet"
  href="https://unpkg.com/@xterm/xterm@6.0.0/css/xterm.css">
<div id="t" style="width:900px;height:500px"></div>
<pre id="out"></pre>
<script type="module">
import { Terminal } from 'https://esm.sh/@xterm/xterm@6.0.0';
import { WebglAddon }
  from 'https://esm.sh/@xterm/addon-webgl@0.19.0';

const q = new URLSearchParams(location.search);
const mode = q.get('r') ?? 'dom';
const term = new Terminal({ scrollback: 1000 });
term.open(document.getElementById('t'));
if (mode === 'webgl') term.loadAddon(new WebglAddon());

const line = (i) =>
  `\x1b[32m[agent]\x1b[0m step ${i} src/f${i % 97}.ts ` +
  `\x1b[33mok\x1b[0m ${'.'.repeat(i % 40)}\r\n`;
const chunks = [];
for (let c = 0; c < 200; c++) {
  let s = '';
  for (let i = 0; i < 1000; i++) s += line(c * 1000 + i);
  chunks.push(s);
}

let frames = 0, worst = 0, last = performance.now();
let running = true;
const tick = (now) => {
  frames++;
  worst = Math.max(worst, now - last);
  last = now;
  if (running) requestAnimationFrame(tick);
};
requestAnimationFrame(tick);

const t0 = performance.now();
for (const chunk of chunks) {
  await new Promise((done) => term.write(chunk, done));
}
running = false;
const ms = performance.now() - t0;
document.getElementById('out').textContent =
  `${mode}: ${ms.toFixed(0)} ms, ${frames} frames, ` +
  `worst gap ${worst.toFixed(1)} ms`;
</script>

Read the three numbers together. Total time is mostly parser time, so expect it to move less than you'd guess. Frame count and worst gap are the renderer's story: how often the page got to paint, and the longest stretch where it couldn't. A long worst gap is the keystroke that shows up late. To mimic five panes, duplicate the div and the terminal five times and write to all of them in the same loop.

I haven't run this across a range of machines, so I won't quote numbers. Run it on yours, and on the oldest laptop you can borrow. The write callback fires when the parser finishes a chunk, per the write API docs, not when pixels hit the screen, so the final frame lands a moment after the total.

Where Hermes IDE sits in this

I build Hermes IDE, so weigh this section with that in mind. Hermes runs each agent (Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity CLI and others) in its own real terminal, with split panes so sessions sit side by side. Those terminals are xterm.js: the package.json pins @xterm/xterm 6.0.0 and depends on @xterm/addon-webgl.
