The README describes the rendering as "GPU-accelerated (WebGL) where the system supports it," which is the same try-WebGL, keep-DOM-as-fallback idea VS Code uses.


Hermes 2.3.4: Codex and Claude Code in split panes, each in its own hermes/ worktree, with the sessions sidebar showing status, context use, cost and branch.

None of that is specific to Hermes. Any app built on xterm.js can load the same addon, and VS Code has done so by default since its 1.55 release. Hermes is free to download, source-available under BSL 1.1, runs on macOS, Windows and Linux, and is not affiliated with any agent vendor. Download it here, or read the code on GitHub.

If this was useful

The glyph atlas is a small system-design lesson hiding in a terminal: a cache keyed on exactly what makes an entry unique, an eviction plan for when it fills, batching a thousand updates into one unit of work per frame, and sharing one expensive resource across tenants with the same config. Those are the trade-offs interviewers want you to say out loud. The System Design Pocket Guide: Interviews walks through 15 real designs step by step, with that reasoning on every page.

articles.title: I built a free Whisper transcription site that runs in the browser: 5 things that broke
articles.description: I'm a YouTube creator, and I got tired of subtitle tools that upload my footage, cap free minutes or...
articles.body_html:
I'm a YouTube creator, and I got tired of subtitle tools that upload my footage, cap free minutes or stamp a watermark on the video. So I built Quietscribe: OpenAI's Whisper running directly in the browser. You get transcripts, SRT/VTT subtitles and even burned-in captions, and the file never leaves your device.

It's a static site on Cloudflare Pages: no backend for the default mode and zero hosting cost. Here are the five things that broke along the way, in case you're building something similar.

The stack

  • Transformers.js v3, running Xenova/whisper-tiny / base / small in a module Web Worker
  • WebGPU when it's trustworthy, otherwise multi-threaded WASM
  • COOP: same-origin + COEP: credentialless headers (via Cloudflare Pages _headers) so crossOriginIsolated is true and WASM can use threads
  • Canvas + MediaRecorder + WebAudio for burning captions into the video (MP4 where the browser supports H.264)

1. "Auto-detect" was silently English

My first Urdu test came back as confident English gibberish. It turned out that when you don't pass a language to a multilingual Whisper model, the library falls back to English with only a console warning:

// TODO: Implement language detection
console.warn('No language specified - defaulting to English (en).');

The fix is to do what Whisper does internally. Take the first ~30 seconds of speech, run a single decoding step after <|startoftranscript|>, and pick the language token with the highest score:

let scores = null;
const capture = (ids, logits) => { if (!scores) scores = logits.data.slice(); return logits; };
await asr.model.generate({
  ...(await asr.processor(clip)),
  decoder_input_ids: [cfg.decoder_start_token_id],
  max_new_tokens: 1,
  logits_processor: [capture],
});
// then argmax over cfg.lang_to_id

2. iPhone Safari just... reloads the page

On iPhone, the model download reached 100% and then the whole page reloaded. There was no error. Safari kills tabs that use too much memory. What fixed it:

  • Phones use one WASM thread (each thread duplicates memory) and default to whisper-tiny
  • Before starting, I write the chosen model to sessionStorage. If the page loads and that flag is still there, the last run crashed, so the site steps down a model size and tells the user why.

3. Small models loop

tiny and base sometimes get stuck repeating one word forever, especially in lower-resource languages. Two layers helped:

  • Detect a loop (4+ identical words in a row, or a very low unique-word ratio) and re-run that piece with no_repeat_ngram_size: 4, repetition_penalty: 1.15
  • Collapse any 1–4-word phrase repeated 3+ times as a final clean-up step

4. Some languages need a bigger model than a phone can hold

For Urdu, the honest answer is that small on-device models aren't good enough, and the large ones don't fit on a phone. So I added an opt-in Cloud mode. The browser decodes the audio to 16 kHz mono, cuts it into ~60-second pieces at the quietest point, and sends each piece to a Cloudflare Worker running @cf/openai/whisper-large-v3-turbo on Workers AI. Nothing is stored. The free tier covers roughly 200 audio minutes a day.

One gotcha: whisper-large-v3-turbo can't translate. task: 'translate' just returns the original language. So the Worker transcribes first, then translates each segment with @cf/meta/m2m100-1.2b.

Being honest about this mattered. The site says "private by default". It used to say "never uploaded", which stopped being true the day Cloud mode shipped.

5. Burned-in captions and MP4

MediaRecorder with plain video/mp4 produced VP9-in-MP4 in some Chromium builds, which many players reject. Requesting explicit avc1 codec strings first, and falling back to WebM, fixed it. Long captions also need to shrink to fit (down to ~65% size) before wrapping, otherwise you get single orphan words on a second line.

Bonus: share target on Android

With a share_target in the web manifest and a tiny service worker that stores the shared file in Cache Storage and redirects to /?shared=1, Android users can tap Share → Quietscribe from their gallery or WhatsApp. The file still never leaves the device.

It's free, with no sign-up. There's a one-tap sample if you want to see it run without uploading anything: quietscribe.pages.dev. I'd love feedback on speed on your hardware and accuracy in your language.

Written by the AI agent that helped build Quietscribe, on behalf of its maker.

articles.title: React Activity Component: The State Between Render and Remount
articles.description: React's Activity component hides a subtree without unmounting it — what state, effects, and renders actually do, plus a copy-paste cheat sheet.
articles.body_html:
You hide a settings panel with {isOpen && <Panel />}. The user reopens it two seconds later, and the unsaved toggle they'd flipped is back to its default. The scroll position is gone. The debounced search they'd typed into a nested filter has vanished. Nothing is broken — React unmounted <Panel /> and mounted a brand new one, exactly as that code tells it to. You just didn't mean to ask for that.

Before React 19.2, there was no built-in way to say "hide this, but keep it exactly as it was." CSS (display: none while the component stays mounted) keeps the state, but its effects keep running in the background — timers ticking, subscriptions open, polling a screen nobody can see. Unmounting runs cleanup correctly but throws the state away. There was no option between "alive and visible" and "gone."

React 19.2 (released October 2025) added <Activity> to close that gap: a built-in way to hide a subtree while keeping its state intact. React 19.3 — released September 2026 and patched to the current npm latest, 19.3.1, in October — shipped several bug fixes for it, including one around useSyncExternalStore updates while hidden, that are worth understanding on their own, because they show exactly where the "hidden but alive" model gets subtle. This is episode eight of React Deep Dive, and it picks up where episode one, on re-render vs. remount, left off: <Activity> is neither of those two things. It's a third state, with its own rules, and treating it like either of the other two is exactly how the 19.3 bugs happened.

What you'll learn

By the end of this article you'll be able to:

  • Explain precisely what <Activity mode="hidden"> preserves and what it tears down — state, effects, refs, and renders are four separate questions, not one
  • Replace a {condition && <Panel/>} pattern with <Activity> when hiding, not destroying, is what you actually want
  • Predict when a hidden subtree still re-renders (and why that's not a bug)
  • Avoid the two traps that the 19.3 patch notes had to fix for the React team itself
  • Use <StrictMode> to catch the effect-cleanup bugs that <Activity> surfaces

Who this is for

You're comfortable with function components, useState, and useEffect, and you've been bitten at least once by state resetting when you only meant to hide something. You don't need to have used <Activity> before.

Table of contents

  • The problem: hiding isn't unmounting, and unmounting isn't hiding
  • The mental model
  • The walkthrough
  • Edge cases and gotchas
  • Best practices
  • FAQ
  • Cheat sheet
  • Key takeaways

The problem: hiding isn't unmounting, and unmounting isn't hiding

Say you're building a dashboard with three report tabs. Each tab has its own view: a filter form, a live-updating counter from a useEffect-driven interval (think "records processed," polled every second), and a draft note the user is typing. Switch tabs, and here's the naive version:

function Dashboard({ activeTab }) {
  return (
    <>
      {activeTab === "sales" && <ReportPanel label="Sales" />}
      {activeTab === "ops" && <ReportPanel label="Ops" />}
      {activeTab === "support" && <ReportPanel label="Support" />}
    </>
  );
}

This works, in the sense that it compiles and nothing throws. But switch from "Sales" to "Ops" and back, and the Sales ReportPanel is a completely new instance. Its counter restarts at zero. Its draft note is empty. Its useEffect cleanup ran when you left, and a fresh mount effect ran when you came back — including any expensive setup it does on mount. You wanted a tab switch; React gave you a demolition and a rebuild.

The instinctive fix is to keep everything mounted and hide the inactive panels with CSS:

function Dashboard({ activeTab }) {
  return (
    <>
      <div style={{ display: activeTab === "sales" ? "block" : "none" }}>
        <ReportPanel label="Sales" />
      </div>
      <div style={{ display: activeTab === "ops" ? "block" : "none" }}>
        <ReportPanel label="Ops" />
      </div>
      <div style={{ display: activeTab === "support" ? "block" : "none" }}>
        <ReportPanel label="Support" />
      </div>
    </>
  );
}

This keeps the state, but now you've traded one bug for another: the Sales panel's interval keeps polling, its effects keep subscribing, and its hidden DOM keeps costing you layout and memory for every tab the user isn't looking at. You've solved the state problem by un-solving the cleanup problem.

<Activity> is React's answer to "I want both": state survives, but effects still tear down and rebuild the way they would for a component you actually cared about keeping correct.

The mental model

The mental model: Render, remount, and <Activity mode="hidden"> are three different operations, and they disagree on three separate things — state, effects, and rendering — not just one axis you can call "aliveness."

Stays mounted (same instance) <Activity mode="hidden"> Unmount (remove from the tree)
State (useState, useReducer) Preserved Preserved Destroyed
Effects (useEffect) Keep running Torn down on hide, re-created on show Torn down, never re-created (new instance builds fresh ones)
Rendering on prop/context change Happens normally Still happens, at lower priority Doesn't happen — there's nothing there
DOM Visible Hidden (display: none), node kept Removed
Refs Point at the live node Still point at the (now hidden) node Become null

Read the middle column again: hidden is not the same as paused, and it is not the same as destroyed. A component inside a hidden <Activity> keeps its state, loses its effects, and — this is the part people get wrong — keeps rendering when something above it changes, just at a priority React considers less urgent than whatever's actually on screen. That last row is the one the 19.3 patch notes had to fix bugs around, because it's the one that breaks the intuition "hidden means nothing happens here."

Here's the shape in code, next to the two things it's between:

import { Activity, useState } from "react";

function Dashboard({ activeTab }) {
  return (
    <>
      <Activity mode={activeTab === "sales" ? "visible" : "hidden"}>
        <ReportPanel label="Sales" />
      </Activity>
      <Activity mode={activeTab === "ops" ? "visible" : "hidden"}>
        <ReportPanel label="Ops" />
      </Activity>
      <Activity mode={activeTab === "support" ? "visible" : "hidden"}>
        <ReportPanel label="Support" />
      </Activity>
    </>
  );
}

Switch tabs now, and the inactive ReportPanels stay mounted as far as state is concerned (the draft note survives), but their effects clean up (the polling interval stops) the moment they go hidden, and start fresh again the moment they're shown. No wasted polling, no lost draft.

Historical aside, labelled: before 19.2 stabilized this, an experimental build exposed the same idea as unstable_Activity. If you see import { unstable_Activity as Activity } from "react" in an older blog post or a pinned pre-19.2 dependency, that's the pre-stable name — don't write it in new code. The stable export is just Activity, no prefix.

The walkthrough

Step 1 — the smallest correct example 

import { Activity, useState } from "react";

function Sidebar({ isOpen }) {
  const [filter, setFilter] = useState("");

  return (
    <Activity mode={isOpen ? "visible" : "hidden"}>
      <input value={filter} onChange={(e) => setFilter(e.target.value)} />
    </Activity>
  );
}

Key concept: mode is the entire API surface for visibility — "visible" or "hidden" (it defaults to "visible" if you omit it). There's no mode="unmounted"; if you want a true unmount, don't render the <Activity> at all. <Activity> only ever answers "show or hide," never "destroy."

Step 2 — proving the effect actually tears down 

function ReportPanel({ label }) {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  const [draft, setDraft] = useState("");

  useEffect(() => {
    const id = setInterval(() => setCount((c) => c + 1), 1000);
    return () => clearInterval(id); // runs when Activity hides this subtree
  }, []);

  return (
    <div>
      <h3>{label}: {count}</h3>
      <textarea value={draft} onChange={(e) => setDraft(e.target.value)} />
    </div>
  );
}

Hide this panel's <Activity> and the interval's cleanup runs immediately — count stops climbing. Show it again, and the effect's setup function runs again, starting a new interval. count and draft were never touched by any of this; they're still sitting in React's fiber for this component, exactly where you left them. The playground below is this exact component, running the real reconciler, so you can watch the counter freeze and the draft survive in real time.

Step 3 — the row people miss: hidden subtrees still render

This is the one the mental model table flags and most tutorials skip. A hidden <Activity> doesn't freeze its children — it keeps re-rendering them when their props or context change, just scheduled at a lower priority than the visible UI. Why would React bother? Two real reasons, both from the official docs:

  • Pre-rendering. A <Activity mode="hidden"> on initial render still renders its children (without mounting their effects), which lets data-fetching components start loading before the user ever opens that tab — so when they do, it's instant instead of a fresh Suspense fallback.
  • Keeping derived UI correct. If a hidden panel's rendered output depends on a prop from its parent (say, a shared "last synced at" timestamp), it should show the right value the instant it's revealed, not a stale one from the moment it was hidden.

The playground's "Bump shared prop" button demonstrates this directly: it changes a value passed into every ReportPanel, visible or hidden, and the hidden panel's render count still climbs — while its effect-mount count does not. Those two counters moving independently is the mental model, observed instead of described.

Step 4 — what the 19.3 bug fixes actually tell you

React 19.3's changelog lists several <Activity> fixes: issues with useSyncExternalStore updates while hidden, portal visibility, metadata hoisting, and error handling. The pattern across them is instructive: every one is a place where "still rendering, but hidden, with effects torn down" created a seam that a feature built on a simpler always-mounted/never-mounted assumption fell through. useSyncExternalStore subscribes to an external store through an effect-like mechanism — exactly what <Activity> tears down on hide — so an update arriving while hidden needs special handling to avoid being silently lost or double-applied on reveal. If you subscribe to anything external (WebSockets, browser APIs, a state manager outside React) inside a component that might live under an <Activity>, assume the subscription is gone while hidden and gets rebuilt from current state when shown.

Edge cases and gotchas

  • Text-only children render nothing when hidden. Hiding works by applying display: "none" to a wrapper — bare text has no element to attach that to, so it just doesn't render. Wrap bare text in an element if it might end up inside an <Activity>.
  • Side effects outside useEffect keep running. A <video>, <audio>, or <iframe> isn't paused by hiding — its DOM node is still alive, still doing whatever it was doing. Pause it explicitly, in a useLayoutEffect cleanup tied to the visual hide.
  • Refs still point at hidden DOM. Unmounting nulls a ref; hiding doesn't — the node still exists, just invisible. Code that treats "ref is set" as "user can see it" will be wrong.
  • StrictMode is how you catch the bugs this exposes. Effects now mount and unmount far more often than a typical lifetime suggests — every hide/show cycle, not just mount/unmount. Any effect that assumed its cleanup never really had to undo everything gets exposed fast. Develop with <StrictMode> so this surfaces before production does.
  • Interaction with <ViewTransition>. If an <Activity> reveal happens inside startTransition, and the tree uses <ViewTransition> (also stable in 19.3), showing it triggers that boundary's enter animation and hiding triggers exit — the two features compose by design.

Best practices

  • Reach for <Activity> when state is expensive to rebuild and the hide is temporary — tabs, a collapsible sidebar, a wizard step, a modal reopened with the same draft. The signal: the user will plausibly come back to this exact state.
  • Don't make it a default replacement for conditional rendering. If the user is done with something for good (a dismissed notification, a finished onboarding step), unmounting is correct and cheaper — nothing left to render at low priority, nothing to reconcile later.
  • Don't treat it as a pause button for real-world side effects (payments in flight, a write to a server). Hiding a subtree doesn't cancel an in-flight promise; it only affects effect lifecycle and state.
  • If a hidden subtree subscribes to anything external, write its effect assuming the subscription is gone while hidden — resync from current state on the next mount rather than assuming buffered delivery.
  • Keep mode a useState/prop-driven value, not something you mutate imperatively — <Activity> reacts to re-renders like anything else in React.

FAQ

Is <Activity> the same thing as display: none?

No. It uses display: none for the visual hiding, but that's one of four things it does — it also tears down effects (plain CSS never does), preserves state across the hide (an unmount never does), and keeps rendering hidden children at lower priority (a component you've stopped rendering can't do at all).

Does <Activity> replace key-based remounting?

No — opposite problems. key forces React to treat something as a new instance, which is right when you want fresh state. <Activity> keeps the same instance alive while hidden. Want a reset? Use key. Want to preserve exactly what's there? Use <Activity>.

Will <Activity> fetch data for a hidden tab before the user opens it?

Under specific conditions: if the hidden children read data through something Suspense-activating — a promise read with use() — a hidden <Activity> can pre-render and start that fetch early. Data fetched inside a useEffect is not: effects don't run while hidden, so effect-based fetching only starts once the subtree becomes visible.

Does hiding with <Activity> cost anything if I never show the content again?

Some — the hidden subtree still occupies a spot in the fiber tree and can still re-render at low priority. For content the user is realistically done with, unmount it; reach for <Activity> specifically because you expect a return visit.

Can I nest <Activity> components?

Yes — visibility composes as expected. A visible <Activity> inside a hidden one is still effectively hidden, because its ancestor is hidden.

Cheat sheet 

import { Activity, useState, useEffect } from "react";

// 1. Import — stable since React 19.2, no prefix.
// import { unstable_Activity as Activity } from "react"; // ❌ pre-19.2 only

// 2. Usage — mode is the whole API.
<Activity mode={isVisible ? "visible" : "hidden"}>
  <ExpensiveSubtree />
</Activity>

// 3. What survives hiding vs. what doesn't:
//    state (useState/useReducer)         → preserved
//    effects (useEffect)                 → torn down on hide, re-created on show
//    rendering on prop/context change    → still happens, lower priority
//    DOM node                            → kept, display: none
//    refs                                → still point at the (hidden) node

// 4. Pick the right tool:
//    "destroy it for good"        → don't render it (plain conditional)
//    "reset it on purpose"        → key={newId}
//    "hide it, keep it alive"     → <Activity mode="hidden">

// 5. Gotchas:
//    - bare text child while hidden renders nothing (no element to hide)
//    - <video>/<audio>/<iframe> keep running while hidden — pause explicitly
//      in a useLayoutEffect cleanup if that matters
//    - external subscriptions (useSyncExternalStore, sockets) are torn down
//      on hide — resync on remount, don't assume buffered delivery
//    - develop with <StrictMode> to catch effects that assumed they'd only
//      ever run once

Key takeaways

  • <Activity mode="hidden"> is a third state, not a point on the line between "mounted" and "unmounted": state is preserved, effects are torn down and rebuilt, and rendering on prop change still happens — just at lower priority.
  • It solves the specific problem of keeping expensive-to-rebuild state alive across a hide/show cycle without paying the cost of a fully-live, always-rendering component.
  • The 19.3 bug fixes for useSyncExternalStore, portals, and metadata under <Activity> all trace back to the same seam: features built assuming "mounted" or "unmounted" as the only two states had to be taught about the third one.
  • Reach for it when the user will plausibly come back; reach for key when you want a clean reset; reach for plain conditional rendering when the content is genuinely done.

That chat-draft bug from episode one and the dashboard tab bug here are mirror images of each other — one was an accidental remount nobody wanted, this one is an accidental unmount nobody wanted. Same underlying lesson both times: React only does what your JSX actually asks for, never what you meant. Have you reached for <Activity> yet, or are you still hiding things with CSS and hoping the effects behave? Tell me what you're using it for in the comments.

Saw Karpathy's HackerTube and wanted the same thing for books. So I had Claude build one (Opus 5.5).It's ~16.5k books that at least two different HN commenters brought up, from 2007 till now. Each book links back to the comments that mentioned it. Data is downloadable from the about page.To be clear: Claude wrote almost all of it, including the data pipeline and the site. I mostly steered and made calls, bought the domain name, etc.It counts mentions, so it's not perfect (praising a book and trashing it both count). If your favourite book is missing or matched to the wrong thing, tell me.

articles.body_html:
After seeing Karpathy's Hackertube and Hackerbooks, I just had to make Wikihack.I scraped all mentions of wikipedia on hackernews and ranked them, and turn them into a scrollable feed to make it a bit more easy to digest / interact with. You can see where people submitted the articles and where people mentioned it in comments.The top shows the most frequently linked articles.Random is random but slightly weighted towards the more frequently linked articles (a little bit like Wikipedia actually).Rising is ranked towards the past 12 months.The entire site is served only through the frontend -- I'll add more features if people enjoy this!
